problems.title: Two Sum
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume each input has exactly one solution and you may not use the same element twice.

bruteForce.explanation: Check every pair of elements to see if they sum to target. Two nested loops iterate over all combinations.

optimal.explanation: Use an unordered_map to store each number and its index. For each number, check if its complement (target - num) already exists in the map — giving O(1) lookup instead of a full scan.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of brackets in the correct order.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly find and remove matched pairs () [] {} from the string until no more are found, then check if the result is empty.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack. Push opening brackets. For each closing bracket, check if the stack top is the matching opening — if so pop, otherwise return false.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.

examples.explanation: Subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] has the largest sum = 6

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible subarrays using two nested loops. For each starting index, accumulate the sum and track the maximum found.

optimal.explanation: Kadane's Algorithm: at each position decide whether to extend the running sum or start fresh. currentSum = max(num, currentSum + num). Track the global max throughout.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.description: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index of the target if found, otherwise return -1.

examples.explanation: 9 exists at index 4

bruteForce.explanation: Linear search: iterate through every element and compare with the target.

optimal.explanation: Binary search: maintain left/right pointers. At each step check the midpoint — if target found return it; if mid < target move left right; if mid > target move right left.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters.

examples.explanation: Substring "abc" has length 3
Substring "b" has length 1
Substring "wke" has length 3

bruteForce.explanation: Try all substrings starting from each index. For each, track characters in a set and stop when a duplicate is encountered.

optimal.explanation: Sliding window with a hash map storing last seen index. When a duplicate is found, jump the left pointer past the previous occurrence instead of starting over.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.description: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

examples.explanation: Two ways: (1+1) or (2)

bruteForce.explanation: Recursive approach: total ways = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Exponential time due to overlapping subproblems.

optimal.explanation: This is the Fibonacci sequence. Track only the previous two values and compute iteratively — no recursion, no extra array needed.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the reversed list.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values into a vector, reverse it, then rebuild the linked list from scratch.

optimal.explanation: Iterate through the list reversing each node's next pointer in-place using prev and curr pointers. No extra space needed.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.

bruteForce.explanation: Compare every pair of elements using nested loops. If any two are equal, return true.

optimal.explanation: Use an unordered_set. As we iterate, if the current element is already in the set return true, otherwise insert it.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0. Constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price=1) and sell on day 5 (price=6), profit = 6-1 = 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every pair of days (i, j) where i < j and compute prices[j] - prices[i], tracking the maximum profit seen.

optimal.explanation: Track the minimum price seen so far as we scan left to right, and at each day compute the profit if we sold today, updating the global maximum.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
problems.description: You are given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day. On each day, you may decide to buy and/or sell the stock. You can only hold at most one share of the stock at any time, but you can buy and sell on the same day. Find and return the maximum profit you can achieve. Constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 3*10^4, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price=1), sell on day 3 (price=5), profit=4. Then buy on day 4 (price=3), sell on day 5 (price=6), profit=3. Total=7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion/DFS to explore every possible buy-sell combination across all days, tracking the maximum profit.

optimal.explanation: Greedily capture every upward price movement by summing all positive differences between consecutive days.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. The product of any prefix or suffix of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and without using the division operation. Constraints: 2 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -30 <= nums[i] <= 30.

bruteForce.explanation: For each index i, iterate through all other elements and multiply them together to compute the answer at position i.

optimal.explanation: Build a prefix product array from the left and multiply with a running suffix product from the right in a second pass, achieving O(n) with O(1) extra space (excluding output).

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.description: Suppose an array of length n sorted in ascending order is rotated between 1 and n times. Given the sorted rotated array nums of unique elements, return the minimum element of this array. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 5000, -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000, all integers are unique.

examples.explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5] rotated 3 times. The minimum is 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Perform a linear scan through the entire array and return the smallest element found.

optimal.explanation: Use binary search: compare the middle element with the rightmost; if mid > right, the minimum is in the right half, otherwise it is in the left half (including mid).

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.description: There is an integer array nums sorted in ascending order (with distinct values) that has been rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the array nums after the possible rotation and an integer target, return the index of target if it is in nums, or -1 if it is not in nums. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4, all values are distinct.

examples.explanation: 0 is found at index 4 in the rotated array.

bruteForce.explanation: Do a linear scan through the array and return the index when the target is found.

optimal.explanation: Use binary search by first determining which half is sorted, then checking if the target lies in that sorted half before narrowing the search window.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.description: You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]). Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store. Constraints: n == height.length, 2 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7) form a container holding min(8,7)*(8-1)=49 units.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every pair of lines (i, j) and compute the water contained as min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i), tracking the maximum.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers starting at both ends; always move the pointer with the smaller height inward, as that is the only way to potentially increase the area.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i, j, and k are all distinct indices and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets. Constraints: 3 <= nums.length <= 3000, -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: nums[0]+nums[1]+nums[2]=-1+0+1=0 and nums[1]+nums[2]+nums[4]=-1+0+1=0 (no duplicates).

bruteForce.explanation: Use three nested loops to check all triplets and use a set to avoid duplicate results.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array, then fix the first element and use two pointers for the remaining pair, skipping duplicates to avoid repeated triplets.

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.description: Given an integer array nums of length n and an integer target, find three integers in nums such that the sum is closest to target. Return the sum of the three integers. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution. Constraints: 3 <= nums.length <= 500, -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000, -10^4 <= target <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The sum that is closest to target=1 is (-1)+2+1=2.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all O(n^3) triplets and keep track of the one whose sum is closest to the target.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array, fix the first element, and use two pointers to find the closest sum in O(n^2) by moving pointers based on whether the current sum is less or greater than target.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Constraints: n == height.length, 1 <= n <= 2*10^4, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: 6 units of rain water are trapped between the bars.

bruteForce.explanation: For each position, find the maximum height to its left and right, then the water at that position is min(leftMax, rightMax) - height[i].

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from both ends; whichever side has the smaller max height determines how much water can be trapped at that pointer's position.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.description: You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the first index of the array. Each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. Return true if you can reach the last index, or false otherwise. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to index 1, then 3 steps to the last index.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion or BFS to try all possible jump lengths from every position and check if the last index can be reached.

optimal.explanation: Greedily track the farthest index reachable so far; if at any point the current index exceeds the farthest reachable, return false.

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.description: You are given a 0-indexed array of integers nums of length n. You are initially positioned at nums[0]. Each element nums[i] represents the maximum length of a forward jump from index i. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach nums[n-1]. The test cases are generated such that you can always reach nums[n-1]. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The minimum number of jumps to reach the last index is 2. Jump from index 0 to 1, then jump 3 to the last index.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS treating each position as a node; level by level, expand all reachable positions and count the number of levels (jumps) needed.

optimal.explanation: Greedy approach: maintain the current jump boundary and the farthest reachable index; increment jump count each time we exhaust the current boundary.

problems.title: Rotate Array
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, rotate the array to the right by k steps, where k is non-negative. You should do this in-place with O(1) extra space. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31-1, 0 <= k <= 10^5.

bruteForce.explanation: Perform k individual rotations, each time moving the last element to the front by shifting all others one position to the right.

optimal.explanation: Reverse the entire array, then reverse the first k elements, and finally reverse the remaining n-k elements to achieve rotation in O(n) time.

problems.title: Move Zeroes
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Note that you must do this in-place without making a copy of the array. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31-1.

examples.explanation: Non-zero elements 1, 3, 12 maintain relative order; zeros are moved to end.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly find the first zero and the next non-zero after it, then swap them; repeat until no such pair exists.

optimal.explanation: Use a slow pointer that tracks the position for the next non-zero element; iterate with a fast pointer and place non-zeros at the slow pointer, then fill the rest with zeros.

problems.title: Find the Duplicate Number
problems.description: Given an array nums containing n+1 integers where each integer is in the range [1, n] inclusive, there is only one repeated number in nums. Return this repeated number. You must solve the problem without modifying the array nums and uses only constant extra space. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, nums.length == n+1, 1 <= nums[i] <= n.

examples.explanation: 2 appears twice in the array.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to record seen numbers; the first number encountered that already exists in the set is the duplicate.

optimal.explanation: Treat the array as a linked list where nums[i] points to nums[nums[i]]; use Floyd's cycle detection algorithm to find the entry point of the cycle, which is the duplicate.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of subarrays whose sum equals to k. A subarray is a contiguous non-empty sequence of elements within an array. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2*10^4, -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000, -10^7 <= k <= 10^7.

examples.explanation: Subarrays [1,1] (indices 0-1) and [1,1] (indices 1-2) each sum to 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use two nested loops: fix the start index, then extend the end index computing the running sum and count whenever it equals k.

optimal.explanation: Use a prefix sum with a hash map: store the frequency of each prefix sum seen so far; for each position, check how many previous prefix sums equal (currentSum - k).

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time. Constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: The longest consecutive sequence is [1,2,3,4] with length 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the array and then do a single pass to find the longest run of consecutive integers.

optimal.explanation: Insert all numbers into a hash set; for each number that is the start of a sequence (num-1 not in set), extend the sequence by incrementing while the next number exists in the set.

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.description: Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0's. You must do it in place. Constraints: m == matrix.length, n == matrix[0].length, 1 <= m, n <= 200, -2^31 <= matrix[i][j] <= 2^31-1.

examples.explanation: Element at (1,1) is 0, so entire row 1 and column 1 are set to 0.

bruteForce.explanation: First collect all positions that contain zero, then set the entire row and column for each such position to zero.

optimal.explanation: Use the first row and first column as markers (with two boolean flags for whether those themselves need zeroing), eliminating the need for extra space beyond O(1).

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.description: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (clockwise starting from the top-left). Constraints: m == matrix.length, n == matrix[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 10, -100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100.

examples.explanation: Traverse: top row left to right, right col top to bottom, bottom row right to left, left col bottom to top, repeat.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a visited matrix to mark cells and simulate movement in spiral direction, changing direction when hitting a boundary or visited cell.

optimal.explanation: Use four boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right) and peel one layer at a time by traversing the four edges and shrinking the boundaries.

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.description: You are given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise. You have to rotate the image in-place, which means you have to modify the input 2D matrix directly. Do not allocate another 2D matrix and do the rotation. Constraints: n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length, 1 <= n <= 20, -1000 <= matrix[i][j] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The matrix rotated 90 degrees clockwise.

bruteForce.explanation: Create a copy of the matrix and place each element at its rotated position: matrix[j][n-1-i] = copy[i][j].

optimal.explanation: First transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row — this gives an in-place 90-degree clockwise rotation.

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.description: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element. The majority element is the element that appears more than n/2 times. You may assume that the majority element always exists in the array. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 5*10^4, -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: 2 appears 4 times out of 7 elements, which is more than 7/2=3.5.

bruteForce.explanation: For each element count how many times it appears in the array; return the element whose count exceeds n/2.

optimal.explanation: Use the Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm: maintain a candidate and a count; increment count for matching elements and decrement for others; when count hits zero pick a new candidate.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.description: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= n, all the numbers of nums are unique.

examples.explanation: n=3. The range [0,3] has 4 numbers. 2 is the only missing one.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the array and check for the first index where nums[i] != i; if all match, the missing number is n.

optimal.explanation: Compute the expected sum 0+1+...+n = n*(n+1)/2 and subtract the actual sum of the array; the difference is the missing number.

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, find a subarray that has the largest product, and return the product. The test cases are generated so that the answer will fit in a 32-bit integer. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2*10^4, -10 <= nums[i] <= 10, the product of any subarray of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: Subarray [2,3] has the largest product = 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible subarrays using two nested loops and compute the product of each, tracking the maximum found.

optimal.explanation: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each position (since a negative * negative can flip to maximum); update the global best at each step.

problems.title: First Missing Positive
problems.description: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest missing positive integer. You must implement an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31-1.

examples.explanation: 1 is present. The smallest missing positive integer is 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to store all numbers in the array, then iterate from 1 upward and return the first positive integer not found in the set.

optimal.explanation: Use the array itself as a hash map: place each number x in position x-1 if 1 <= x <= n, then scan for the first index where nums[i] != i+1.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.description: Given an array nums with n objects colored red (0), white (1), or blue (2), sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent, with the colors in the order red, white, and blue. You must solve this problem without using the library's sort function. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 300, nums[i] is either 0, 1, or 2.

examples.explanation: All 0s, then 1s, then 2s.

bruteForce.explanation: Count the occurrences of 0s, 1s, and 2s, then overwrite the array with the correct number of each value in order.

optimal.explanation: Dutch National Flag algorithm: use three pointers (low, mid, high) to partition the array into 0s, 1s, and 2s in a single pass.

problems.title: Next Permutation
problems.description: A permutation of an array of integers is an arrangement of its members into a sequence or linear order. The next permutation of an array of integers is the next lexicographically greater permutation of its integer. If no next permutation exists, rearrange it to the lowest possible order (sorted in ascending order). The replacement must be in place and use only constant extra memory. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 100.

examples.explanation: The next permutation of [1,2,3] is [1,3,2].

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of the array, find the current one, and return the next one in sorted order (or the first if current is the last).

optimal.explanation: Find the rightmost index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1]; swap nums[i] with the smallest element to its right that is greater than nums[i]; then reverse the suffix after position i.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. Two intervals overlap if one starts before or when the other ends. The input may not be sorted.

examples.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so they are merged into [1,6].

bruteForce.explanation: Sort intervals, then repeatedly scan the list to find and merge any pair of overlapping intervals until no more merges are possible.

optimal.explanation: Sort intervals by start time, then do a single linear pass merging overlapping intervals in place, which is optimal since sorting is the bottleneck.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.description: Given a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, insert the new interval into the list and merge any overlapping intervals. The list is sorted by start time and no intervals overlap before insertion. Return the resulting list of non-overlapping intervals.

examples.explanation: [2,5] overlaps with [1,3] so they merge into [1,5]; [6,9] is untouched.

bruteForce.explanation: Add the new interval to the list, sort all intervals by start time, then merge overlapping intervals using the standard merge algorithm.

optimal.explanation: Use a single linear pass: add all intervals ending before the new one starts, merge all overlapping intervals with the new interval, then add the remaining intervals.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.description: Given an array of intervals intervals[i] = [starti, endi], return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping. Two intervals that only touch at a point are considered non-overlapping. Intervals can have 1 <= starti < endi <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Removing [1,3] leaves [1,2],[2,3],[3,4] which are non-overlapping.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of intervals to find the largest subset of non-overlapping intervals, then subtract its size from total count.

optimal.explanation: Greedy: sort by end time and greedily keep intervals that end earliest and do not overlap with the previous kept interval, minimizing removals.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.description: Given an array of meeting time intervals intervals[i] = [starti, endi], determine if a person could attend all meetings without any two meetings overlapping. Two meetings overlap if one starts before the other ends. Return true if all meetings can be attended, false otherwise.

examples.explanation: [0,30] and [5,10] overlap so a person cannot attend both.

bruteForce.explanation: Check every pair of meetings to see if they overlap; if any pair overlaps return false.

optimal.explanation: Sort intervals by start time, then do a single pass checking if any interval starts before the previous one ends.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.description: Given an array of meeting time intervals intervals[i] = [starti, endi], return the minimum number of conference rooms required to hold all meetings simultaneously. A room can be reused after a meeting ends. Intervals are given as half-open [start, end) ranges.

examples.explanation: Meetings [5,10] and [15,20] can share a room, but [0,30] needs its own room.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort by start time and use a list to track end times of all active rooms, scanning for an available room for each meeting.

optimal.explanation: Sort by start time and use a min-heap of end times; if the earliest-ending meeting ends before the current meeting starts, reuse that room, otherwise allocate a new one.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element. You must solve it in O(n) average time complexity. 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: [6,5,4,3,2,1], so the 2nd largest is 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the array in descending order and return the element at index k-1.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap of size k; after processing all elements, the heap's top is the kth largest element in O(n log k) time.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order. It is guaranteed that the answer is unique and 1 <= k <= number of unique elements <= nums.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times and 2 appears 2 times, making them the top 2 frequent elements.

bruteForce.explanation: Count frequencies using a hash map, then sort elements by frequency descending, and return the first k elements.

optimal.explanation: Use bucket sort: count frequencies then place elements into buckets indexed by frequency, and collect from highest frequency bucket down until k elements are gathered.

problems.title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
problems.description: Given an integer array nums of length n where all integers are in the range [1, n] and each integer appears once or twice, return an array of all integers that appear twice. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and uses only O(1) extra space (output array does not count).

examples.explanation: 2 appears at indices 5, and 3 appears at indices 2 and 6, so both are duplicates.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to track seen numbers; the second time a number is encountered, add it to the result.

optimal.explanation: Use the array itself as a sign map: for each number, negate the value at index abs(num)-1; if that value is already negative, the number is a duplicate.

problems.title: Pascal's Triangle
problems.description: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it. The first and last elements of each row are always 1. 1 <= numRows <= 30.

examples.explanation: Each interior element is the sum of the two elements directly above it in the previous row.

bruteForce.explanation: Build each row from scratch by computing each element as the sum of elements from the previous row at positions j-1 and j.

optimal.explanation: The same row-by-row approach is already optimal since each element must be computed and stored; no asymptotic improvement is possible over O(n^2).

problems.title: H-Index
problems.description: Given an array of integers citations where citations[i] is the number of citations a researcher received for their ith paper, return the researcher's h-index. The h-index is defined as the maximum value h such that the researcher has published at least h papers that have each been cited at least h times.

examples.explanation: Three papers have at least 3 citations each (3, 6, 5), and the remaining two have fewer than 3 citations, so h = 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort citations in descending order and find the largest index i where citations[i] >= i+1.

optimal.explanation: Use counting sort with a bucket of size n+1; bucket i accumulates papers with exactly i citations (capping at n), then scan from high to low to find h.

problems.title: Wiggle Sort II
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, reorder it such that nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3]... You may assume the input always has a valid answer. The reordering must be done in-place. 1 <= nums.length <= 5 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: After reordering: 1 < 6 > 1 < 5 > 1 < 4, satisfying the wiggle condition.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the array, then interleave the smaller half and larger half by placing the smaller half at even indices and the larger half at odd indices.

optimal.explanation: Find the median using nth_element in O(n), then use a 3-way Dutch National Flag partition with index mapping to place elements in wiggle order in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.description: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar heights where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram. 1 <= heights.length <= 10^5 and 0 <= heights[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The largest rectangle has area 10, formed by bars of height 5 and 6 (width 2, height 5 gives 10).

bruteForce.explanation: For each pair of bars (i, j), find the minimum height in that range and compute the rectangle area as min_height * (j - i + 1), tracking the maximum.

optimal.explanation: Use a monotonic increasing stack; when a shorter bar is encountered, pop taller bars and compute the area they can form as the limiting height.

problems.title: Candy
problems.description: There are n children standing in a line. Each child is assigned a rating value given in the array ratings. You are giving candies to these children such that each child must have at least one candy, and children with a higher rating than their adjacent neighbor must get more candies. Return the minimum number of candies required. 1 <= n <= 2 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Give candies [2,1,2]: middle child has rating 0 (lowest) so gets 1; children on sides get more.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the array and update candy counts until no more updates are needed, ensuring all constraints are satisfied.

optimal.explanation: Two-pass greedy: first pass left-to-right ensures right neighbors with higher ratings get more; second pass right-to-left ensures left neighbors with higher ratings get more.

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.description: There are n gas stations along a circular route. You are given two integer arrays gas and cost where gas[i] is the gas at station i and cost[i] is the cost to travel to the next station. Return the starting station index if you can travel around the circuit once, otherwise return -1. The solution is guaranteed to be unique if it exists.

examples.explanation: Starting at station 3, you can collect 4 gas, travel to 4 (net: 3), collect 5 (net: 6), travel to 0 (net: 4), etc., completing the circuit.

bruteForce.explanation: Try each station as a starting point and simulate the full circuit to see if enough gas is available at every step.

optimal.explanation: If total gas >= total cost a solution exists; greedily track the running tank and reset the start to the next station whenever the tank goes negative.

problems.title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if there exists a triple of indices (i, j, k) such that i < j < k and nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]. If no such indices exist, return false. The algorithm should run in O(n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: Any triplet such as (1,2,3) satisfies the increasing condition.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all combinations of three indices with i < j < k to see if nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k].

optimal.explanation: Maintain two variables for the smallest and second-smallest values seen so far; if any element exceeds both, a triplet exists.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.description: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order. 1 <= nums.length <= 10 and -10 <= nums[i] <= 10.

examples.explanation: All 2^3 = 8 subsets of [1,2,3] are returned including the empty set.

bruteForce.explanation: Use backtracking: at each step either include or exclude the current element and recurse, collecting all complete subsets.

optimal.explanation: Use bit manipulation: iterate through all 2^n bitmasks; for each mask, include nums[i] if bit i is set, generating each subset in O(n) time.

problems.title: Summary Ranges
problems.description: Given a sorted unique integer array nums, return the smallest sorted list of ranges that cover all the numbers in the array exactly. Each range [a,b] should be output as 'a->b' if a != b, otherwise 'a'. The array is sorted and has no duplicates. 0 <= nums.length <= 20.

examples.explanation: Consecutive runs [0,2] and [4,5] form ranges; 7 stands alone.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate through the array tracking the start of each consecutive run; when a gap is found, record the range and start a new one.

optimal.explanation: The single-pass approach above is already optimal at O(n); we can make it slightly cleaner using two-pointer style with explicit end tracking.

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return an integer array counts where counts[i] is the number of smaller elements to the right of nums[i]. 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5 and -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: For 5: [2,1] are smaller. For 2: [1] is smaller. For 6: [1] is smaller. For 1: none.

bruteForce.explanation: For each element, scan all elements to its right and count how many are smaller.

optimal.explanation: Use a modified merge sort that counts inversions: when merging, every time a right-half element is placed before a left-half element, increment counts for all remaining left-half elements.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.description: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray of which the sum is greater than or equal to target. If there is no such subarray, return 0 instead. 1 <= target <= 10^9 and 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,3] has sum 7 and length 2, which is the minimum.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays by iterating over every start and end index, accumulating sums and tracking the minimum length that meets the target.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window: expand the right pointer to grow the window and shrink the left pointer whenever the sum meets the target, updating the minimum length.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.description: Given an array nums of n integers and a target, return all unique quadruplets [nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]] such that a, b, c, d are all distinct indices and nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] + nums[d] == target. The solution set must not contain duplicate quadruplets. -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: These are all unique quadruplets that sum to 0.

bruteForce.explanation: Use four nested loops over all index combinations and collect unique quadruplets that sum to target using a set for deduplication.

optimal.explanation: Sort then use two nested loops for the first two elements and a two-pointer approach for the remaining two, skipping duplicates at each level.

problems.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
problems.description: Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number sorted in non-decreasing order. The array may contain negative numbers. Follow up: can you solve it in O(n) time? -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Squaring gives [16,1,0,9,100] and sorting gives [0,1,9,16,100].

bruteForce.explanation: Square each element and then sort the resulting array.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers at both ends: the largest square must come from either the leftmost or rightmost element; fill the result array from back to front in O(n).

problems.title: Find Peak Element
problems.description: A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given a 0-indexed integer array nums, find a peak element and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index of any peak. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time. nums[-1] and nums[n] are considered -infinity.

examples.explanation: Index 2 has value 3 which is greater than its neighbors 2 and 1, so it is a peak.

bruteForce.explanation: Scan linearly and return the index of the first element that is greater than both its neighbors.

optimal.explanation: Use binary search: if the middle element is less than its right neighbor, a peak exists in the right half; otherwise it exists in the left half or at mid.

problems.title: Two Sum II Input Array Is Sorted
problems.description: Given a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific target. Return the indices of the two numbers as an integer array [index1, index2] (1-indexed). You must use only constant extra space. There is exactly one solution.

examples.explanation: numbers[1] + numbers[2] = 2 + 7 = 9, so return [1, 2].

bruteForce.explanation: Check every pair of indices (i, j) with i < j to find the two numbers that sum to target.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers at both ends of the sorted array; move the left pointer right if the sum is too small, and the right pointer left if too large.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.description: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid. The word can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically) and each cell may only be used once. 1 <= m, n <= 6 and 1 <= word.length <= 15.

examples.explanation: The word ABCCED can be traced starting at (0,0) going right then down through the grid.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every cell as a starting point and use DFS backtracking to check if the word can be formed by visiting adjacent unvisited cells.

optimal.explanation: The DFS backtracking approach is already optimal in practice; an improvement is to check character frequency first to prune impossible cases early before any DFS.

problems.title: Pascal's Triangle II
problems.description: Given an integer rowIndex, return the rowIndex-th (0-indexed) row of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it. Follow up: can you optimize your space to O(rowIndex)? 0 <= rowIndex <= 33.

examples.explanation: Row 3 of Pascal's triangle is [1,3,3,1] (0-indexed: row 0=[1], row 1=[1,1], row 2=[1,2,1], row 3=[1,3,3,1]).

bruteForce.explanation: Build all rows of Pascal's triangle up to rowIndex, storing each row, then return the last one.

optimal.explanation: Use a single array of size rowIndex+1 and update it in-place from right to left so each cell is updated before it is used as a source.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word, using all original letters exactly once. Both strings consist of lowercase English letters and their lengths can be up to 5 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Both strings contain the same characters with the same frequencies.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort both strings and compare them character by character; if they are equal the strings are anagrams.

optimal.explanation: Use a frequency count array of size 26 to count characters in s and decrement for t; if all counts are zero the strings are anagrams, achieving linear time.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.description: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together and return them in any order. Two strings are anagrams if one can be formed by rearranging the letters of the other. The input length is between 1 and 10^4 and each string length is between 0 and 100.

examples.explanation: eat, tea, and ate are anagrams; tan and nat are anagrams; bat stands alone.

bruteForce.explanation: For each pair of strings, sort both and compare to group them; use a visited array to avoid reprocessing strings, resulting in O(n^2 * k log k) time.

optimal.explanation: Use a hash map where the key is the sorted version of each string; all anagrams share the same sorted key, allowing grouping in O(n * k log k) time.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.description: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. The string length is between 1 and 1000 and consists of digits and English letters.

examples.explanation: "bab" is a palindrome of length 3; "aba" is also a valid answer.

bruteForce.explanation: Check every possible substring by iterating over all start and end indices and verify if it is a palindrome, tracking the longest one found.

optimal.explanation: Expand around each center (both odd and even length palindromes) to find the longest palindrome in O(n) center expansions each taking O(n) time worst case giving O(n^2) overall.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.description: Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it. A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. The length of s is between 1 and 1000.

examples.explanation: The palindromic substrings are: "a", "a", "a", "aa", "aa", "aaa".

bruteForce.explanation: Check every possible substring by iterating over all pairs of indices and verify if it is a palindrome, incrementing a counter for each one found.

optimal.explanation: Expand around each center for both odd and even length palindromes, counting each valid expansion, reducing the complexity to O(n^2) with O(1) space.

problems.title: Encode and Decode Strings
problems.description: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings to a single string and decode that single string back to the original list. The encoded string must be transmittable over a network and should correctly handle strings containing any character including special characters. The list can have up to 200 strings each up to 200 characters long.

examples.explanation: Encode produces a single string; decode reconstructs the original list exactly.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a delimiter that is unlikely to appear in the strings (e.g., a special sequence), splitting on it during decode; this fails if strings contain the delimiter.

optimal.explanation: Prefix each string with its length followed by a separator character; during decode read the length first then extract exactly that many characters, making it robust to any character in strings.

problems.title: Reverse Words in a String
problems.description: Given an input string s, reverse the order of the words. A word is defined as a sequence of non-space characters. The words in s will be separated by at least one space and the returned string should have words separated by a single space with no leading or trailing spaces.

examples.explanation: Leading and trailing spaces are removed and words are reversed in order with single spaces.

bruteForce.explanation: Split the string by spaces into a list of words (ignoring empty tokens), then reverse the list and join with a single space.

optimal.explanation: Reverse the entire string in place, then reverse each individual word in place, and finally clean up spaces, achieving O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix
problems.description: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string. The array will have between 1 and 200 strings, each with length between 0 and 200, consisting only of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: All three strings share the prefix "fl" which is the longest common prefix.

bruteForce.explanation: Compare every pair of strings character by character to find the pairwise common prefix, then take the minimum across all pairs; this is redundant and slow.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and only compare the first and last strings lexicographically; the common prefix of these two is the longest common prefix of the entire array.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.description: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome, or false otherwise. The string length is between 1 and 2 * 10^5.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: After filtering, the string becomes "amanaplanacanalpanama" which is a palindrome.

bruteForce.explanation: Build a cleaned string by keeping only alphanumeric characters in lowercase, then compare it with its reverse.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing case-insensitively, avoiding the need to build an auxiliary string.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
problems.description: Given a string s, return true if the string can be a palindrome after deleting at most one character from it. The string consists only of lowercase English letters and has length between 1 and 10^5.

examples.explanation: Deleting the character 'c' or 'b' at the right position makes the string a palindrome.

bruteForce.explanation: Try removing each character one at a time and check if the resulting string is a palindrome; return true if any removal works.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers; when a mismatch is found, check if skipping either the left or right character results in a palindrome, solving it in O(n) time.

problems.title: String to Integer atoi
problems.description: Implement the myAtoi(string s) function which converts a string to a 32-bit signed integer. The algorithm reads leading whitespace, optional sign, and digits, stopping at the first non-digit; it clamps to INT_MIN or INT_MAX on overflow. The input string length is between 0 and 200.

examples.explanation: Leading spaces are skipped, '-' sign is read, digits '42' are converted to give -42.

bruteForce.explanation: Manually iterate through the string following the specified rules: skip whitespace, read sign, read digits, and use a long long to detect overflow before clamping.

optimal.explanation: Same linear scan but detect overflow during digit accumulation using the condition before multiplying to avoid any long long usage, keeping it strictly in int range.

problems.title: Implement strStr
problems.description: Given two strings haystack and needle, return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or -1 if needle is not part of haystack. The lengths of haystack and needle are between 0 and 10^4 and both consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The needle "sad" first appears at index 0 in the haystack.

bruteForce.explanation: Slide a window of size needle.length over the haystack and compare each window with the needle character by character.

optimal.explanation: Use the KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) algorithm with a failure function to skip redundant comparisons, achieving O(n + m) time.

problems.title: Roman to Integer
problems.description: Given a roman numeral string s, convert it to an integer. Roman numerals use seven symbols I, V, X, L, C, D, M and follow the rule that when a smaller value precedes a larger one it is subtracted. The input is guaranteed to be in the range 1 to 3999.

bruteForce.explanation: Scan left to right with a map lookup; if the current symbol is less than the next, subtract it, otherwise add it.

optimal.explanation: Scan right to left, keeping track of the previous value; if current value is less than previous, subtract it to handle subtractive notation cleanly without a map.

problems.title: Integer to Roman
problems.description: Given an integer num, convert it to a roman numeral string. Roman numerals are formed by combining symbols in descending order value and using subtractive notation for values like 4, 9, 40, 90, 400, and 900. The input num is in the range 1 to 3999.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a series of conditional checks or repeated subtraction for each roman numeral symbol from largest to smallest, appending the symbol each time.

optimal.explanation: Use lookup tables for thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones digits to directly build the roman numeral in O(1) time without any loops.

problems.title: Largest Number
problems.description: Given a list of non-negative integers nums, arrange them such that they form the largest number and return it as a string. Since the result may be very large, return it as a string. The list can have between 1 and 100 integers each in the range 0 to 10^9.

examples.explanation: By placing 9 first, then 5, then 34, then 3, then 30, we get the largest possible number.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of the numbers, concatenate each to form a string, and return the maximum; this is factorial time and only feasible for very small inputs.

optimal.explanation: Sort the numbers using a custom comparator: for two numbers a and b, prefer a before b if the concatenation a+b is lexicographically greater than b+a; then concatenate in sorted order.

problems.title: Add Binary
problems.description: Given two binary strings a and b, return their sum as a binary string. The inputs are non-empty binary strings without leading zeros (except the number 0 itself). Each string can have length up to 10^4.

examples.explanation: Binary 11 + 1 = 100, which is 3 + 1 = 4 in decimal.

bruteForce.explanation: Convert both binary strings to integers, add them, and convert the result back to a binary string; this fails for very large inputs that exceed integer range.

optimal.explanation: Simulate binary addition from the least significant bit using two pointers and a carry variable, building the result string directly without overflow risk.

problems.title: Multiply Strings
problems.description: Given two non-negative integers num1 and num2 represented as strings, return the product of num1 and num2, also represented as a string. You must not convert the inputs to integers directly. The lengths of num1 and num2 are between 1 and 200 and they do not have leading zeros (except for 0 itself).

examples.explanation: 123 * 456 = 56088, computed via digit-by-digit multiplication.

bruteForce.explanation: Multiply each digit of num2 by num1 (like long multiplication), shift appropriately, and add all partial results as strings.

optimal.explanation: Use a position array of size n+m to store intermediate products; the product of digits at positions i and j goes to positions i+j and i+j+1, then convert the array to a string.

problems.title: Zigzag Conversion
problems.description: The string "PAYPALISHIRING" is written in a zigzag pattern on a given number of rows. Read line by line to produce the output. Given the string s and the number of rows numRows, return the string read line by line. The string length is between 1 and 1000 and numRows is between 1 and 1000.

examples.explanation: Writing in zigzag with 3 rows and reading row by row gives PAHNAPLSIIGYIR.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate the zigzag pattern by placing each character in its appropriate row using a direction flag, then concatenate all rows.

optimal.explanation: Directly compute the cycle length (2*numRows-2) and jump to the correct positions in the original string for each row without building row arrays, saving memory allocations.

problems.title: Reverse String
problems.description: Write a function that reverses a string. The input is given as an array of characters and you must do it in place with O(1) extra memory. The array length is between 1 and 10^5 and consists of printable ASCII characters.

examples.explanation: The array is reversed in place by swapping characters from both ends.

bruteForce.explanation: Create a copy of the array and write characters from back to front into the original array; this uses O(n) extra space.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from both ends and swap characters until the pointers meet, reversing in place with O(1) extra space.

problems.title: First Unique Character in a String
problems.description: Given a string s, find the first non-repeating character in it and return its index. If it does not exist, return -1. The string consists only of lowercase English letters and has length between 1 and 10^5.

examples.explanation: The first non-repeating character is 'l' at index 0.

bruteForce.explanation: For each character, scan the entire string to check if it appears more than once; return the index of the first character that appears exactly once.

optimal.explanation: Count the frequency of each character in one pass, then scan the string a second time to find the first character with frequency 1.

problems.title: Ransom Note
problems.description: Given two strings ransomNote and magazine, return true if ransomNote can be constructed by using the letters from magazine and false otherwise. Each letter in magazine can only be used once. Both strings consist of lowercase English letters and have length between 1 and 10^5.

examples.explanation: Magazine has two 'a' characters so ransomNote 'aa' can be formed.

bruteForce.explanation: For each character in ransomNote, scan magazine to find a match and mark it as used; this is O(n*m) time.

optimal.explanation: Count character frequencies in magazine using an array of size 26, then decrement counts for each character in ransomNote; return false if any count goes negative.

problems.title: Is Subsequence
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if s is a subsequence of t, or false otherwise. A subsequence is a sequence derived by deleting some (or no) characters without changing the relative order of the remaining characters. The length of s is between 0 and 100 and t is between 0 and 10^4.

examples.explanation: Characters a, c, e appear in t in order without overlapping.

bruteForce.explanation: Use dynamic programming to check if s is a subsequence of t by building a 2D table tracking how many characters of s have been matched up to each position in t.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers: advance the pointer in s whenever a character matches the current character in t; if the s pointer reaches the end, s is a subsequence.

problems.title: Compare Version Numbers
problems.description: Given two version strings version1 and version2, compare them. Versions are split by dots into revisions and compared from left to right numerically; missing revisions are treated as 0. Return 1 if version1 > version2, -1 if version1 < version2, and 0 if they are equal.

examples.explanation: The second revision of version1 is 2 and of version2 is 10; since 2 < 10, version1 is smaller.

bruteForce.explanation: Split both version strings by '.' into arrays of revision strings, convert each to integer, and compare element by element padding with zeros where needed.

optimal.explanation: Parse revisions on-the-fly using two pointers into the version strings without building auxiliary arrays, reducing space to O(1).

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.description: A message containing letters A-Z can be encoded to numbers using the mapping A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26. Given a string s of digits, return the number of ways to decode it. The string can have length between 1 and 100 and may contain the digit '0'.

examples.explanation: 226 can be decoded as BZ(2,26), VF(22,6), or BBF(2,2,6).

bruteForce.explanation: Use plain recursion: at each position try taking one digit (if valid) or two digits (if valid), summing the results; this has exponential time due to overlapping subproblems.

optimal.explanation: Use dynamic programming where dp[i] is the number of ways to decode s[0..i-1]; transitions consider single-digit and two-digit decodings, solving in O(n) time and space.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.description: Given a string s and a dictionary of strings wordDict, return true if s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. Words in the dictionary may be reused multiple times. The string length is between 1 and 300 and the dictionary has between 1 and 1000 words.

examples.explanation: "leetcode" can be split into "leet" and "code", both of which are in the dictionary.

bruteForce.explanation: Use plain recursion trying all possible prefixes at each position to see if they are in the dictionary, then recursively check the remaining suffix; exponential due to repeated subproblems.

optimal.explanation: Use a boolean DP array where dp[i] is true if s[0..i-1] can be segmented; for each position check all substrings ending there that are in the dictionary, achieving O(n^2) time.

problems.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
problems.description: Given a string s, check if it can be constructed by taking a substring of it and appending multiple copies of the substring together. The string length is between 1 and 10^4 and consists only of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The string is constructed by repeating "abc" four times.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every possible substring length from 1 to n/2; for each, check if the string is composed entirely of repetitions of that substring.

optimal.explanation: Concatenate s with itself to form t = s + s, then check if s appears in t[1..2n-2] (i.e., excluding the first and last character); using KMP this check is O(n).

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string. The answer is guaranteed to be unique. Constraints: 1 <= s.length, t.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: The minimum window substring BANC includes A, B, and C from string t.

bruteForce.explanation: Check every possible substring of s and verify if it contains all characters of t, tracking the minimum valid window found.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window with two pointers; expand the right pointer to include characters and shrink the left pointer once all characters of t are covered, updating the minimum window at each valid state.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.description: Given a string s and an integer k, you can replace at most k characters in the string with any letter. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter you can get after performing the above operations. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^5, 0 <= k <= s.length.

examples.explanation: Replace the one 'A' in the middle with 'B' to form AABBBBA, but the longest window is ABBB or BBBA of length 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all substrings and for each one find the most frequent character, then check if replacing the rest (length - maxFreq) is within k.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window maintaining the count of the most frequent character; shrink the window from the left when replacements needed exceed k.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.description: Given two strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1 as a substring, or false otherwise. In other words, return true if one of the permutations of s1 is a substring of s2. Constraints: 1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: s2 contains one permutation of s1 ("ba") as a substring starting at index 3.

bruteForce.explanation: For every substring of s2 with length equal to s1, sort both and compare to check if they are anagrams.

optimal.explanation: Use a fixed-size sliding window of length s1 over s2, maintaining character frequency arrays and comparing them in O(1) per step.

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.description: Given two strings s and p, return an array of all the start indices of p's anagrams in s. You may return the answer in any order. An anagram is a permutation of a string. Constraints: 1 <= s.length, p.length <= 3 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: The substring at index 0 is 'cba' and at index 6 is 'bac', both anagrams of 'abc'.

bruteForce.explanation: For each starting index in s, extract the substring of length p, sort it, and compare it to the sorted version of p.

optimal.explanation: Use a fixed-size sliding window maintaining character frequency counts; record start index whenever window frequencies match p's frequencies.

problems.title: Regular Expression Matching
problems.description: Given an input string s and a pattern p, implement regular expression matching with support for '.' and '*'. '.' matches any single character, '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element. The matching should cover the entire input string. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 20, 1 <= p.length <= 30.

examples.explanation: c* matches zero c's, a* matches two a's, and b matches b.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try all possible matches at each position, handling '.' and '*' by branching into possible interpretations.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D dynamic programming where dp[i][j] means s[0..i-1] matches p[0..j-1], filling the table bottom-up to avoid redundant recursive calls.

problems.title: Wildcard Matching
problems.description: Given an input string s and a pattern p, implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*'. '?' matches any single character, '*' matches any sequence of characters (including empty). The matching should cover the entire input string. Constraints: 0 <= s.length, p.length <= 2000.

examples.explanation: The first '*' matches empty string, 'a' matches 'a', second '*' matches 'dce', 'b' matches 'b'.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively match the string and pattern character by character, branching on '*' to match zero or more characters of s.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] represents whether s[0..i-1] matches p[0..j-1], handling '*' as matching empty or extending the match.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.description: Given a string s, partition s such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitioning of s. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 16, s consists of only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Both partitions have all substrings as palindromes.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try every possible prefix at each position, check if it's a palindrome, and recurse on the remaining string.

optimal.explanation: Precompute a DP table for all palindrome substrings to answer isPalindrome queries in O(1), then use backtracking to enumerate partitions efficiently.

problems.title: Remove Duplicate Letters
problems.description: Given a string s, remove duplicate letters so that every letter appears once and only once. You must make sure your result is the smallest in lexicographical order among all possible results. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^4, s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Removing duplicate letters while maintaining smallest lexicographic order gives 'abc'.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all subsequences that contain each character exactly once and return the lexicographically smallest one.

optimal.explanation: Use a greedy monotonic stack approach: track last occurrence of each character and use a visited set to skip duplicates, popping larger characters from the stack when a smaller one can still appear later.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.description: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations (insert, delete, or replace a character) required to convert word1 to word2. Constraints: 0 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500.

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace h with r), rorse -> rose (remove r), rose -> ros (remove e).

bruteForce.explanation: Use plain recursion to try all three operations (insert, delete, replace) at each position and return the minimum.

optimal.explanation: Build a 2D DP table where dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i chars of word1 and first j chars of word2, filling it bottom-up.

problems.title: Shortest Palindrome
problems.description: Given a string s, you can prepend any number of characters in front of it to make it a palindrome. Return the shortest palindrome you can find by performing this transformation. Constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Prepend one 'a' to the front to get the shortest palindrome.

bruteForce.explanation: For each prefix of s from longest to shortest, check if it is a palindrome; once found, prepend the reverse of the remaining suffix to s.

optimal.explanation: Use KMP failure function on the string s + '#' + reverse(s) to find the longest palindromic prefix in O(n), then prepend the minimum characters needed.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s which equals t. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit number. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000, 1 <= t.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: There are 3 ways to generate 'rabbit' from 'rabbbit' by choosing which of the three b's to include.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: for each character in s either match it with the current character in t or skip it, counting all ways to form t.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the number of ways to form t[0..j-1] from s[0..i-1], building the table bottom-up in O(m*n).

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.description: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is a sequence derived from one string by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements. Constraints: 1 <= text1.length, text2.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is 'ace' which has length 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try matching or skipping each character and return the maximum length common subsequence.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] stores the LCS length of text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1], computed bottom-up using previously computed values.

problems.title: Interleaving String
problems.description: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2. An interleaving of two strings s and t is a configuration where all characters of s and t are divided into n+m substrings and merged in the original order. Constraints: 0 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 100, 0 <= s3.length <= 200.

examples.explanation: s3 can be formed by interleaving s1 and s2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: at each step pick the next character from s1 or s2 that matches s3, and recurse; return true if all of s3 is matched.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] means s3[0..i+j-1] can be formed by interleaving s1[0..i-1] and s2[0..j-1], filling the table bottom-up.

problems.title: Word Break II
problems.description: Given a string s and a dictionary of strings wordDict, add spaces in s to construct a sentence where each word is a valid dictionary word and return all such possible sentences in any order. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 20, 1 <= wordDict.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Both sentences use words from the dictionary and cover the full string.

bruteForce.explanation: Use plain recursion to try every prefix at each position, check if it's in the dictionary, and recurse on the suffix collecting all valid sentences.

optimal.explanation: Use memoized recursion (top-down DP) where results for each starting index are cached to avoid recomputation of overlapping subproblems.

problems.title: Reverse Vowels of a String
problems.description: Given a string s, reverse only all the vowels in the string and return it. The vowels are 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', and 'u', and they can appear in both lowercase and uppercase. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 3 * 10^5.

examples.explanation: The vowels 'e' and 'o' are swapped.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all vowels in order, then iterate over the string again and replace vowels with the collected vowels in reverse order.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from both ends of the string, swapping vowels when both pointers point to vowels, advancing them inward until they meet.

problems.title: String Compression
problems.description: Given an array of characters chars, compress it using the following algorithm: for each group of consecutive repeating characters, write the character followed by the count if the count is greater than 1. Modify the array in-place and return the new length. Constraints: 1 <= chars.length <= 2000.

examples.explanation: The array becomes ['a','2','b','2','c','3'] and the function returns 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Build the compressed string separately using a string builder, then copy back to the array at the end.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers: a read pointer to scan the array and a write pointer to overwrite in-place, converting counts to digits directly without extra space.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Steps to Make Two Strings Anagram
problems.description: Given two strings s and t of equal length, return the minimum number of steps to make t an anagram of s. In one step you can choose any character of t and replace it with another character. Constraints: 1 <= s.length == t.length <= 5 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Replace the first 'a' in t with 'b', t becomes 'bba' which has the same characters as 'bab'.

bruteForce.explanation: Count character frequencies for both strings and for each character compute the excess in t compared to s, summing all excesses as the required replacements.

optimal.explanation: Use a fixed-size array of 26 for character frequency differences between s and t, then sum the positive differences to get the answer with O(1) space.

problems.title: Reverse Words in a String III
problems.description: Given a string s, reverse the order of characters in each word within a sentence while still preserving whitespace and initial word order. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4, s contains printable ASCII characters.

examples.explanation: Each word in the string is reversed while whitespace positions are preserved.

bruteForce.explanation: Split the string by spaces into words, reverse each word individually, then join them back with spaces.

optimal.explanation: Traverse the string in-place, identifying word boundaries and reversing each word directly within the string without extra splitting overhead.

problems.title: Text Justification
problems.description: Given an array of strings words and a width maxWidth, format the text such that each line has exactly maxWidth characters and is fully (left and right) justified. Pack as many words as possible in each line. Extra spaces should be distributed as evenly as possible between words, and extra spaces go to the left slots. The last line should be left-justified. Constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 300, 1 <= words[i].length <= 20.

examples.explanation: Each line except the last is fully justified with spaces distributed evenly.

bruteForce.explanation: Greedily pack words into lines, then for each non-last line compute the required spaces between words and distribute them left to right.

optimal.explanation: The greedy line-packing approach is already optimal; this implementation is cleaner with explicit tracking of lines and space distribution without extra passes.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.description: Given an encoded string, return its decoded string. The encoding rule is k[encoded_string], where the encoded_string inside the square brackets is repeated exactly k times. You may assume that the input data is always valid. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 30, k is in the range [1, 300].

examples.explanation: 2[c] decodes to cc, so a2[c] becomes acc, and 3[acc] becomes accaccacc.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the string for the innermost bracket pair, decode it, replace it in the string, and repeat until no brackets remain.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack to process characters left to right: push characters until ']', then pop to find the matching '[' and the repeat count, build the repeated string, and push it back.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.description: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists. Return the head of the merged linked list. Both lists contain nodes with integer values in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: The merged sorted list interleaves the nodes from both lists maintaining sorted order.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all values from both lists into an array, sort the array, then build a new linked list from the sorted values.

optimal.explanation: Use a two-pointer iterative approach with a dummy head node, comparing values from both lists and linking the smaller node each step, achieving linear time without extra space for values.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.description: Given head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it. A cycle exists if some node can be reached again by continuously following the next pointer. Return true if there is a cycle, otherwise return false. The number of nodes can be up to 10^4.

examples.explanation: The tail node links back to the node at index 1, forming a cycle.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to store visited node addresses; if we encounter a node already in the set, a cycle exists.

optimal.explanation: Use Floyd's slow and fast pointer algorithm: if there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually meet the slow pointer, using constant extra space.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle II
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return null. Do not modify the linked list. The number of nodes can be up to 10^4 and node values are in range [-10^5, 10^5].

examples.explanation: The cycle begins at the node with value 2 (index 1).

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to track visited nodes; the first node visited a second time is the start of the cycle.

optimal.explanation: Use Floyd's cycle detection: after slow and fast pointers meet, reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time until they meet again at the cycle entrance.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node. The number of nodes in the list is between 1 and 100.

examples.explanation: The middle node is node 3; returning the node at position 3 gives [3,4,5].

bruteForce.explanation: Traverse the entire list to count nodes, then traverse again to reach the node at position count/2.

optimal.explanation: Use slow and fast pointers: fast moves two steps while slow moves one; when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle, completing this in a single pass.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return its head. The number of nodes in the list is sz and 1 <= n <= sz <= 30. Node values are in range [0, 100].

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end is node 4, so it is removed.

bruteForce.explanation: Traverse the list to find its length, then traverse again to the (length - n)th node and remove the next node.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers separated by n nodes; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is just before the node to remove, solving it in one pass.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.description: You are given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked lists into one sorted linked list and return it. k is between 0 and 10^4 and the total number of nodes across all lists is between 0 and 10^4.

examples.explanation: All three sorted lists are merged into a single sorted linked list.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values into a vector, sort them, and rebuild a new linked list — simple but does not leverage the pre-sorted property.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap (priority queue) of size k to always extract the smallest node among current list heads, achieving O(N log k) time by exploiting the sorted order.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers
