problems.description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order and each node contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list. The number of nodes in each list is between 1 and 100 and each node value is a digit 0-9.

examples.explanation: 342 + 465 = 807, stored in reverse as [7,0,8].

bruteForce.explanation: Extract numbers from both lists into strings, convert to big integers, add them, then convert the sum back into a linked list in reverse order.

optimal.explanation: Directly simulate digit-by-digit addition with a carry variable, processing both lists simultaneously and creating new nodes for the result.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers II
problems.description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers where digits are stored in forward (most significant digit first) order. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list in the same forward order. The number of nodes in each list is between 1 and 100.

examples.explanation: 7243 + 564 = 7807, stored in forward order as [7,8,0,7].

bruteForce.explanation: Use two stacks to reverse both lists, perform digit-by-digit addition with carry, push results onto a result stack, then build the linked list from the stack.

optimal.explanation: Reverse both input lists, add digits with carry like Add Two Numbers, then reverse the result list — same complexity but conceptually cleaner without extra stack structure.

problems.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
problems.description: Given the heads of two singly linked lists headA and headB, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If the two linked lists have no intersection at all, return null. The lists have no cycles. The number of nodes in listA is m and in listB is n, both between 1 and 3*10^4.

examples.explanation: The two lists share the suffix [8,4,5] starting at the node with value 8.

bruteForce.explanation: Store all nodes from list A in a hash set, then traverse list B and return the first node found in the set.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers that switch to the other list's head upon reaching the end; they will meet at the intersection node (or both reach null) after traversing m+n nodes each.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if it is a palindrome or false otherwise. The number of nodes in the list is between 1 and 10^5 and each node value is between 0 and 9.

examples.explanation: The list reads the same forwards and backwards.

bruteForce.explanation: Copy all node values into a vector, then check if the vector equals its reverse using two pointers.

optimal.explanation: Find the middle using slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half in-place, compare both halves, then optionally restore the list — achieves O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
problems.description: A linked list of length n is given such that each node also has a random pointer which could point to any node in the list or null. Construct a deep copy of the list. The deep copy should consist of new nodes and none of the new nodes' next or random pointers should point to nodes in the original list. n is between 0 and 1000.

examples.explanation: A deep copy where each node's random pointer mirrors the original structure.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash map from original nodes to their copies; first pass creates all copies, second pass sets next and random pointers.

optimal.explanation: Interleave clone nodes between original nodes (A->A'->B->B'->...), set random pointers for clones, then detach the cloned list — eliminates the hash map for O(1) extra space.

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.description: Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement the LRUCache class with get(key) returning the value if key exists or -1, and put(key, value) inserting or updating the key-value pair and evicting the LRU key when capacity is exceeded. 1 <= capacity <= 3000 and 0 <= key, value <= 10^4.

examples.input: LRUCache(2), put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: Cache capacity is 2; inserting key 3 evicts key 2 (LRU), inserting key 4 evicts key 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Use an ordered map or vector of pairs to track access order, scanning linearly to find and evict the LRU element on each put operation.

optimal.explanation: Use a doubly linked list for O(1) insertion/deletion and a hash map for O(1) lookup, giving O(1) time for both get and put operations.

problems.title: Reorder List
problems.description: You are given the head of a singly linked list. Reorder it so that nodes at positions 0, 1, 2, ... n are rearranged to 0, n, 1, n-1, 2, n-2, ... Do this in-place without altering node values. The number of nodes is between 1 and 5*10^4.

examples.explanation: The list is reordered by interleaving the original list with its reverse.

bruteForce.explanation: Copy all nodes into a vector, then use two pointers (front and back) to rebuild the list by alternately taking from the front and back of the vector.

optimal.explanation: Find the middle, reverse the second half in-place, then merge both halves alternately — achieves the same result with O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Sort List
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, return the list after sorting it in ascending order. The number of nodes is between 0 and 5*10^4 and node values are between -10^5 and 10^5. Try to sort the list in O(n log n) time and O(1) space.

examples.explanation: The linked list is sorted in ascending order.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values into a vector, sort the vector, then update each node's value with the sorted values in order.

optimal.explanation: Apply bottom-up merge sort on the linked list: repeatedly merge sublists of increasing size (1, 2, 4, ...) until the whole list is sorted, achieving O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Rotate List
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, rotate the list to the right by k places. The number of nodes in the list is between 0 and 500 and node values are between -100 and 100. k is between 0 and 2*10^9.

examples.explanation: Rotating right by 2 moves the last 2 elements to the front.

bruteForce.explanation: Perform k individual one-step right rotations by moving the last node to the front each time (with k reduced by list length modulo).

optimal.explanation: Connect the tail to the head to form a circle, then find the new tail at position (n - k%n - 1) and break the circle there, achieving O(n) time.

problems.title: Partition List
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list and a value x, partition it such that all nodes less than x come before nodes greater than or equal to x. You should preserve the original relative order of the nodes in each of the two partitions. The number of nodes is between 0 and 200 and node values are between -100 and 100.

examples.explanation: Nodes with values less than 3 (1,2,2) come before nodes with values >= 3 (4,3,5).

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all values less than x and all values >= x separately maintaining order, then concatenate them to form the partitioned list.

optimal.explanation: Maintain two dummy-headed lists (less and greater-or-equal), append each node to the appropriate list, then connect them — O(1) extra space using original nodes.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List II
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list and two integers left and right where left <= right, reverse the nodes of the list from position left to position right, and return the reversed list. The number of nodes is n and 1 <= left <= right <= n <= 500. Node values are in [-500, 500].

examples.explanation: The sublist from position 2 to 4 ([2,3,4]) is reversed to [4,3,2].

bruteForce.explanation: Extract the values of the sublist from left to right, reverse them, then put them back into the corresponding nodes.

optimal.explanation: Use a one-pass approach: navigate to the node before position left, then repeatedly insert the next node at the front of the reversed section using pointer manipulation.

problems.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
problems.description: Given a linked list, swap every two adjacent nodes and return its head. You must solve the problem without modifying the values in the list's nodes (only nodes themselves may be changed). The number of nodes is between 0 and 100 and node values are between 0 and 100.

examples.explanation: Every pair of adjacent nodes is swapped: (1,2) becomes (2,1) and (3,4) becomes (4,3).

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all nodes into a vector, swap adjacent pairs in the vector by swapping node values, then return the head.

optimal.explanation: Use a dummy head and iteratively swap each pair of nodes using pointer manipulation without altering values, achieving O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time and return the modified list. k is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k, the remaining nodes at the end should stay as-is. You may not alter the values in the list's nodes, only nodes themselves may be changed.

examples.explanation: Every group of 2 nodes is reversed; the last node stays as-is since it cannot form a complete group.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all nodes into a vector, reverse each chunk of size k in-place by swapping values, then reconstruct the list.

optimal.explanation: Check if k nodes remain, reverse the k-node group in-place using pointer manipulation, then recursively process the rest — O(1) extra space per group.

problems.title: Remove Linked List Elements
problems.description: Given the head of a linked list and an integer val, remove all nodes of the linked list that have val as their value and return the new head. The number of nodes in the list is between 0 and 10^4 and node values are between 1 and 50. val is between 1 and 50.

examples.explanation: All nodes with value 6 are removed from the list.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values not equal to val into a new list by creating new nodes for each valid value.

optimal.explanation: Use a dummy head and a single pointer; skip nodes with the target value by adjusting the next pointer in-place, using O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Odd Even Linked List
problems.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, group all the nodes with odd indices together followed by the nodes with even indices, and return the reordered list. The first node is considered odd and the second is even and so on. The relative order inside both the odd and even groups should remain as it is in the input. The number of nodes is between 0 and 10^4.

examples.explanation: Odd-indexed nodes (1,3,5) come first, followed by even-indexed nodes (2,4).

bruteForce.explanation: Separate node values at odd and even positions into two vectors, concatenate them, and update node values in the original list.

optimal.explanation: Maintain two separate chains (odd and even) using pointers, interleave them in-place, and connect the even chain to the end of the odd chain — O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Delete Node in a Linked List
problems.description: You are given a node to delete in a singly linked list. You will not be given access to the head of the list, only access to the node to be deleted. All node values in the list are unique, and the node is guaranteed not to be the tail node. The number of nodes is between 2 and 1000.

examples.explanation: Node 5 is deleted by copying the next node's value and skipping the next node.

bruteForce.explanation: Since we have no access to the previous node or head, the only approach is to copy the next node's value and redirect to skip the next node — this is also the only viable solution.

optimal.explanation: Copy the value from the next node into the current node and skip the next node — this effectively deletes the current node in O(1) time and space.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
problems.description: Given the head of a sorted linked list, delete all duplicates such that each element appears only once. Return the linked list sorted as well. The number of nodes is between 0 and 300 and node values are between -100 and 100. The list is guaranteed to be sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: All duplicate values are removed, keeping only the first occurrence of each value.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a hash set to track seen values; rebuild a new list containing only the first occurrence of each value.

optimal.explanation: Since the list is sorted, traverse with one pointer and skip consecutive nodes with the same value — no extra space needed.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
problems.description: Given the head of a sorted linked list, delete all nodes that have duplicate numbers, leaving only distinct numbers from the original list. Return the linked list sorted as well. The number of nodes is between 0 and 300 and node values are between -100 and 100.

examples.explanation: All nodes with values 3 and 4 are removed because they appear more than once.

bruteForce.explanation: Count the frequency of each value using a map, then rebuild a new list keeping only values that appear exactly once.

optimal.explanation: Use a dummy head and predecessor pointer; whenever a run of equal values is detected, skip all of them in one pass without extra storage for frequencies.

problems.title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
problems.description: You are given a doubly linked list where each node has a next pointer, a prev pointer, and a child pointer that may point to a separate doubly linked list (also with child pointers). Flatten the list so that all the nodes appear in a single-level doubly linked list. Return the head of the flattened list. The total number of nodes is between 0 and 1000.

examples.explanation: Child lists are inserted after the parent node before continuing with the rest of the parent list.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a recursive DFS approach: for each node with a child, recursively flatten the child list and insert it between the current node and its next.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative approach with a stack: push the next node before diving into the child list to avoid recursion overhead and stack depth issues.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.description: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time. Implement the MinStack class with push(val), pop(), top(), and getMin() operations. All operations must run in O(1) time complexity.

examples.input: MinStack minStack = new MinStack(); minStack.push(-2); minStack.push(0); minStack.push(-3); minStack.getMin(); minStack.pop(); minStack.top(); minStack.getMin();
examples.explanation: After pushing -2, 0, -3, getMin() returns -3. After pop(), top() is 0 and getMin() is -2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a single stack and scan all elements each time getMin() is called to find the minimum value.

optimal.explanation: Use two stacks: one for elements and one to track minimums. Push to the min stack whenever the new value is <= current min, achieving O(1) getMin.

problems.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
problems.description: Implement a FIFO queue using only two stacks. The implemented queue should support push(x), pop(), peek(), and empty() operations. You must use only standard stack operations (push to top, peek/pop from top, size, and is empty).

examples.input: MyQueue queue = new MyQueue(); queue.push(1); queue.push(2); queue.peek(); queue.pop(); queue.empty();
examples.explanation: peek() returns 1 (front), pop() removes and returns 1, empty() returns false since 2 remains.

bruteForce.explanation: On every push, move all elements from stack1 to stack2, push new element to stack1, then move all back. This makes push O(n) but pop/peek O(1).

optimal.explanation: Use two stacks with lazy transfer: push to input stack, and only transfer all elements to output stack when output is empty (amortized O(1) per operation).

problems.title: Implement Stack using Queues
problems.description: Implement a LIFO stack using only two queues. The implemented stack should support push(x), pop(), top(), and empty() operations. You must use only standard queue operations (push to back, peek/pop from front, size, and is empty).

examples.input: MyStack stack = new MyStack(); stack.push(1); stack.push(2); stack.top(); stack.pop(); stack.empty();
examples.explanation: top() returns 2 (last pushed), pop() removes and returns 2, empty() returns false since 1 remains.

bruteForce.explanation: Use two queues. On push, enqueue to q2, then move all elements from q1 to q2, then swap q1 and q2, making q1 always maintain LIFO order.

optimal.explanation: Use a single queue. After pushing, rotate the queue by moving all previous elements to the back, so the new element is always at the front.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation. Valid operators are +, -, *, and /. Each operand may be an integer or another expression. Division between two integers truncates toward zero.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively find the last operator, split the tokens array into left and right sub-expressions, and evaluate them recursively. This approach is inefficient due to repeated array scanning.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack: push numbers onto the stack, and when an operator is encountered, pop two values, apply the operator, and push the result back. This is iterative and clean.

problems.title: Basic Calculator
problems.description: Given a string s representing a valid mathematical expression containing digits, +, -, (, and ), implement a basic calculator to evaluate it. The expression is guaranteed to be valid and may contain spaces. No multiplication or division is involved.

examples.explanation: Evaluating all additions and subtractions respecting parentheses gives 23.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively find matching parentheses, replace them with their evaluated value, and repeat until no parentheses remain. This involves repeated string scanning and is very slow.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack to handle parentheses: push the current result and sign onto the stack when encountering '(', reset, and pop to combine when encountering ')'. Single pass O(n).

problems.title: Basic Calculator II
problems.description: Given a string s representing a valid mathematical expression with integers and operators +, -, *, /, implement a basic calculator. The integer division should truncate toward zero. The expression does not contain parentheses.

examples.explanation: 5/2 = 2 (truncated), then 3 + 2 = 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Split the expression by + and - first, then evaluate each sub-expression (which may contain * and /) separately, and combine results. This requires two passes over the string.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack with a single pass: push positive numbers for '+', negative for '-', and immediately compute * and / by popping the top. Sum the stack at the end.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.description: Given an array of integers temperatures representing daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after the ith day to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future day with a warmer temperature, answer[i] = 0. 1 <= temperatures.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: For day 0 (73), the next warmer day is day 1 (74), so answer[0]=1. For day 2 (75), next warmer is day 6 (76), so answer[2]=4.

bruteForce.explanation: For each day, scan all subsequent days to find the first one with a higher temperature. This nested loop approach is O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Use a monotonic decreasing stack storing indices. When a warmer temperature is found, pop indices from the stack and record the distance. Single pass O(n).

problems.title: Next Greater Element I
problems.description: Given two distinct arrays nums1 and nums2, where nums1 is a subset of nums2, find all next greater numbers for nums1's elements in the corresponding places in nums2. The next greater element of x in nums2 is the first greater element to its right. If no such element exists, return -1 for that number.

examples.explanation: 4 has no next greater element. 1's next greater is 3. 2 has no next greater element.

bruteForce.explanation: For each element in nums1, find its position in nums2, then scan right to find the first greater element. This is O(m*n) where m and n are the lengths of nums1 and nums2.

optimal.explanation: Precompute next greater elements for all elements of nums2 using a monotonic stack and a hash map, then answer queries in O(1) each.

problems.title: Next Greater Element II
problems.description: Given a circular integer array nums (i.e., the next element of nums[nums.length - 1] is nums[0]), return the next greater number for every element. The next greater number of a number x is the first greater number to its traversing-order next in the array. If it doesn't exist, return -1 for this number.

examples.explanation: The next greater number for 1 is 2. For 2, there is no greater number. For the last 1, looking circularly, the next greater is 2.

bruteForce.explanation: For each element, scan the next n-1 elements circularly using modular indexing to find the first greater element. This is O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Traverse the array twice (simulate circularity) using a monotonic decreasing stack of indices. The second pass handles wrap-around lookups.

problems.title: Asteroid Collision
problems.description: Given an array asteroids of integers representing asteroids in a row, find out the state after all collisions. Each asteroid's absolute value represents size and the sign represents direction (positive = right, negative = left). Two asteroids collide if one moves right and the next moves left. The larger one survives; equal ones both explode.

examples.explanation: 10 and -5 collide; 10 survives. 5 and 10 don't collide since both move right.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the array and resolve the first collision found until no collisions remain. This requires multiple passes and is O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Use a stack to simulate collisions in a single pass. When a left-moving asteroid meets right-moving ones on the stack, resolve collisions until the stack is stable.

problems.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
problems.description: Given a string s, repeatedly remove all adjacent duplicate characters until no more adjacent duplicates exist. Return the final string. The order of the remaining characters is preserved.

examples.explanation: Remove 'bb' to get 'aaca', then remove 'aa' to get 'ca'.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the string and remove adjacent duplicates until no more are found. Each pass is O(n) and may require O(n) passes in the worst case, giving O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Use a stack (or build result string as a stack): push characters one by one; if the top equals current character, pop it (remove pair). Single pass O(n).

problems.title: Car Fleet
problems.description: There are n cars going to the same destination along a one-lane road. You are given arrays position and speed of length n, and an integer target. A car fleet is a group of cars driving at the same position and speed. A faster car catching up to a slower car merges into that fleet. Return the number of car fleets that arrive at the destination.

examples.explanation: Cars at 10 and 8 form one fleet, car at 0 forms another, and car at 5 and 3 form another, arriving as 3 fleets.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort cars by position, then for each pair check if the faster car behind catches up to the slower car ahead before reaching target. Track fleet merging iteratively with O(n^2) comparisons.

optimal.explanation: Sort cars by position descending. Compute each car's time to target. Use a stack: if the current car's time > stack top, it forms a new fleet. This is clean O(n log n) due to sort.

problems.title: Score of Parentheses
problems.description: Given a balanced parentheses string s, return the score of the string based on these rules: () has score 1, AB has score A + B where A and B are balanced strings, and (A) has score 2 * A. The string length is between 2 and 50.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively find balanced substrings, compute their scores, and combine. For each position, find matching closing bracket and recurse into the inner and outer parts. O(n^2) due to repeated scanning.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack initialized with 0. On '(' push 0; on ')' pop v: if v==0 push 1, else push 2*v, then add to new top. Single pass O(n).

problems.title: Online Stock Span
problems.description: Design an algorithm that collects daily price quotes for some stock and returns the span of that stock's price for the current day. The span of the stock's price today is the maximum number of consecutive days (including today) for which the stock price was less than or equal to today's price.

examples.input: StockSpanner(); next(100); next(80); next(60); next(70); next(60); next(75); next(85);
examples.explanation: For price 85 on day 7, looking back: 75, 60, 70, 60, 80 -- first 4 consecutive are <= 85 then 80 also <= 85, so span is 6.

bruteForce.explanation: For each new price, scan back through all previous prices until finding one greater than current. Count the days traversed including today. O(n) per call in worst case.

optimal.explanation: Use a monotonic stack storing (price, span) pairs. When a new price arrives, pop all pairs with price <= current and accumulate their spans. Amortized O(1) per call.

problems.title: Validate Stack Sequences
problems.description: Given two integer arrays pushed and popped each with distinct values, return true if this could have been the result of a sequence of push and pop operations on an initially empty stack. Both arrays have the same length between 1 and 1000.

examples.explanation: We can push 1-4, pop 4, push 5, pop 5,3,2,1 to match the popped sequence.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible interleavings of push and pop operations using backtracking and check if any matches the popped sequence. This is exponential time.

optimal.explanation: Simulate the process with a stack: push elements greedily and pop whenever the stack top matches the next expected popped element. Check if all pops are satisfied.

problems.title: Backspace String Compare
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return true if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors. '#' means a backspace character. Note that after backspacing an empty text, the text will continue empty.

examples.explanation: Both s and t become "ac" after processing backspaces.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate typing for both strings using a stack/string, building the final text by processing each character including backspaces, then compare the two results.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from the end of both strings, counting backspaces. Skip characters accordingly, comparing remaining characters without extra space. O(1) space.

problems.title: Make the String Great
problems.description: Given a string s of lower and upper case English letters, make the string great by repeatedly removing adjacent pairs of the same letter with different cases (e.g., 'aA' or 'Aa'). Return the resulting string. A string is great if there are no adjacent pairs of same letter with different case.

examples.explanation: 'eE' is removed first giving 'leeetcode', then another 'eE'... eventually 'leetcode'.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the string and remove the first adjacent bad pair found until no such pair exists. Each pass is O(n) and there can be O(n) passes, giving O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Use a stack: push each character, and if the top of the stack forms a bad pair with the current character, pop instead of pushing. Single pass O(n).

problems.title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string s of '(', ')' and lowercase English characters, remove the minimum number of parentheses (in any positions) so that the resulting string is valid. Return any valid string. A string is valid if it is empty, contains only lowercase characters, or is wrapped in matched parentheses.

examples.explanation: Remove the last ')' to make the string valid.

bruteForce.explanation: Try removing each subset of parentheses and check if the result is valid, returning the one with minimum removals. This is exponential in the number of parentheses.

optimal.explanation: Two-pass approach: first mark unmatched ')' by scanning left to right with a counter, then mark unmatched '(' by scanning right to left. Build result by skipping marked indices.

problems.title: Monotone Increasing Digits
problems.description: An integer has monotone increasing digits if and only if each pair of adjacent digits satisfies digits[i] <= digits[i+1]. Given an integer n, return the largest number that is less than or equal to n with monotone increasing digits. 0 <= n <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: 332 has non-monotone digits (3 > 2). The largest monotone number <= 332 is 299.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate downward from n, checking each number for monotone increasing property until one is found. This is O(n) in the worst case.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n * d) where d is number of digits

optimal.explanation: Work on the digit string: find the rightmost position where a digit is greater than the next, decrement it, and set all subsequent digits to '9'. Greedy O(d) where d is number of digits.

problems.title: 132 Pattern
problems.description: Given an array of n integers nums, a 132 pattern is a subsequence of three integers nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] where i < j < k. Return true if there is a 132 pattern in nums, otherwise return false. 1 <= nums.length <= 2*10^5.

examples.explanation: The sequence [1,4,2] satisfies nums[i]=1 < nums[k]=2 < nums[j]=4 with i=1, j=2, k=3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use three nested loops to check all triplets (i, j, k) with i < j < k and verify if nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]. O(n^3) time.

optimal.explanation: Traverse from right to left with a monotonic stack. Maintain a variable 'third' (nums[k]) as the maximum value popped from the stack. If any nums[i] < third, we found the pattern.

problems.title: Design Circular Queue
problems.description: Design your implementation of the circular queue with enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, and isFull operations. The circular queue is a linear data structure in which the operations are performed based on FIFO principle and the last position is connected to the first position to make a circle. 1 <= k <= 1000.

examples.input: MyCircularQueue(3); enQueue(1); enQueue(2); enQueue(3); enQueue(4); Rear(); isFull(); deQueue(); enQueue(4); Rear();
examples.output: true, true, true, false, 3, true, true, true, 4
examples.explanation: Queue of size 3 fills up with 1,2,3. enQueue(4) fails (full). After deQueue, enQueue(4) succeeds and Rear() is 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a vector with head and tail indices, shifting elements on dequeue to keep head at index 0. This makes dequeue O(n) but is simple to implement.

optimal.explanation: Use a fixed-size array with head and tail pointers that wrap around using modular arithmetic. All operations become O(1).

problems.title: Maximum Frequency Stack
problems.description: Design a stack-like data structure to push elements to the stack and pop the most frequent element from the stack. Implement FreqStack with push(val) that pushes an integer onto the stack, and pop() that removes and returns the most frequent element. If there is a tie, the element closest to the top of the stack is removed.

examples.input: FreqStack fs; push(5); push(7); push(5); push(7); push(4); push(5); pop(); pop(); pop(); pop();
examples.explanation: 5 appears 3 times, 7 appears 2 times. pop() returns 5, then 7 (now tied frequency), then 5, then 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Maintain a list of all elements in order. On pop, scan all to find max frequency, then among those find the most recently pushed. O(n) per pop.

optimal.explanation: Use a frequency map and a group map (frequency -> stack of elements at that frequency). Track maxFreq. Push: update freq and group. Pop: pop from group[maxFreq] and update. O(1) per operation.

problems.title: Simplify Path
problems.description: Given a string path, which is an absolute path (starting with '/') to a file or directory in a Unix-style file system, convert it to the simplified canonical path. The canonical path must start with '/', not end with '/', and have no double slashes or '.' or '..' components except resolved ones.

examples.explanation: Double slash and trailing slash are removed. The canonical path is /home/foo.

bruteForce.explanation: Split the path by '/', process each component by simulating directory traversal with a list (go back on '..', stay on '.', push otherwise), then join. This is essentially the optimal approach.

optimal.explanation: Use a stack to process path components: split by '/', skip empty and '.', pop on '..', push otherwise. Join stack contents with '/' for the result.

problems.title: Remove K Digits
problems.description: Given string num representing a non-negative integer and an integer k, return the smallest possible integer after removing k digits from num. The result should not have leading zeros. If the result is empty, return '0'. 1 <= k <= num.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Remove digits 4, 3, and 2 to get 1219, which is the smallest possible.

bruteForce.explanation: For each removal, scan the number and remove the first digit that is greater than the next digit (or the last digit if monotone). Repeat k times. O(k*n) time.

optimal.explanation: Use a monotonic increasing stack: greedily remove larger digits before smaller ones. Pop from stack when current digit is smaller and k > 0. Build result from stack.

problems.title: 132 Pattern Detection
problems.description: Given an array of n integers nums, determine if there exist indices i < j < k such that nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]. This is the 132 pattern. Return true if such a pattern exists, otherwise false. Use an approach based on tracking prefix minimums for an efficient solution.

examples.explanation: No 132 pattern exists since the array is strictly increasing.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all pairs (j, k) with j < k where nums[j] > nums[k], then check if there exists any i < j where nums[i] < nums[k]. This uses a prefix minimum array and is O(n^2).

optimal.explanation: Scan from right to left with a monotonic stack. Keep track of the best 'k' candidate (third = largest popped value). If nums[i] < third at any point, the pattern exists.

problems.title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the inorder traversal of its nodes' values. Inorder traversal visits nodes in the order: left subtree, root, right subtree. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: Inorder traversal visits left, then root, then right. Node 1 has no left child, so we visit 1, then go right to 2, but 2 has left child 3, so we visit 3 then 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive DFS: recursively traverse the left subtree, then visit the current node, then recursively traverse the right subtree, collecting values in a result vector.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative approach with an explicit stack to simulate the recursion, achieving the same O(n) time but avoiding function call overhead and stack overflow risk on deep trees.

problems.title: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the preorder traversal of its nodes' values. Preorder traversal visits nodes in the order: root, left subtree, right subtree. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: Preorder visits root first (1), then left subtree (none), then right subtree: visits 2, then 2's left child 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive DFS: visit the current node first, then recursively traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative approach with an explicit stack, pushing right child before left child so left is processed first, eliminating recursion overhead.

problems.title: Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the postorder traversal of its nodes' values. Postorder traversal visits nodes in the order: left subtree, right subtree, root. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: Postorder visits left subtree first (none for node 1), then right subtree: 3 then 2, then finally root 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive DFS: recursively traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the current node.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative approach: push root, push left before right, collect in reverse order (like a reverse preorder), then reverse the result at the end.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, level by level). The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Level 0 has node 3, level 1 has nodes 9 and 20, level 2 has nodes 15 and 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS with a level parameter to insert each node's value into the correct index of the result 2D vector, traversing the entire tree recursively.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS with a queue, processing nodes level by level: for each level, record the current queue size, process exactly that many nodes, and enqueue their children.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: The longest path is 3 -> 20 -> 15 (or 3 -> 20 -> 7), which has 3 nodes.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively compute the maximum depth: the depth of an empty tree is 0, and the depth of a non-empty tree is 1 plus the maximum of the depths of its left and right subtrees.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative BFS with a queue, counting the number of levels processed — each level corresponds to one unit of depth, avoiding recursion stack overhead.

problems.title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.description: Given a binary tree, find its minimum depth. The minimum depth is the number of nodes along the shortest path from the root node down to the nearest leaf node. Note that a leaf node has no children. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^5] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The shortest path to a leaf is 3 -> 9 (node 9 is a leaf), which has depth 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: if a node has only one child, return 1 plus the depth of that child (not 0 for the missing child), and if it has two children, return 1 plus the minimum of both subtree depths.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS: the first leaf node encountered during BFS is at the minimum depth, so we can stop early without visiting all nodes.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree (mirror it), and return its root. Inverting means swapping the left and right children of every node in the tree. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: Every node's left and right children are swapped: root's children become 7,2 instead of 2,7, and this is applied recursively.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: for each node, swap its left and right children, then recursively invert both subtrees.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative BFS with a queue to swap children of each node level by level, avoiding recursion stack usage for very deep trees.

problems.title: Symmetric Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (i.e., symmetric around its center). A tree is symmetric if the left subtree is a mirror image of the right subtree. The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: The tree is symmetric: the left subtree [2,3,4] mirrors the right subtree [2,4,3].

bruteForce.explanation: Use a recursive helper that checks if two subtrees are mirrors of each other: they must have the same root value, with one's left matching the other's right and vice versa.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative approach with a queue storing pairs of nodes to compare, avoiding recursion stack by processing node pairs level by level.

problems.title: Path Sum
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals targetSum. A leaf is a node with no children. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The path 5 -> 4 -> 11 -> 2 sums to 22.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS recursion: subtract the current node's value from targetSum, and if we reach a leaf node with remaining sum equal to 0, we found the path.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative DFS with a stack of (node, remaining sum) pairs, which eliminates recursion overhead and has the same asymptotic complexity but avoids call stack depth issues.

problems.title: Path Sum II
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values in the path equals targetSum. Each path should be returned as a list of node values. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS backtracking: maintain a current path and subtract values as we go deeper; when we reach a leaf with remaining sum 0, add the current path to results.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative DFS with a stack storing (node, remaining sum, current path), which avoids deep recursion and collects all valid root-to-leaf paths efficiently.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.description: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes has an edge between them. The path must contain at least one node and does not need to pass through the root. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum. The number of nodes is in the range [1, 3*10^4] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The optimal path is 15 -> 20 -> 7 with sum 42.

bruteForce.explanation: For every node, compute the max path sum passing through that node by considering all root-to-leaf paths through it, leading to an O(n^2) solution due to repeated subproblem computation.

optimal.explanation: Use a single DFS pass: for each node, compute the max gain from left and right subtrees, update global max with the path through the current node, and return the max one-sided gain to the parent.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.description: Given a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes p and q. The LCA is defined as the lowest node that has both p and q as descendants (where a node is a descendant of itself). All node values are unique and both p and q will exist in the tree.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is the LCA of nodes 5 and 1 since 5 is in the left subtree and 1 is in the right subtree of 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Find the path from root to p and from root to q, then compare paths to find the last common node — this requires two DFS traversals and extra storage.

optimal.explanation: Use a single DFS: if the current node is p or q, return it; otherwise combine results from left and right subtrees — if both are non-null, the current node is the LCA.

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problems.description: Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree. Serialization converts a tree to a string, and deserialization reconstructs the tree from the string. There is no restriction on how your serialization/deserialization algorithm should work. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The tree is serialized to a string like '1,2,3,null,null,4,5' and deserialized back to the original tree structure.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS level-order traversal for serialization, encoding null nodes explicitly, and rebuild the tree by reading nodes level by level during deserialization.

optimal.explanation: Use preorder DFS for serialization with null markers; during deserialization, use an index pointer or stringstream to reconstruct the tree in O(n) time with less overhead than BFS.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
problems.description: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder where preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree. All values in the arrays are unique and 1 <= preorder.length <= 3000.

examples.explanation: The root is 3 (first element of preorder). In inorder, 9 is left of 3, and [15,20,7] is right of 3. This determines the tree structure recursively.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively: the first element of preorder is the root; find it in inorder to split into left and right subtrees; rebuild each subtree recursively with linear search each time.

optimal.explanation: Use a hash map to store inorder indices for O(1) lookup, reducing the overall time complexity from O(n^2) to O(n).

problems.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, flatten the tree into a linked list in-place. The linked list should use the same TreeNode class where the right child pointer points to the next node in the list and the left child pointer is always null. The nodes should be in the same order as a preorder traversal. The number of nodes is in [0, 2000] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: The tree is flattened following preorder: 1,2,3,4,5,6 connected via right pointers with all left pointers set to null.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all nodes in preorder traversal into a list, then rewire the nodes so each node's right points to the next and left is null.

optimal.explanation: Use Morris-like traversal: for each node with a left child, find the rightmost node in the left subtree, attach the current right subtree there, then move the left subtree to the right — O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the right side of it and return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom. You can see the rightmost node at each level. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: From the right side: level 0 shows 1, level 1 shows 3 (rightmost), level 2 shows 4 (rightmost).

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS, traversing right subtree before left; for each depth, only record the first node seen (which will be the rightmost due to right-first traversal).

optimal.explanation: Use BFS level-order traversal and record only the last node of each level, which directly corresponds to the right side view without any extra bookkeeping.

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter is the length of the longest path between any two nodes, measured in number of edges. The path may or may not pass through the root. The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: The longest path is [4,2,1,3] or [5,2,1,3] with length 3 edges.

bruteForce.explanation: For every node, compute the height of left and right subtrees separately, and track the maximum sum of those heights; this runs O(n^2) due to recomputing heights.

optimal.explanation: Combine height computation and diameter update in a single DFS: each node returns its height while updating the global maximum diameter, achieving O(n) time.

problems.title: Balanced Binary Tree
problems.description: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than 1. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000] and -10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The left subtree has height 1 and right subtree has height 2; difference is 1, so it's balanced.

bruteForce.explanation: For every node, compute the height of its left and right subtrees and check if their difference exceeds 1; recurse on both children — O(n^2) due to redundant height computations.

optimal.explanation: Use a single DFS that returns -1 if a subtree is unbalanced or its height otherwise, propagating the unbalanced flag up without recomputing heights.

problems.title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
problems.description: Given the root of a complete binary tree, return the number of nodes in the tree. In a complete binary tree, every level except possibly the last is completely filled, and all nodes in the last level are as far left as possible. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5*10^4].

examples.explanation: The tree has 6 nodes. The last level has nodes 4, 5, 6 which are as far left as possible.

bruteForce.explanation: Simply traverse all nodes using DFS or BFS and count them, ignoring the complete binary tree property.

optimal.explanation: Exploit the complete binary tree property: compute left height and right height by going leftmost and rightmost; if equal, subtree is perfect (2^h - 1 nodes); otherwise recurse on children, achieving O(log^2 n) time.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal II
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the bottom-up level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, level by level from leaf to root). The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000] and -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Level order from bottom: leaf level [15,7], then [9,20], then root [3].

bruteForce.explanation: Perform standard level-order traversal collecting each level, then reverse the entire result array at the end.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS but insert each level at the front of the result using a deque or by front-inserting, avoiding the final reverse step for slightly cleaner logic.

problems.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the zigzag level order traversal of its nodes' values, i.e., from left to right then right to left for the next level, alternating. The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000] and -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: Level 0: left to right [3]. Level 1: right to left [20,9]. Level 2: left to right [15,7].

bruteForce.explanation: Perform standard BFS level order, then reverse every odd-indexed level in the result array.

optimal.explanation: Use a deque for each level: for left-to-right levels push to back, for right-to-left push to front — no reversal needed at the end of each level.

problems.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
problems.description: You are given a binary tree containing digits from 0 to 9 only. Each root-to-leaf path represents a number. For example, the path 1->2->3 represents the number 123. Return the total sum of all root-to-leaf numbers. The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000] and 0 <= Node.val <= 9.

examples.explanation: The path 1->2 represents 12 and 1->3 represents 13. Sum = 12 + 13 = 25.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS with backtracking, building each root-to-leaf number as a string, converting it to an integer at leaf nodes and summing them all up.

optimal.explanation: Use DFS passing the current accumulated number as an integer (multiply by 10 and add digit), avoiding string operations and achieving the same O(n) time with less overhead.

problems.title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum width of the given tree. The width of one level is defined as the length between the end-nodes (the leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes), where null nodes between the end-nodes that would be present in a complete binary tree are also counted. The number of nodes is in [1, 3000] and 0 <= Node.val <= 100.

examples.explanation: The third level has nodes 5, 3, null, 9. The width is 4 (from index 0 to index 3 in a 0-indexed complete tree).

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS, assigning position indices (left child = 2*pos, right child = 2*pos+1) and recording the min and max positions per level to compute width.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS with (node, index) pairs; normalize each level by subtracting the leftmost index to prevent integer overflow, then compute width as last index minus first index plus 1.

problems.title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, a target node, and an integer k, return an array of the values of all nodes that have a distance k from the target node. The answer can be returned in any order. All node values are unique and the number of nodes is in [1, 500].

examples.explanation: Nodes 7 and 4 are distance 2 from target 5 going down; node 1 is distance 2 going up through node 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Build a graph by treating the binary tree as an undirected graph (each edge bidirectional), then run BFS from the target node to find all nodes at exactly distance k.

optimal.explanation: Use DFS to annotate each node with parent pointers, then BFS from the target node using parent pointers to traverse upward as well as downward, all in O(n) time and space.

problems.title: Binary Tree Cameras
problems.description: You are given the root of a binary tree. We install cameras on the tree nodes where each camera at a node can monitor its parent, itself, and its children. Return the minimum number of cameras needed to monitor all nodes of the tree. The number of nodes is in [1, 1000] and Node.val is always 0.

examples.explanation: One camera placed at node index 1 (the middle node) can cover nodes 0, 1, 3, and 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible camera placements using a bitmask over all nodes, and check for each placement whether all nodes are covered, taking the minimum count — exponential in the number of nodes.

optimal.explanation: Use greedy DFS with states (0=not covered, 1=covered no camera, 2=has camera): greedily place cameras at leaf parents first (bottom-up), minimizing camera count.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A valid BST is defined as follows: the left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key, the right subtree contains only nodes with keys greater than the node's key, and both subtrees must also be valid BSTs. Node values are in the range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].

examples.explanation: Node 1 is less than 2 (left child) and node 3 is greater than 2 (right child), so it is a valid BST.

bruteForce.explanation: Perform an inorder traversal and collect all values into a list, then check if the list is strictly increasing. This works because inorder traversal of a BST yields sorted values.

optimal.explanation: Use recursive DFS passing valid min/max bounds for each node, which avoids storing all values and validates in a single pass.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.description: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the kth smallest value (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree. The number of nodes in the tree is n, and 1 <= k <= n <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The inorder traversal gives [1,2,3,4], so the 1st smallest element is 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values via inorder traversal into a sorted array, then return the element at index k-1.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative inorder traversal with a stack, stopping early as soon as we reach the kth element, saving time on large trees.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
problems.description: Given a binary search tree (BST), find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes p and q. The LCA is defined as the lowest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants (where we allow a node to be a descendant of itself). All node values are unique and both p and q will exist in the BST.

examples.explanation: The LCA of nodes 2 and 8 is 6 since 6 is the first node that splits the path to 2 and 8.

bruteForce.explanation: Find the path from root to p and from root to q, then find the last common node in both paths. This does not leverage BST properties.

optimal.explanation: Leverage BST property: if both p and q are smaller than current node go left, if both larger go right, otherwise current node is the LCA. This runs in O(h) time.

problems.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
problems.description: Given an integer array nums where the elements are sorted in ascending order, convert it to a height-balanced binary search tree. A height-balanced binary tree is one where the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than one. The length of nums is between 1 and 10^4.

examples.explanation: The middle element 0 becomes the root, making the BST height-balanced.

bruteForce.explanation: Insert elements one by one into a BST in sorted order, which creates a degenerate (skewed) tree requiring rebalancing afterward.

optimal.explanation: Recursively pick the middle element as root so both halves become left and right subtrees, guaranteeing height balance in O(n) time.

problems.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
problems.description: Implement the BSTIterator class that represents an iterator over the in-order traversal of a BST. next() returns the next smallest number and hasNext() returns whether there is a next number. Both operations should run in average O(1) time and use O(h) space, where h is the height of the tree.

examples.input: BSTIterator([7,3,15,null,null,9,20]), next(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext()
examples.explanation: Inorder traversal yields 3,7,9,15,20 and hasNext is true until exhausted.

bruteForce.explanation: Precompute the entire inorder traversal into a list and use a pointer to iterate, using O(n) space.

optimal.explanation: Use an explicit stack to simulate inorder traversal lazily, maintaining only the nodes on the path to the next smallest — O(h) space.

problems.title: Delete Node in a BST
problems.description: Given a root node reference of a BST and a key, delete the node with the given key in the BST and return the updated root. The number of nodes in the tree is in [0, 10^4], and all node values are unique. Guarantee the key may or may not exist in the BST.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is deleted and replaced by its inorder successor 4, maintaining BST property.

bruteForce.explanation: Convert the BST to a sorted array, remove the key, then rebuild the BST from scratch — O(n) time but with high constant factor.

optimal.explanation: Recursively find the node; if it has two children replace its value with the inorder successor then delete the successor from the right subtree.

problems.title: Insert into a BST
problems.description: Given the root node of a BST and a value to insert, insert the value into the BST and return the root. The value does not exist in the original BST. The number of nodes is between 0 and 10^4, and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: 5 is greater than 4 so we go right, less than 7 so we insert as 7's left child.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all values, add the new one, sort the array, then rebuild a balanced BST from scratch — far more work than needed.

optimal.explanation: Traverse the BST iteratively (or recursively) comparing the value at each node to find the correct leaf position and insert there in O(h) time.

problems.title: Search in a BST
problems.description: Given the root node of a BST and an integer val, find the node in the BST where the node's value equals val and return the subtree rooted at that node. If no such node exists, return null. The number of nodes is in [1, 5000] and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: Node with value 2 is found and its subtree [2,1,3] is returned.

bruteForce.explanation: Do a full BFS or DFS over all nodes and return the one whose value matches — does not use BST properties.

optimal.explanation: Use BST property to eliminate half the tree at each step: go left if val is smaller, right if larger, achieving O(h) time.

problems.title: Two Sum IV Input is a BST
problems.description: Given the root of a BST and an integer k, return true if there exist two elements in the BST such that their sum is equal to k. The number of nodes is in [1, 10^4], node values are in [-10^4, 10^4], and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: 3 + 6 = 9, so the answer is true.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all node values into a list and use a nested loop to check every pair for the target sum.

optimal.explanation: Use a hash set to store visited values during DFS; for each node check if k minus the current value is already in the set, giving O(n) time.

problems.title: Range Sum of BST
problems.description: Given the root node of a BST and two integers low and high, return the sum of values of all nodes with a value in the inclusive range [low, high]. The number of nodes is in [1, 2*10^4] and all node values are unique.

examples.explanation: Nodes 7, 10, and 15 are within [7,15] and their sum is 32.

bruteForce.explanation: Traverse every node in the tree and add its value to the sum if it falls within the range, visiting all nodes regardless of BST property.

optimal.explanation: Use BST property to prune subtrees: skip the left subtree if current value <= low, skip right subtree if current value >= high, reducing unnecessary work.

problems.title: Unique Binary Search Trees
problems.description: Given an integer n, return the number of structurally unique BSTs which have exactly n nodes of unique values from 1 to n. These are the Catalan numbers. The input n is in [1, 19].

examples.explanation: There are 5 structurally unique BSTs with values 1,2,3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive computation: for each possible root i from 1 to n, the count is the product of counts for left subtree (1..i-1) and right subtree (i+1..n), with exponential overlapping subproblems.

optimal.explanation: Use dynamic programming to compute the nth Catalan number: dp[i] = sum of dp[j-1]*dp[i-j] for j in 1..i, filling the table bottom-up in O(n^2).

problems.title: Unique Binary Search Trees II
problems.description: Given an integer n, return all the structurally unique BSTs which have exactly n nodes of unique values from 1 to n. Return the answer in any order. The input n is in [1, 8].

examples.explanation: All 5 structurally unique BSTs with nodes 1,2,3 are returned.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of 1..n, build a BST from each permutation, and collect unique structures — extremely slow due to n! permutations.

optimal.explanation: Use memoization with a map keyed on (lo,hi) to cache and reuse previously generated subtrees, avoiding redundant tree construction.

problems.title: Recover Binary Search Tree
problems.description: You are given the root of a BST where exactly two nodes were swapped by mistake. Recover the tree without changing its structure. The number of nodes is in [2, 1000] and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: 3 and 1 are swapped; after recovery the BST property is restored.

bruteForce.explanation: Do inorder traversal and collect all values, find the two misplaced values, then do another inorder traversal and swap them back — O(n) space.

optimal.explanation: Use Morris traversal to do inorder traversal with O(1) extra space while tracking the two swapped nodes via a previous pointer.

problems.title: Convert BST to Greater Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a Binary Search Tree (BST), convert it to a Greater Sum Tree where every key is replaced by the sum of all keys greater than or equal to it. The number of nodes is in [0, 10^4] and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: Each node value is replaced by the sum of all BST values greater than or equal to it.

bruteForce.explanation: Collect all values, compute prefix sums from right, then traverse the tree and update each node by looking up the precomputed sum.

optimal.explanation: Perform reverse inorder traversal (right-root-left) keeping a running cumulative sum, updating each node in place — O(n) time and O(h) space.

problems.title: Construct Binary Search Tree from Preorder Traversal
problems.description: Given an array of integers preorder, which represents the preorder traversal of a BST, construct the BST and return its root. It is guaranteed that there is always possible to find a binary search tree with the given requirements for the given test cases. The length of preorder is in [1, 100].

examples.explanation: 8 is the root; values less than 8 go left (5,1,7) and greater go right (10,12).

bruteForce.explanation: Insert each element of the preorder array into a BST one by one, which produces the correct BST in O(n^2) worst-case time.

optimal.explanation: Use a recursive approach with an upper bound: the first element is the root; partition remaining elements using the bound and recurse, achieving O(n log n) with monotonic stack giving O(n).

problems.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, calculate the vertical order traversal. For each node at position (row, col), its left child is at (row+1, col-1) and right child at (row+1, col+1). Nodes in the same position are sorted by value. Return the vertical order traversal as a list of lists from leftmost to rightmost column.

examples.explanation: Columns from left to right: col=-1 has [9], col=0 has [3,15], col=1 has [20], col=2 has [7].

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS with (node, row, col) tuples, collect all entries, sort globally by (col, row, val), then group by column — O(n log n) due to sorting.

optimal.explanation: Use DFS to collect (col, row, val) tuples, then sort once using a single comparator — same asymptotic complexity but avoids BFS queue overhead and is cleaner.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
problems.description: Given two integer arrays inorder and postorder where inorder is the inorder traversal of a binary tree and postorder is the postorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree. The length of both arrays is in [1, 3000] and all values are unique.

examples.explanation: Last element of postorder (3) is root; split inorder around 3 to get left and right subtrees recursively.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively identify the root as the last postorder element and find its position in inorder with a linear scan, giving O(n^2) due to repeated scanning.

optimal.explanation: Build a hash map from value to inorder index for O(1) lookup, reducing the overall complexity to O(n) for the construction.

problems.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node
problems.description: You are given a perfect binary tree where all leaves are on the same level and every parent has two children. Populate each next pointer to point to its next right node. If there is no next right node, the next pointer should be set to NULL. The tree has at most 2^12 - 1 nodes.

examples.explanation: Each node's next pointer is connected to its right neighbor at the same level.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS level-order traversal, and for each level connect consecutive nodes via their next pointers — O(n) time but O(n) space for the queue.

optimal.explanation: Use O(1) space by leveraging the already-set next pointers of the current level to traverse and set the next level's pointers.

problems.title: Binary Tree Pruning
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the same tree where every subtree not containing a 1 has been removed. A subtree of a node is that node plus every node that is a descendant. The number of nodes is in [1, 200] and each value is 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: The subtree rooted at the left child of 0 contains only zeros and is pruned.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly scan the tree and prune leaf nodes with value 0 until no more pruning is possible — O(n^2) due to multiple passes.

optimal.explanation: Single postorder traversal: prune children first, then return null for the current node if it has no children and value is 0 — O(n) time.

problems.title: Cousins in Binary Tree
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree with unique values and the values of two different nodes x and y, return true if the nodes corresponding to x and y are cousins. Two nodes are cousins if they have the same depth with different parents. The number of nodes is in [2, 100].

examples.explanation: 4 is at depth 2 with parent 2, and 3 is at depth 1 with parent 1 — different depths so not cousins.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS to find depth and parent of both x and y separately in two passes, then compare — O(n) but with two traversals.

optimal.explanation: Single BFS pass tracking parent and depth for each node, stopping early once both nodes are found — O(n) but with early termination.

problems.title: Sum of Left Leaves
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the sum of all left leaves. A left leaf is a leaf node that is the left child of its parent. The number of nodes is in [1, 1000] and node values are in [-1000, 1000].

examples.explanation: There are two left leaves: 9 and 15, with sum 9 + 15 = 24.

bruteForce.explanation: Do a full DFS collecting all leaves and checking whether each is a left child by tracking parent and direction — correct but verbose.

optimal.explanation: Check from the parent: if the left child exists and is a leaf, add its value; otherwise recurse into both children — clean and O(n) with O(h) stack space.

problems.title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the leftmost value in the last row (bottom row) of the tree. The number of nodes is in [1, 10^4] and node values are in [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].

examples.explanation: The bottom row has values [1,3] and the leftmost value is 1.

bruteForce.explanation: DFS tracking the current depth; update the result whenever we reach a new maximum depth (taking the first — leftmost — node at that depth).

optimal.explanation: BFS right-to-left level order traversal: the last node visited is the leftmost node at the deepest level — O(n) with clean logic.

problems.title: Path Sum III
problems.description: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return the number of paths where the sum of the values along the path equals targetSum. The path does not need to start or end at the root or a leaf, but it must go downwards. The number of nodes is in [0, 1000] and values are in [-10^9, 10^9].

examples.explanation: There are 3 paths that sum to 8: 5->3, 5->2->1, and -3->11.

bruteForce.explanation: For every node, start a DFS counting paths that sum to targetSum; then recurse to children — O(n^2) due to nested traversals.

optimal.explanation: Use prefix sum with a hash map: for each node compute the running sum and check how many previous prefix sums differ by targetSum — O(n) time.

problems.title: House Robber III
problems.description: The thief has found himself a new place for his thievery and it is a binary tree of houses. Each house has a certain amount of money. Adjacent houses (connected directly) cannot both be robbed. Given the root of the binary tree, return the maximum amount of money the thief can rob without alerting the police. The number of nodes is in [1, 10^4].

examples.explanation: Rob nodes 3 (root), 3 (right of 2), and 1 for total 3+3+1=7.

bruteForce.explanation: For each node recursively compute the max by trying both rob (skip children) and don't-rob options, with exponential overlapping subproblems.

optimal.explanation: Return a pair {rob, skip} from each node in a single DFS postorder, avoiding recomputation — O(n) time.

problems.title: Distribute Coins in Binary Tree
problems.description: You are given the root of a binary tree with n nodes where each node has node.val coins. There are n coins total. In one move, we may choose two adjacent nodes and move one coin between them. Return the minimum number of moves to make every node have exactly one coin. The number of nodes is in [1, 100] and node values are in [0, 100].

examples.explanation: From the root with 3 coins, move one coin to each child, requiring 2 moves.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate coin distribution by repeatedly moving coins along edges until every node has exactly one — O(n * max_coins) moves in the worst case.

optimal.explanation: Postorder DFS: each node returns its excess coins (val - 1 + left excess + right excess); the number of moves equals the sum of absolute excesses flowing through each edge — O(n) and O(h) space.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.description: Design a class to find the kth largest element in a stream. Note that it is the kth largest element in the sorted order, not the kth distinct element. Implement KthLargest class with constructor taking k and an initial array, and an add method that adds a new value and returns the kth largest. Constraints: 1 <= k <= 10^4, 0 <= nums.length <= 10^4, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: After adding 3 the 3rd largest is 4; after adding 5 it becomes 5; after adding 10 it stays 5; after adding 9 it becomes 8; after adding 4 it stays 8.

bruteForce.explanation: Store all elements in a sorted list. On each add, insert the element maintaining sorted order and return the kth element from the end.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n log n) per add due to insertion

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap of size k. The top of the heap is always the kth largest element. On each add, push the value and pop if size exceeds k.

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.description: Design a data structure that supports adding numbers from a data stream and finding the median of all elements so far. Implement MedianFinder with addNum(int num) and findMedian() methods. The median is the middle value in a sorted list; if even count, it is the average of the two middle values. Constraints: -10^5 <= num <= 10^5, at most 5*10^4 calls to addNum and findMedian.

examples.explanation: After [1,2] the median is (1+2)/2 = 1.5; after [1,2,3] the median is 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Store all numbers in a vector. On each findMedian call, sort the vector and return the middle element or average of two middle elements.

optimal.explanation: Use two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, keeping them balanced so the median can be retrieved in O(1).
optimal.timeComplexity: O(log n) per addNum, O(1) per findMedian

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.description: Given an array of points where points[i] = [xi, yi] represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer k, return the k closest points to the origin (0, 0). The distance is the Euclidean distance. You may return the answer in any order. Constraints: 1 <= k <= points.length <= 10^4, -10^4 <= xi, yi <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Distance of (1,3) is sqrt(10); distance of (-2,2) is sqrt(8). So (-2,2) is closer.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort all points by their squared distance from the origin, then return the first k points.

optimal.explanation: Use a max-heap of size k. Iterate through all points; if a point is closer than the heap's top, replace it. The heap holds the k closest points.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.description: Given a list of tasks CPU needs to do, with a cooldown interval n between two same tasks, find the minimum number of intervals the CPU will take to finish all tasks. The CPU can be idle between tasks if needed. Constraints: 1 <= tasks.length <= 10^4, tasks[i] is uppercase English letter, 0 <= n <= 100.

examples.explanation: A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B. Total 8 intervals.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate the scheduling process using a priority queue to always pick the most frequent available task, tracking cooldown with a queue.

optimal.explanation: Use the math formula: result = max(tasks.length, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countOfMaxFreq). This avoids simulation entirely.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.description: Given an array of strings words and an integer k, return the k most frequent words. Return the answer sorted by frequency from highest to lowest. Sort words with the same frequency by their lexicographical order. Constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 500, 1 <= words[i].length <= 10, words[i] consists of lowercase English letters, 1 <= k <= unique words count.

examples.explanation: "i" appears 2 times, "love" appears 2 times, both more than other words. "i" comes before "love" lexicographically.

bruteForce.explanation: Count frequencies using a map, then sort words by frequency descending and lexicographic order ascending, return first k.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap of size k with a custom comparator. This avoids sorting all elements and only maintains k elements in the heap.

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
problems.description: You have an array of stones where stones[i] is the weight of the ith stone. Each turn, smash the two heaviest stones. If they are equal, both are destroyed; otherwise the heavier one remains with weight difference. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain. Constraints: 1 <= stones.length <= 30, 1 <= stones[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Smash 8 and 7 -> 1. Stones: [2,4,1,1,1]. Smash 4 and 2 -> 2. Stones: [2,1,1,1]. Smash 2 and 1 -> 1. Stones: [1,1,1]. Smash 1 and 1. Stones: [1]. Answer is 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the array each iteration, pick the two largest, compute difference, and repeat until at most one stone remains.

optimal.explanation: Use a max-heap to efficiently always access the two largest stones in O(log n) per operation.

problems.title: Ugly Number II
problems.description: An ugly number is a positive integer whose prime factors are limited to 2, 3, and 5. Given an integer n, return the nth ugly number. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1690.
