examples.explanation: The first 10 ugly numbers are [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12], so the 10th is 12.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate through all positive integers and check if each is an ugly number by dividing by 2, 3, and 5 until the result is 1. Count until nth.

optimal.explanation: Use dynamic programming with three pointers (p2, p3, p5). Generate ugly numbers in order by picking the minimum of dp[p2]*2, dp[p3]*3, dp[p5]*5.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
problems.description: Given an n x n matrix where each row and column is sorted in ascending order, return the kth smallest element in the matrix. Note that it is the kth smallest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element. Constraints: n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length, 1 <= n <= 300, -10^9 <= matrix[i][j] <= 10^9, 1 <= k <= n^2.

examples.explanation: The sorted list is [1,5,9,10,11,12,13,13,15], and the 8th element is 13.

bruteForce.explanation: Flatten the matrix into a single array, sort it, and return the element at index k-1.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap initialized with the first element of each row. Pop k-1 times, each time pushing the next element in the same row.

problems.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
problems.description: Given a string s, sort it in decreasing order based on the frequency of the characters. Return any valid sorted string where characters with higher frequency appear first. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^5, s consists of uppercase and lowercase English letters and digits.

examples.explanation: 'e' appears twice while 'r' and 't' appear once. "eetr" is also a valid answer.

bruteForce.explanation: Count frequency of each character, then sort characters by frequency in descending order, and build the result string.

optimal.explanation: Use bucket sort by frequency. Since max frequency is bounded by string length, create buckets for each frequency and fill from highest to lowest.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
problems.description: You have some number of sticks with positive integer lengths. You can connect any two sticks of lengths x and y into one stick by paying a cost of x + y. Return the minimum cost to connect all sticks into one stick. Constraints: 1 <= sticks.length <= 10^4, 1 <= sticks[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Connect 2+3=5 (cost 5). Connect 5+4=9 (cost 9). Total = 14.

bruteForce.explanation: Repeatedly find the two smallest sticks by sorting, combine them, and add the cost until one stick remains.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap (similar to Huffman coding). Always combine the two smallest sticks, add cost, and push the combined stick back. This greedy approach is optimal.

problems.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
problems.description: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 sorted in ascending order and an integer k, return the k pairs (u, v) with the smallest sums where u is from nums1 and v is from nums2. Return the pairs in any order. Constraints: 1 <= nums1.length, nums2.length <= 10^5, -10^9 <= nums1[i], nums2[i] <= 10^9, 1 <= k <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The first 3 pairs with smallest sums are (1+2)=3, (1+4)=5, (1+6)=7.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all possible pairs, sort by sum, and return the first k pairs.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap initialized with pairs (nums1[i], nums2[0]) for all i. Each time we pop a pair (i, j), push (i, j+1) if valid. This avoids generating all pairs.

problems.title: Super Ugly Number
problems.description: A super ugly number is a positive integer whose prime factors are in the given array primes. Given an integer n and an array of integers primes, return the nth super ugly number. The nth super ugly number is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, 1 <= primes.length <= 15, 2 <= primes[i] <= 100, all primes[i] are distinct primes.

examples.explanation: The first 12 super ugly numbers are [1,2,4,7,8,13,14,16,19,26,28,32].

bruteForce.explanation: Use a min-heap to generate super ugly numbers in order. Start with 1, then for each popped number multiply by all primes and push if not seen.

optimal.explanation: Use DP with k pointers (one per prime). Generate the next ugly number as the minimum of dp[ptr[i]] * primes[i] and advance all pointers that produced the minimum.

problems.title: IPO
problems.description: Given k projects to do, each with a profit and minimum capital requirement, and starting capital w, maximize capital after completing at most k projects. You can only start a project if you have enough capital. Constraints: 1 <= k <= 10^5, 0 <= w <= 10^9, n == profits.length == capital.length, 1 <= n <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Start project 0 (capital=0, profit=1), w becomes 1. Then start project 2 (capital=1, profit=3), w becomes 4.

bruteForce.explanation: For each of the k rounds, scan all available projects (those with capital <= w), pick the one with maximum profit, add it to w.

optimal.explanation: Sort projects by capital. Use a min-heap for capital and a max-heap for profits. For each round, push all affordable projects into the max-heap and pick the best profit.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(n log n + k log n)

problems.title: Furthest Building You Can Reach
problems.description: Given heights of buildings, bricks, and ladders, move from building to building. If the next building is taller, use bricks (difference) or one ladder. Return the furthest building index reachable. Constraints: 1 <= heights.length <= 10^5, 1 <= heights[i] <= 10^6, 0 <= bricks <= 10^9, 0 <= ladders <= heights.length.

examples.explanation: Going from 4 to 2: no cost. 2 to 7: use ladder. 7 to 6: no cost. 6 to 9: use 3 bricks. 9 to 14: need 5 bricks but only have 2, cannot proceed.

bruteForce.explanation: Try a greedy simulation: always use ladders for the largest jumps. Use a sorted structure to track which jumps had ladders and swap to bricks when possible.

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap to track ladder-assigned jumps. Assign ladders greedily to the largest jumps seen; when we exceed ladders, reassign the smallest ladder jump to bricks.

problems.title: Reorganize String
problems.description: Given a string s, rearrange its characters so that no two adjacent characters are the same. Return any valid rearrangement, or an empty string if not possible. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 500, s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Rearranging 'a', 'a', 'b' to 'aba' ensures no two adjacent characters are the same.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of the string and return the first one where no two adjacent characters are equal. This is exponential and impractical for large inputs.

optimal.explanation: Use a max-heap by frequency. Alternately pick the most frequent char and the second most frequent to build the result, ensuring no adjacent duplicates.

problems.title: Single Threaded CPU
problems.description: Given n tasks with enqueueTime[i] and processingTime[i], a single-threaded CPU picks the task with the smallest processing time (ties broken by index) from available tasks. Return the order in which tasks are processed. Constraints: tasks.length == n, 1 <= n <= 10^5, 1 <= enqueueTime[i], processingTime[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: At time 1, task 0 is available. Process task 0 (finishes at 3). At time 3, tasks 1,2 available. Pick task 2 (smaller processing). Finish at 5. At 5, tasks 1 and 3 available. Pick 3 (smaller processing). Finish at 6. Process task 1 last.

bruteForce.explanation: At each time step advance the clock to the next available task if CPU is idle, then scan all available tasks to pick the one with smallest processing time.

optimal.explanation: Sort tasks by enqueue time. Use a min-heap sorted by (processingTime, index) for available tasks. Advance clock when CPU is idle and no tasks are available.

problems.title: Design Twitter
problems.description: Design a simplified version of Twitter with postTweet, getNewsFeed (10 most recent tweets from user and followees), follow, and unfollow operations. Constraints: 1 <= userId, followerId, followeeId <= 500, 0 <= tweetId <= 10^4, all Twitter functions will be called with valid parameters, at most 3*10^4 calls.

examples.input: postTweet(1,5), getNewsFeed(1), follow(1,2), postTweet(2,6), getNewsFeed(1), unfollow(1,2), getNewsFeed(1)
examples.explanation: User 1 sees their own tweets and followees' tweets in the news feed.

bruteForce.explanation: Store all tweets in a list with timestamps. For getNewsFeed, collect all tweets from user and followees, sort by time descending, and return top 10.

optimal.explanation: Use a max-heap merging the most recent tweet from each relevant user's list, advancing pointers lazily. This avoids loading all tweets at once.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(k log k) per getNewsFeed where k is followees count

problems.title: Minimum Number of Refueling Stops
problems.description: A car starts at position 0 with startFuel liters of fuel. There are gas stations on the way, each with a position and fuel amount. The car can travel one mile per liter of fuel. Return the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach target, or -1 if impossible. Constraints: 1 <= target <= 10^9, 1 <= startFuel <= 10^9, 0 <= stations.length <= 500.

examples.explanation: Stop at station 0 (fuel = 10+60 = 70), drive to station 3 (fuel = 70-50 = 20), stop there (fuel = 20+40 = 60), reach target (fuel = 60-40 = 20).

bruteForce.explanation: Use DP where dp[i] is the furthest position reachable with exactly i stops. For each station, update dp values in reverse order.

optimal.explanation: Greedy with max-heap: drive as far as possible; when out of fuel, greedily refuel from the station with the most fuel seen so far using a max-heap.

problems.title: Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array
problems.description: Given an array of strings nums representing large integers and an integer k, return the kth largest integer as a string. Note that duplicate numbers should be counted distinctly. Constraints: 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^4, 1 <= nums[i].length <= 100, nums[i] consists of only digits without leading zeros.

examples.explanation: The integers in order from largest to smallest are 10, 7, 6, 3. The 4th largest is 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the strings using a custom comparator that compares numeric values (first by length, then lexicographically), then return the kth element.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n log n * L) where L is max string length

optimal.explanation: Use a min-heap of size k with the numeric string comparator. The heap top is always the kth largest, avoiding full sort.

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Half Array Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, in one operation you can halve any element of nums. Return the minimum number of operations to reduce the sum of nums by at least half. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^7.

examples.explanation: Initial sum = 33, target <= 16.5. Halve 19 -> 9.5 (sum=23.5). Halve 9.5 -> 4.75 (sum=18.75). Halve 8 -> 4 (sum=14.75 <= 16.5). 3 operations.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort in descending order and repeatedly halve the largest element. Recalculate the maximum each time and check if sum is halved.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n * ops) where ops can be O(n log maxVal)

optimal.explanation: Use a max-heap to always halve the largest element efficiently. Each halve operation takes O(log n) and we stop once sum is reduced by at least half.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(n log n + ops * log n)

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.description: Given an m x n 2D binary grid where '1' represents land and '0' represents water, return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.

examples.explanation: There are two islands: one formed by the top-left connected 1s, and one at the bottom-right.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate over each cell; when a '1' is found, use a recursive DFS to mark all connected land cells as visited, incrementing the island count each time.

optimal.explanation: Use Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) to union adjacent land cells, then count the number of distinct roots among all land cells, which avoids deep recursion stacks.

problems.title: Max Area of Island
problems.description: Given an m x n binary matrix grid where 0 represents water and 1 represents land, return the maximum area of an island in the grid. An island is a group of 1s connected 4-directionally. If there is no island, return 0.

examples.explanation: The largest island has 4 connected land cells.

bruteForce.explanation: For each unvisited land cell, perform a DFS to count the size of its island, tracking the maximum found so far.

optimal.explanation: Use an iterative BFS with a queue to explore each island and count its area, avoiding recursion stack overflow for large grids.

problems.title: Clone Graph
problems.description: Given a reference of a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy (clone) of the graph. Each node in the graph contains a value (int) and a list of its neighbors. The number of nodes ranges from 0 to 100.

examples.explanation: The cloned graph has the same structure and neighbor connections as the original.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS with a hash map to map original nodes to their clones; recursively clone neighbors while avoiding revisiting already-cloned nodes.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative BFS with a hash map to clone nodes level by level, which avoids recursion overhead and is more stack-safe for large graphs.

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.description: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. Given prerequisites pairs [a,b] meaning you must take course b before a, determine if it is possible to finish all courses. This reduces to detecting a cycle in a directed graph.

examples.explanation: Take course 0 first, then course 1. No cycle exists.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS with a visited/in-progress coloring scheme: for each unvisited node, explore via DFS and detect back edges (cycles) by checking if a neighbor is currently in the DFS stack.

optimal.explanation: Use Kahn's algorithm (topological sort via BFS): count in-degrees, process nodes with 0 in-degree, and check if all nodes are processed; if not, a cycle exists.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.description: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1 with prerequisite pairs. Return the ordering of courses to finish all of them, or an empty array if impossible. This is a topological sort problem on a directed graph.

examples.explanation: One valid ordering; course 0 first, then 1 and 2, then 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS-based topological sort: perform post-order DFS and push nodes to a stack after all their dependencies are processed, then reverse the stack.

optimal.explanation: Use Kahn's BFS-based topological sort: enqueue all zero-in-degree nodes and iteratively reduce in-degrees, collecting the ordering in BFS order.

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.description: Given an m x n matrix of heights, water can flow to adjacent cells with equal or lower height. Find all cells from which water can flow to both the Pacific ocean (top/left borders) and the Atlantic ocean (bottom/right borders).

examples.explanation: These cells can reach both oceans by flowing to equal or lower adjacent cells.

bruteForce.explanation: For each cell, run DFS/BFS to check if water can reach each ocean separately (by flowing to lower/equal neighbors), then collect cells reachable by both.

optimal.explanation: Reverse the flow: BFS/DFS from ocean borders inward (water flows uphill in reverse), finding all cells reachable from each ocean, then intersect the two sets.

problems.title: Surrounded Regions
problems.description: Given an m x n board of 'X' and 'O', capture all regions of 'O' that are surrounded by 'X' (not connected to any border 'O'). Flip all captured 'O's to 'X'. Regions connected to the border are not captured.

examples.explanation: The center 'O' is surrounded by 'X' on all sides and gets flipped.

bruteForce.explanation: For every 'O' cell, run a DFS to check if the connected region touches any border; if not, flip all cells in the region to 'X'.

optimal.explanation: Start DFS/BFS from all border 'O' cells, marking connected 'O's as safe (e.g., 'S'), then flip all remaining 'O's to 'X' and restore 'S' back to 'O' in one pass.

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.description: In a grid, 0 represents empty, 1 a fresh orange, and 2 a rotten orange. Each minute, any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh oranges remain, or -1 if impossible.

examples.explanation: The rot spreads outward from the initial rotten orange, taking 4 minutes to reach all fresh oranges.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate the process minute by minute: each pass over the grid marks newly rotten oranges, repeating until no changes occur or no fresh oranges remain.

optimal.explanation: Use multi-source BFS starting from all initially rotten oranges simultaneously, tracking elapsed time and fresh orange count for an O(m*n) solution.

problems.title: Walls and Gates
problems.description: You are given an m x n grid initialized with -1 (wall), 0 (gate), or INF (empty room). Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate. If impossible to reach a gate, leave as INF. INF = 2^31 - 1.

examples.explanation: Each room is filled with the shortest distance to the nearest gate.

bruteForce.explanation: For each empty room (INF), run BFS to find the nearest gate and update the distance; this results in O(m^2*n^2) total work.

optimal.explanation: Use multi-source BFS starting from all gates simultaneously; distances naturally propagate outward, filling each room with the minimum distance in one O(m*n) pass.

problems.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problems.description: Given n nodes (labeled 0 to n-1) and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components in the graph. Each node is connected if there exists a path between them.

examples.explanation: Components are {0,1,2} and {3,4}, so there are 2 connected components.

bruteForce.explanation: Build adjacency list, then use DFS from each unvisited node to mark all reachable nodes, counting the number of DFS calls initiated.

optimal.explanation: Use Union-Find: initialize n components, union connected nodes, decrement component count on each successful union, returning the final count in nearly O(V+E) time.

problems.title: Graph Valid Tree
problems.description: Given n nodes (0 to n-1) and a list of undirected edges, determine if these edges make up a valid tree. A valid tree must be connected and have exactly n-1 edges with no cycles.

examples.explanation: The graph is connected with 4 edges and no cycles, forming a valid tree.

bruteForce.explanation: Check if there are exactly n-1 edges, then verify the graph is fully connected using DFS from node 0, checking all nodes are visited.

optimal.explanation: Use Union-Find: a valid tree has exactly n-1 edges and no cycle; union each edge and return false if a union fails (cycle detected), otherwise check edge count.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.description: Given a tree with n nodes that has one extra edge added (making it a graph with a cycle), find and return the redundant edge that can be removed to restore the tree. If multiple answers exist, return the last one in the input.

examples.explanation: Removing edge [2,3] restores the tree structure.

bruteForce.explanation: Try removing each edge one at a time and check if the remaining graph is a valid tree (connected, n-1 edges, no cycle); return the last valid removal.

optimal.explanation: Process edges with Union-Find; the first edge whose two endpoints already share the same root is the redundant connection forming the cycle.

problems.title: Find the Town Judge
problems.description: In a town of n people, the town judge trusts nobody and is trusted by everyone else. Given a list of trust pairs [a,b] meaning a trusts b, find and return the judge's label, or -1 if no judge exists.

examples.explanation: Person 3 is trusted by persons 1 and 2 and trusts nobody, making them the judge.

bruteForce.explanation: For each person, check if they trust nobody and are trusted by all n-1 others by scanning the trust list; O(n * trust.size()) overall.

optimal.explanation: Track in-degree (trusted by) and out-degree (trusts) for each person; the judge has out-degree 0 and in-degree n-1, findable in O(n + T).

problems.title: Evaluate Division
problems.description: Given equations like A/B = k and a list of queries, return the answers to each query or -1.0 if it cannot be determined. Build a weighted graph where each edge represents a division relationship and use BFS/DFS to answer queries.

bruteForce.explanation: For each query, perform a DFS on the weighted graph from source to target, multiplying edge weights along the path to compute the result.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS for each query to find the weighted path in the graph; BFS ensures shortest path and the same time complexity but is iterative and avoids recursion overhead.

problems.title: Number of Provinces
problems.description: Given an n x n adjacency matrix isConnected where isConnected[i][j]=1 if cities i and j are directly connected, return the total number of provinces (groups of directly or indirectly connected cities).

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 form one province; city 2 is isolated and forms its own province.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS from each unvisited city, marking all reachable cities in the same province as visited, and count the number of DFS calls.

optimal.explanation: Apply Union-Find on all direct connections; each union reduces the province count by one, giving nearly O(n^2) with small constants due to the matrix traversal.

problems.title: Keys and Rooms
problems.description: There are n rooms (0 to n-1) and you start in room 0 (unlocked). Each room has a set of keys to other rooms. Determine if you can visit all rooms. Room 0 is always unlocked; use BFS/DFS to explore reachable rooms.

examples.explanation: Start in room 0, get key 1, visit room 1, get key 2, visit room 2, get key 3, visit room 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS from room 0, tracking visited rooms; if all n rooms are visited after DFS, return true.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative BFS with a count of visited rooms; once BFS completes, check if the visited count equals n, avoiding recursion stack usage.

problems.title: Find Eventual Safe States
problems.description: In a directed graph, a node is eventually safe if every path from that node leads to a terminal node (no outgoing edges) or another safe node. Return all eventually safe nodes in sorted order.

examples.explanation: Nodes 2, 4, 5, 6 are safe because all paths from them eventually terminate.

bruteForce.explanation: For each node, use DFS to check if any path leads to a cycle using a coloring scheme (unvisited/visiting/safe/unsafe); collect nodes marked safe.

optimal.explanation: Reverse all edges, then use topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) on the reversed graph; nodes that appear in the topological order of the reversed graph are safe in the original.

problems.title: Is Graph Bipartite
problems.description: Given an adjacency list of an undirected graph, determine if the graph is bipartite. A graph is bipartite if nodes can be split into two groups such that every edge connects nodes from different groups. The graph may be disconnected.

examples.explanation: The graph contains an odd-length cycle, so it cannot be 2-colored.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS-based 2-coloring: assign alternating colors to nodes; if two adjacent nodes have the same color, the graph is not bipartite.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS-based 2-coloring: process each component with BFS, assigning alternating colors; if a conflict is detected, return false immediately.

problems.title: All Paths From Source to Target
problems.description: Given a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of n nodes, find all possible paths from node 0 to node n-1 and return them in any order. Each node has edges only to higher-numbered nodes (DAG property).

examples.explanation: There are two paths from node 0 to node 3: 0->1->3 and 0->2->3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use backtracking DFS: explore all paths from node 0, and when node n-1 is reached, record the current path.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative DFS with an explicit stack storing (node, current path); this avoids recursion overhead while maintaining the same complexity for DAG path enumeration.

problems.title: Count Sub Islands
problems.description: Given two binary grids grid1 and grid2 of the same size, an island in grid2 is a sub-island if every cell of that island also exists as land in grid1. Return the number of sub-islands in grid2.

examples.explanation: The single island in grid2 is fully covered by land in grid1, so it counts as a sub-island.

bruteForce.explanation: For each unvisited land cell in grid2, DFS to find the whole island, simultaneously checking if every cell is also land in grid1; count islands where all cells match.

optimal.explanation: First mark all grid2 land cells that are water in grid1 as water (flood fill), eliminating non-sub-island parts; then count remaining islands in grid2 with standard DFS.

problems.title: Making a Large Island
problems.description: Given an n x n binary matrix, you may change at most one 0 to 1. Return the size of the largest island after this change. An island is a group of connected 1s (4-directionally).

examples.explanation: Changing one 0 to 1 can connect both islands into one island of size 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Try flipping each 0 to 1, then compute the largest island size using DFS; return the maximum over all flips. O(n^4) overall.

optimal.explanation: Label each island with a unique ID and record its size; for each 0 cell, sum the sizes of distinct neighboring islands plus 1 to find the best flip, achieving O(n^2).

problems.title: Flood Fill
problems.description: Given an image represented as an m x n integer grid, a starting pixel (sr, sc), and a new color, perform a flood fill. Color the starting pixel and all connected pixels (4-directionally) with the same original color to the new color.

examples.explanation: All 1s connected to (1,1) are replaced with 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive DFS from the starting pixel; change the color of each visited pixel with the original color to the new color.

optimal.explanation: Use iterative BFS with a queue; fill each dequeued pixel and enqueue its same-color neighbors, achieving the same complexity without recursion stack risk.

problems.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
problems.description: A gene string consists of 8 characters from {A, C, G, T}. Given a start gene, an end gene, and a bank of valid mutations, find the minimum number of single-character mutations to reach the end gene. Return -1 if impossible.

examples.explanation: One mutation changes the last T to A, which is in the bank.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all possible single-character mutations at each step using DFS, tracking visited states; return the minimum depth at which endGene is reached.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS level-by-level: each level represents one mutation step; the first time endGene is reached gives the minimum number of mutations.

problems.title: Detect Cycle in Directed Graph
problems.description: Given a directed graph with V vertices and a list of edges, determine if the graph contains a cycle. A cycle exists if there is a path from a vertex back to itself following directed edges.

examples.explanation: Vertices 0->1->2->0 form a cycle in the directed graph.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS with a recursion stack (inStack array): mark nodes as being visited in the current DFS path; if a neighbor is already in the stack, a cycle is detected.

optimal.explanation: Use Kahn's topological sort (BFS): if not all V nodes can be processed (some remain with non-zero in-degree), a cycle must exist in the directed graph.

problems.title: Topological Sort
problems.description: Given a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with V vertices and E edges, return a valid topological ordering of the vertices. In a topological ordering, for every directed edge u->v, vertex u appears before vertex v in the ordering.

examples.explanation: One valid topological order where each node appears before all nodes it points to.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS-based topological sort: perform post-order DFS from each unvisited node and push nodes to a stack; reverse the stack to get the topological order.

optimal.explanation: Use Kahn's BFS algorithm: compute in-degrees, enqueue zero-in-degree nodes, and process them iteratively while reducing neighbors' in-degrees; produces topological order without recursion.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.description: Given two words, beginWord and endWord, and a dictionary wordList, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord such that only one letter can be changed at a time and each transformed word must exist in the wordList. Return 0 if no such sequence exists. All words have the same length and contain only lowercase letters.

examples.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog, which is 5 words long.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS from beginWord, exploring all possible one-letter transformations and checking each against the word list using a set.

optimal.explanation: Use bidirectional BFS, expanding from both beginWord and endWord simultaneously to reduce the search space significantly.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.description: You are given a network of n nodes labeled from 1 to n, and a list of travel times as directed edges times[i] = (ui, vi, wi) where wi is the travel time. Find how long it takes for all nodes to receive a signal sent from node k. Return -1 if it is impossible for all nodes to receive the signal.

examples.explanation: Starting from node 2, all nodes receive the signal after 2 time units.

bruteForce.explanation: Use Bellman-Ford algorithm to compute shortest paths from source k to all nodes, running n-1 relaxation passes.

optimal.explanation: Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue to efficiently compute shortest paths from k to all nodes.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.description: There are n cities connected by some flights. Given an array flights where flights[i] = [fromi, toi, pricei], find the cheapest price from src to dst with at most k stops. Return -1 if no such route exists. There are no duplicate flights and no self loops.

examples.explanation: The cheapest route with at most 1 stop is 0->1->3 costing 700.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS/BFS with state tracking of stops, exploring all paths from src to dst limited to k stops.

optimal.explanation: Use Bellman-Ford with k+1 iterations, maintaining a copy of distances at each relaxation step to enforce the stop constraint.

problems.title: Critical Connections in a Network
problems.description: There are n servers numbered from 0 to n-1 connected by undirected server-to-server connections forming a network where connections[i] = [ai, bi] represents a connection between servers ai and bi. A critical connection is a connection that, if removed, will make some servers unable to reach some other server. Return all critical connections in the network in any order.

examples.explanation: Removing connection [1,3] disconnects server 3 from the rest of the network.

bruteForce.explanation: For each edge, remove it temporarily and check if the graph remains connected using DFS/BFS; if not, it is a critical connection.

optimal.explanation: Use Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm with DFS, tracking discovery times and low-link values to identify bridges in O(V+E).

problems.title: Swim in Rising Water
problems.description: You are given an n x n integer matrix grid where grid[i][j] represents the elevation at that point. At time t, the depth of water everywhere is t. You can swim from a square to another 4-directionally adjacent square if and only if the elevation of both squares individually is at most t. Return the minimum time until you can reach from the top left to the bottom right.

examples.explanation: At time 3, you can swim from (0,0) to (0,1) to (1,1) since all elevations are <= 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Binary search on the answer t and use BFS/DFS to check if there is a path from top-left to bottom-right where all cells have elevation <= t.

optimal.explanation: Use Dijkstra's algorithm treating the cost to reach each cell as the maximum elevation seen on the path from start to that cell.

problems.title: Path With Minimum Effort
problems.description: You are given a rows x columns matrix of heights. A route's effort is the maximum absolute difference in heights between two consecutive cells of the route. Return the minimum effort required to travel from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. You can move up, down, left, or right.

examples.explanation: The route 1->3->5->3->5 has a maximum absolute difference of 2 in consecutive cells.

bruteForce.explanation: Binary search on the answer (effort) and use BFS to check if there exists a path where all consecutive differences are <= mid.

optimal.explanation: Use Dijkstra's algorithm where the cost to reach each cell is the minimum possible maximum effort along the path from start.

problems.title: Accounts Merge
problems.description: Given a list of accounts where each element accounts[i] is a list of strings where the first element is a name and the rest are emails, merge accounts that share any email address. After merging, return the accounts in any order with emails sorted and the name as the first element.

examples.explanation: The first two John accounts share johnsmith@mail.com so they are merged.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS/BFS: build a graph where emails are nodes connected if they appear in the same account, then find connected components.

optimal.explanation: Use Union-Find (DSU) to union emails that belong to the same account, then group emails by their root representative efficiently.

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.description: Given a list of strings words sorted lexicographically by the rules of a new alien language, derive the order of letters in this language. Return the characters in the correct order, or an empty string if there is no valid ordering or the input is inconsistent. All letters are lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: From adjacent words we derive: t<f, w<e, r<t, e<r, giving the order wertf.

bruteForce.explanation: Compare adjacent words to extract ordering constraints, then use DFS-based topological sort to determine the character order.

optimal.explanation: Use Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based topological sort) with in-degree tracking for a cleaner iterative approach.

problems.title: Minimum Height Trees
problems.description: Given a tree with n nodes labeled 0 to n-1 and an array of n-1 edges, find all nodes that can be tree roots minimizing the tree height. A tree's height is the number of edges on the longest downward path from root to a leaf. Return all such root labels in any order.

examples.explanation: Node 1 as root gives height 1, which is the minimum possible.

bruteForce.explanation: For each node, do BFS to compute the height of the tree rooted at that node, and return nodes achieving minimum height.

optimal.explanation: Iteratively prune leaf nodes layer by layer (like topological sort) until 1 or 2 nodes remain; these are the centroid roots.

problems.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.description: Given a list of airline tickets represented by pairs [from, to], reconstruct the itinerary in order starting from JFK. You must use all tickets exactly once. If there are multiple valid itineraries, return the one with the smallest lexical order. It is guaranteed that at least one valid itinerary exists.

examples.explanation: Starting from JFK, follow the only possible path visiting all airports.

bruteForce.explanation: Use backtracking: sort destinations lexicographically, then try each possible next flight and backtrack if a dead end is reached before using all tickets.

optimal.explanation: Use Hierholzer's algorithm for Eulerian path: greedily visit smallest destination first and build the path in reverse via post-order DFS.

problems.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
problems.description: Given an n x n binary matrix grid, return the length of the shortest clear path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. A clear path consists only of cells with value 0, and you can move 8-directionally. Return -1 if no clear path exists. The path length is the number of cells visited.

examples.explanation: The shortest path is (0,0) -> (1,1) with length 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS from (0,0) exploring all 8 directions, counting steps until reaching (n-1,n-1) or exhausting all reachable cells.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS with in-place marking (setting visited cells to 1) to avoid the extra visited array and reduce memory usage.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.description: Given an m x n integers matrix, return the length of the longest increasing path in the matrix. From each cell, you can move in four directions. You may not move diagonally or move outside the boundary. The path must be strictly increasing.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing path is [1, 2, 6, 9], length 4.

bruteForce.explanation: For each cell, run DFS to find the longest increasing path starting from that cell, exploring all four directions where the next cell is strictly greater.

optimal.explanation: Use DFS with memoization: cache the longest increasing path starting from each cell to avoid recomputation.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
problems.description: You are in a city with n intersections numbered from 0 to n-1. Given roads where roads[i] = [ui, vi, timei] describes a bidirectional road, find the number of ways you can travel from intersection 0 to intersection n-1 in the shortest amount of time. Return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: There are 4 shortest paths from node 0 to node 6, each with total time 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS to enumerate all paths from 0 to n-1, tracking total time, then count paths matching the minimum time found.

optimal.explanation: Use Dijkstra's algorithm while simultaneously counting the number of shortest paths to each node using a ways array.

problems.title: Bus Routes
problems.description: You are given an array routes where routes[i] is a bus route that the ith bus repeats forever. You start at the bus stop source and want to reach the bus stop target. Return the minimum number of buses you must take to travel from source to target. Return -1 if it is not possible.

examples.explanation: Take the first bus from stop 1 to stop 7, then take the second bus from stop 7 to stop 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Build a graph between bus stops and use BFS to find the minimum number of stops, treating each stop-to-stop as a unit.

optimal.explanation: Use BFS on routes instead of stops: treat each route as a node, find which routes serve source, then BFS by transferring between routes that share stops.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in a Grid
problems.description: Given an m x n grid where each cell has a sign pointing right (1), left (2), down (3), or up (4), it costs 0 to follow the sign and 1 to change the direction. Starting from cell (0,0), find the minimum cost to reach cell (m-1,n-1). You can move in any of the four directions.

examples.explanation: You need to change direction 3 times to reach (3,3) from (0,0).

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS with cost tracking, exploring all four directions from each cell with cost 0 if following the sign and cost 1 if changing direction.

optimal.explanation: Use 0-1 BFS with a deque: push to front when following the sign (cost 0) and push to back when changing direction (cost 1) for O(m*n) time.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.description: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed, and the only constraint is that adjacent houses have security systems connected — if two adjacent houses are broken into on the same night, the police will be alerted. Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money in each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob without alerting the police. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 400.

examples.explanation: Rob house 1 (money=2), skip house 2, rob house 3 (money=9), skip house 4, rob house 5 (money=1). Total = 2+9+1 = 12.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try all subsets of non-adjacent houses, computing the maximum sum over all valid subsets.

optimal.explanation: Use dynamic programming with two variables to track the best rob amount up to the previous and current house, avoiding O(n) space array.

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.description: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses arranged in a circle. Each house has a certain amount of money, and adjacent houses (including the first and last) cannot both be robbed. Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money, return the maximum amount you can rob. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: You cannot rob house 1 (money=2) and house 3 (money=2) because they are adjacent in a circle. Rob house 2 (money=3) for maximum.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of non-adjacent houses respecting the circular constraint by brute-force enumeration.

optimal.explanation: Split the circular problem into two linear House Robber subproblems: houses 0..n-2 and houses 1..n-1, take the maximum of both.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence is derived from the array by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2500, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing subsequence is [2,3,7,101], which has length 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a DP array where dp[i] is the LIS length ending at index i, comparing each element with all previous elements.

optimal.explanation: Use patience sorting with binary search to maintain a tails array, achieving O(n log n) time.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.description: You are given an integer array coins representing coins of different denominations and an integer amount representing a total amount of money. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If that amount cannot be made up by any combination of coins, return -1. You may assume you have an infinite number of each kind of coin. Constraints: 1 <= coins.length <= 12, 1 <= coins[i] <= 2^31 - 1, 0 <= amount <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Use 25 + 10 + 1 = 36 with 3 coins.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization, trying all coin denominations at each step to find the minimum number of coins.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP building a table from 0 to amount, filling each cell as the minimum coins needed, eliminating recursion overhead.

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.description: You are given an integer array coins representing different coin denominations and an integer amount. Return the number of combinations that make up that amount. If no combination can make up that amount, return 0. You may assume each coin can be used an infinite number of times. Constraints: 1 <= coins.length <= 300, 1 <= coins[i] <= 5000, 0 <= amount <= 5000.

examples.explanation: There are four combinations: 5=5, 5=2+2+1, 5=2+1+1+1, 5=1+1+1+1+1.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to enumerate all combinations of coins that sum to the target amount, counting valid ones.

optimal.explanation: Use 1D DP where dp[i] represents the number of ways to make amount i, iterating each coin and updating the table in place.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if you can partition the array into two subsets such that the sum of elements in both subsets is equal. If it is not possible, return false. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 200, 1 <= nums[i] <= 100.

examples.explanation: The array can be partitioned as [1,5,5] and [11] both summing to 11.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try all subsets and check if any subset sums to half of the total.

optimal.explanation: Use a bitset DP where each bit represents whether a given sum is achievable, shifting and ORing for each number.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.description: You are given an integer array nums and an integer target. You want to build an expression using + or - before each integer and return the number of different ways to assign symbols such that the result equals target. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 20, 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000, 0 <= sum(nums[i]) <= 1000, -1000 <= target <= 1000.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion to try both + and - assignments for each number and count the combinations that reach the target.

optimal.explanation: Use a DP map from current sum to count of ways, updating for each number by adding and subtracting, in O(n * sum) time.

problems.title: Perfect Squares
problems.description: Given an integer n, return the least number of perfect square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, ...) that sum to n. A perfect square is an integer that is the square of an integer. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, using three perfect squares.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS starting from 0, expanding by each perfect square at each level, returning the level when n is reached.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP where dp[i] is the minimum squares needed for i, filling each entry by trying all squares up to i.

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.description: A robot is located at the top-left corner of an m x n grid. It can only move either down or right at any point in time. The robot is trying to reach the bottom-right corner of the grid. How many possible unique paths are there? Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 100.

examples.explanation: There are 28 unique paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3x7 grid moving only right or down.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion where from each cell we can move right or down, counting all paths that reach the destination.

optimal.explanation: Use a 1D DP array representing one row, updating left to right as we simulate moving through each row of the grid.

problems.title: Unique Paths II
problems.description: You are given an m x n integer array grid where grid[i][j] is either 0 (empty) or 1 (obstacle). A robot starts at the top-left and must reach the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Count the number of unique paths avoiding obstacles. Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 100, grid[i][j] is 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: There are two ways to reach the bottom-right corner, going around the obstacle at [1][1].

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization, trying all valid right/down moves while skipping obstacle cells.

optimal.explanation: Use in-place DP modifying the grid itself, so no extra space is used beyond the input array.

problems.title: Minimum Path Sum
problems.description: Given an m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from the top-left to the bottom-right which minimizes the sum of all numbers along the path. You can only move either down or right at any point in time. Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 200, 0 <= grid[i][j] <= 200.

examples.explanation: The path 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1 -> 1 minimizes the sum to 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization, computing the minimum path sum from each cell to the bottom-right.

optimal.explanation: Use in-place DP filling the grid from top-left, each cell becomes the minimum cost to reach it from the start.

problems.title: Triangle
problems.description: Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. At each step you may move to an adjacent number on the row below. Adjacent means index i leads to index i or i+1 in the next row. Constraints: 1 <= triangle.length <= 200, triangle[i].length == i + 1, -10^4 <= triangle[i][j] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The minimum path sum from top to bottom is 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 11.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion exploring all paths from top to bottom and returning the minimum sum path.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP starting from the last row, updating a 1D array upward, so only O(n) extra space is needed.

problems.title: Maximal Square
problems.description: Given an m x n binary matrix filled with '0's and '1's, find the largest square containing only '1's and return its area. Constraints: m == matrix.length, n == matrix[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 300, matrix[i][j] is '0' or '1'.

examples.explanation: The maximal square of all '1's has side length 3, giving area 9.

bruteForce.explanation: For every cell containing '1', expand outward to check if larger squares of all '1's exist, tracking the maximum side length.

optimal.explanation: Use DP where dp[i][j] = side length of the largest square with bottom-right corner at (i,j), defined by the recurrence min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1.

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.description: Given an integer n, return an array ans of length n+1 such that for each i (0 <= i <= n), ans[i] is the number of '1's in the binary representation of i. Constraints: 0 <= n <= 10^5.

bruteForce.explanation: For each number from 0 to n, count its set bits using __builtin_popcount or bit shifting.

optimal.explanation: Use DP: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), leveraging the fact that i has one more or same number of bits as i/2 depending on the last bit.

problems.title: Paint House
problems.description: There are n houses along a street, and each house can be painted with one of three colors: red, blue, or green. No two adjacent houses can have the same color. The cost of painting house i with color j is given by costs[i][j]. Return the minimum cost to paint all houses. Constraints: costs.length == n, costs[i].length == 3, 1 <= n <= 100, 1 <= costs[i][j] <= 20.

examples.explanation: Paint house 0 blue (cost 2), house 1 green (cost 5), house 2 blue (cost 3). Total = 10.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion trying all color choices for each house, ensuring no two adjacent houses share a color.

optimal.explanation: Use DP updating three running cost variables for each color, each time taking the min of the other two previous colors.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
problems.description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the stock price on day i. Find the maximum profit you can achieve with the constraint that after you sell, you must wait one day (cooldown) before buying again. You may not hold multiple stocks simultaneously. Constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 5000, 0 <= prices[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 0, sell on day 1, cooldown on day 2, buy on day 3, sell on day 4. Profit = 1 + 2 = 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization tracking current day and whether holding a stock, modeling the cooldown state explicitly.

optimal.explanation: Use three state variables (hold, sold, rest) updated each day representing having stock, just sold, or in cooldown/rest state.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
problems.description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the stock price on day i, and an integer fee representing a transaction fee for each buy-sell transaction. Find the maximum profit you can achieve. You may complete as many transactions as you like, but you must pay the fee for each transaction. Constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 5 * 10^4, 1 <= prices[i] <= 5 * 10^4, 0 <= fee <= 5 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1, sell at 8 (profit 5), buy at 4, sell at 9 (profit 3). Total profit = 5 + 3 = 8.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization tracking day and holding state, subtracting the fee on each sell operation.

optimal.explanation: Use two variables: cash (max profit when not holding) and hold (max profit when holding stock), updated each day in O(1) space.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
problems.description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the stock price on day i. Find the maximum profit you can achieve with at most two transactions (buy-sell pairs). You may not engage in multiple transactions simultaneously. Constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 4 (price=0), sell on day 6 (price=3), buy on day 7 (price=1), sell on day 8 (price=4). Profit = 3+3 = 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all ways to split the array into at most two non-overlapping buy-sell intervals and take the maximum total profit.

optimal.explanation: Track four state variables: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2 representing the best profit at each stage of up to two transactions.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
problems.description: You are given an integer k and an array prices where prices[i] is the stock price on day i. Find the maximum profit using at most k transactions. You may not engage in multiple transactions simultaneously. Constraints: 0 <= k <= 100, 0 <= prices.length <= 1000, 0 <= prices[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 0 (price=2), sell on day 1 (price=4), buy on day 2 (price=1), sell on day 3 (price=7). Profit = 2+6 = 8.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization over (day, transactions remaining, holding state) to try all buy/sell/skip choices.

optimal.explanation: Use DP with arrays buy[k] and sell[k] representing the best profit at each transaction count, updated greedily in one pass.

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.description: You are given n balloons indexed from 0 to n-1. Each balloon has a number painted on it given by nums[i]. Bursting balloon i yields nums[i-1]*nums[i]*nums[i+1] coins. Balloons at boundaries use 1 as the out-of-bounds value. Return the maximum coins obtainable by bursting all balloons. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 300, 0 <= nums[i] <= 100.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization over intervals, trying every balloon as the last to burst in the interval.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up interval DP building solutions for increasing interval lengths, filling the table without recursion overhead.

problems.title: Stone Game
problems.description: Alice and Bob take turns picking from either end of a pile of stones, with Alice going first. They always play optimally. The player with more stones at the end wins. Alice always wins when there are an even number of piles; return true if Alice wins. Constraints: 2 <= piles.length <= 500, piles.length is even, 1 <= piles[i] <= 500, sum(piles[i]) is odd.

examples.explanation: Alice always wins in this configuration with optimal play; mathematically Alice always wins with even piles.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization simulating optimal play for both players, tracking whose turn it is and the score difference.

optimal.explanation: Since piles.length is even and the first player can always pick all odd-indexed or all even-indexed piles, Alice always wins — return true directly.

problems.title: Stone Game II
problems.description: Alice and Bob take turns (Alice goes first), and on each turn a player can take the first X piles where 1 <= X <= 2*M, and M is updated to max(M, X). Both play optimally to maximize their own total. Return the maximum stones Alice can get. Constraints: 1 <= piles.length <= 100, 1 <= piles[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Alice takes 2 piles (2+7=9), Bob takes all remaining (9+4+4=17)... with optimal play Alice gets 10.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization over (index, M) state where each player picks 1 to 2*M piles, maximizing their own total.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP with suffix sums, filling a 2D table dp[i][M] = max stones the current player can get from index i with parameter M.

problems.title: Integer Break
problems.description: Given an integer n, break it into the sum of k positive integers (k >= 2) and maximize the product of those integers. Return the maximum product you can get. Constraints: 2 <= n <= 58.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization, trying all possible first parts from 1 to n-1 and recursively computing the best product for the rest.

optimal.explanation: Use a mathematical greedy approach: break n into as many 3s as possible (using 2s when n mod 3 == 1 or 2), since 3s maximize the product.

problems.title: Arithmetic Slices
problems.description: An integer array is called arithmetic if it consists of at least three elements and the difference between consecutive elements is constant. Given an integer array nums, return the number of arithmetic subarrays of nums. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000, -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The arithmetic slices are [1,2,3], [2,3,4], and [1,2,3,4].

bruteForce.explanation: Check every subarray of length >= 3 to see if it is arithmetic, counting valid ones.

optimal.explanation: Use DP where dp[i] is the number of arithmetic slices ending at i; if nums[i]-nums[i-1] == nums[i-1]-nums[i-2], then dp[i] = dp[i-1]+1.

problems.title: Jump Game VI
problems.description: You are given a 0-indexed integer array nums and an integer k. You start at index 0, and in each step you can jump at most k steps forward. You want to reach the last index. Your score is the sum of all nums[i] for each index i you visit. Return the maximum score you can get. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4, 1 <= k <= nums.length.

examples.explanation: Jump from index 0 to 3 to 5 visiting values 1+4+3=8... optimal path gives 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion with memoization, at each index trying all k possible previous positions and taking the maximum.

optimal.explanation: Use DP with a monotonic deque (sliding window maximum) to get the best dp value in the last k positions in O(1) per step.

problems.title: Zero One Knapsack Problem
problems.description: Given N items each with a weight and value, and a knapsack with capacity W, find the maximum value you can achieve by selecting items such that total weight does not exceed W. Each item can be selected at most once. Constraints: 1 <= N <= 1000, 1 <= W <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Select items with weight 1 (value 10) and weight 3 (value 30) for total weight 4 and value 50.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try including or excluding each item and take the maximum value across all combinations.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP table where dp[i][w] represents the max value using first i items with capacity w, reducing to polynomial time.

problems.title: Unbounded Knapsack Problem
problems.description: Given N items each with a weight and value, and a knapsack with capacity W, find the maximum value achievable where each item can be selected unlimited times. Constraints: 1 <= N <= 1000, 1 <= W <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Select the item with weight 1 and value 10 four times for total value 40.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try taking each item multiple times or skipping it, exploring all combinations.

optimal.explanation: Use 1D DP where dp[w] is the max value for capacity w, iterating forward to allow item reuse.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence DP
problems.description: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is a sequence derived by deleting some characters without changing the relative order. Constraints: 1 <= text1.length, text2.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is 'ace' with length 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively compare characters and explore all subsequences of both strings, checking for common ones.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP table where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of text1[0..i-1] and text2[0..j-1], filling bottom-up.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.description: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s which equals t. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000, 1 <= t.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: There are 3 ways to generate 'rabbit' from 'rabbbit' by removing one of the three 'b's.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try matching each character of t with characters of s, exploring all possible matches.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] counts distinct ways to form t[0..j-1] from s[0..i-1], processing row by row.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
problems.description: Given a string s, partition it such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return the minimum number of cuts needed. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 2000, s contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: The palindrome partitioning ['aa','b'] requires just 1 cut.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try all possible cut positions, check if the prefix is a palindrome, and find the minimum cuts.

optimal.explanation: Precompute palindrome table using DP, then compute minimum cuts with another DP array in O(n^2).

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
problems.description: Given a string s, find the longest palindromic subsequence's length. A subsequence is obtained by deleting some characters without changing relative order. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000, s consists only of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: One possible longest palindromic subsequence is 'bbbb' with length 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively check if end characters match and expand inward, exploring both skip options otherwise.

optimal.explanation: Use interval DP where dp[i][j] is the LPS length of s[i..j], filling diagonals bottom-up.

problems.title: Scramble String
problems.description: We can scramble a string s to get string t using a recursive splitting process. Given two strings s1 and s2 of the same length, return true if s2 is a scrambled string of s1. Constraints: s1.length == s2.length, 1 <= s1.length <= 30.

examples.explanation: Splitting 'great' at index 1 gives 'g' and 'reat'; swapping gives 'reat' and 'g', then 'rgeat' is obtained.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try all split positions and check if swapped or unswapped substrings form valid scramble pairs.

optimal.explanation: Use memoization with a hash map storing results for (s1, s2) pairs to avoid recomputing overlapping subproblems.

problems.title: Minimum ASCII Delete Sum for Two Strings
problems.description: Given two strings s1 and s2, return the lowest ASCII sum of deleted characters to make two strings equal. Constraints: 1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 1000, s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Deleting 's' from s1 (115) and 't' from s2 (116) gives 'ea' == 'ea', cost = 231.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try deleting characters from both strings when they don't match, accumulating ASCII costs.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] stores minimum delete cost to equalize s1[0..i-1] and s2[0..j-1].

problems.title: Shortest Common Supersequence
problems.description: Given two strings str1 and str2, return the shortest string that has both str1 and str2 as subsequences. If there are multiple valid answers, return any of them. Constraints: 1 <= str1.length, str2.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: 'cabac' contains both 'abac' and 'cab' as subsequences and is the shortest such string.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively build the supersequence by always taking the smaller option of appending from str1 or str2.

optimal.explanation: Compute LCS with DP, then reconstruct the supersequence by merging both strings using the LCS as a backbone.

problems.title: Dungeon Game
problems.description: A knight starts at the top-left of an m x n grid. Each cell has an integer (negative = loses health, positive = gains health). Find the minimum initial health so the knight can reach bottom-right alive (health >= 1 at all times). Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 200, -1000 <= dungeon[i][j] <= 1000.

examples.explanation: With initial health 7, the knight follows the path right->right->down->down, always maintaining at least 1 health.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively explore all paths from top-left to bottom-right and compute the minimum health required for each path.

optimal.explanation: Work backwards from bottom-right, computing the minimum health needed at each cell using bottom-up DP.

problems.title: Cherry Pickup
problems.description: You have an n x n grid with cherries (1), empty (0), or thorns (-1). Start at (0,0), reach (n-1,n-1) picking cherries, then return. Find the maximum cherries collectible. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50, grid[i][j] is -1, 0, or 1.

examples.explanation: Going right, down, down picks 3 cherries; returning via up, up, left picks 2 more for total 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively simulate both the forward and return trip, trying all paths and keeping track of collected cherries.

optimal.explanation: Simulate two simultaneous forward trips using DP on (t, r1, r2) where t is the step count, computing optimal cherry collection.

problems.title: K Inverse Pairs Array
problems.description: Given n and k, return the number of different arrays consisting of numbers 1 to n such that there are exactly k inverse pairs. An inverse pair is a pair (i, j) where i < j and nums[i] > nums[j]. Return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, 0 <= k <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Arrays [1,3,2] and [2,1,3] each have exactly 1 inverse pair.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of 1 to n and count those with exactly k inverse pairs.

optimal.explanation: Use DP with prefix sums where dp[i][j] counts arrays of length i with j inverse pairs, using sliding window for efficiency.

problems.title: Minimum Cost for Tickets
problems.description: You have planned travels on some days of a year (1-365). Tickets cost: 1-day pass, 7-day pass, 30-day pass. Find the minimum cost to travel all the given days. Constraints: 1 <= days.length <= 365, 1 <= days[i] <= 365, costs.length == 3.

examples.explanation: Buy a 1-day pass on day 1 (cost 2), a 7-day pass on day 4 covering days 4-10 (cost 7), and a 1-day pass on day 20 (cost 2), total 11.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively decide which ticket to buy for each travel day and explore all combinations.

optimal.explanation: Use DP array over days 1-365 where dp[i] is the minimum cost to cover travel up to day i.

problems.title: Remove Boxes
problems.description: You have a row of colored boxes. Each turn, remove k consecutive boxes of the same color to earn k*k points. Return the maximum points you can get. Constraints: 1 <= boxes.length <= 100, 1 <= boxes[i] <= 100.

examples.explanation: Remove boxes[2..4] (three 2s) for 9 points, then boxes[1][5] (two 3s together with new neighbor) for more points totaling 23.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try removing each contiguous group of same-colored boxes and compute the maximum score.

optimal.explanation: Use memoized interval DP with state (l, r, k) where k is the count of same-colored boxes attached to boxes[r] from the right.

problems.title: Strange Printer
problems.description: A printer can only print a sequence of the same characters each turn, and each new turn overwrites previous characters. Given a string s, return the minimum number of turns the printer needs to print it. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 100, s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Print 'aaa' in one turn, then overwrite the middle with 'b' in a second turn.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try all split points for the string and compute minimum turns for each segment combination.

optimal.explanation: Use memoized interval DP; if s[l]==s[k], merging saves a turn, finding the minimum over all splits.

problems.title: Video Stitching
problems.description: You are given clips from a video, each with a start and end time. Return the minimum number of clips needed to cover the entire range [0, time], or -1 if impossible. Constraints: 1 <= clips.length <= 100, 0 <= clips[i][0] <= clips[i][1] <= 100, 1 <= time <= 100.

examples.explanation: Use clips [0,2], [1,9], and [8,10] to cover [0,10] with 3 clips.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of clips, check if they cover [0, time], and return the size of the smallest valid subset.

optimal.explanation: Greedy interval covering: at each position, pick the clip that starts at or before current end and extends farthest.

problems.title: Ones and Zeroes
problems.description: You are given an array of binary strings strs, and two integers m and n. Return the size of the largest subset where there are at most m zeros and n ones in total. Constraints: 1 <= strs.length <= 600, 1 <= strs[i].length <= 100, 0 <= m, n <= 100.

examples.explanation: The largest subset with at most 5 zeros and 3 ones is {"10","0001","1","0"} of size 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of strings, count zeros and ones, and track the largest valid subset.

optimal.explanation: 2D 0/1 knapsack DP where dp[i][j] is the max strings using at most i zeros and j ones.

problems.title: Super Egg Drop
problems.description: You have k eggs and n floors. Find the minimum number of moves to determine the critical floor (highest floor from which an egg won't break). An egg that doesn't break can be reused. Constraints: 1 <= k <= 100, 1 <= n <= 10000.

examples.explanation: With 1 egg, you must test floor 1 then floor 2 sequentially, requiring 2 moves in the worst case.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursive DP trying every floor as the test floor, taking minimum over all choices and maximum of two outcomes.

optimal.explanation: Reframe as: with k eggs and t moves, what is the max floors we can check? Find minimum t such that f(t,k) >= n.

problems.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
problems.description: You have n jobs each with a startTime, endTime, and profit. Find the maximum profit from non-overlapping jobs. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50000, 1 <= startTime[i] < endTime[i] <= 10^9, 1 <= profit[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Select jobs [1,3,50] and [3,6,70] for total profit 120.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try taking or skipping each job (sorted by end time), finding the maximum profit.

optimal.explanation: Sort by end time, use DP with binary search to find the latest non-overlapping job for each position.

problems.title: Frog Jump
problems.description: A frog starts at stone 0 and wants to reach the last stone. If the frog jumped k units last step, next jump can be k-1, k, or k+1 units. Given stone positions, determine if the frog can cross. Constraints: 2 <= stones.length <= 2000, 0 <= stones[i] <= 2^31-1.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try all valid jumps from each stone and check if the last stone is reachable.

optimal.explanation: Use a map from stone position to set of valid jump sizes to reach it; propagate reachable jump sizes forward.

problems.title: Best Team with No Conflicts
problems.description: A team has players with scores and ages. No conflicts occur when for any two players chosen, the older player has a score >= the younger player's score. Return the highest overall score of all possible teams. Constraints: 1 <= scores.length == ages.length <= 1000, 1 <= ages[i] <= 1000, 1 <= scores[i] <= 10^6.

examples.explanation: Choose all players (ages 2,1,2,1 with scores 4,5,6,5) since for same age there is no conflict and older players have higher scores.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of players, verify no conflict within each subset, and return the maximum score sum.

optimal.explanation: Sort players by age then score; use LIS-style DP where dp[i] is max score using player i as the last selected.

problems.title: Count All Valid Pickup and Delivery Options
problems.description: Given n orders, each with a pickup and delivery, count valid sequences where each delivery Di occurs after its pickup Pi. Return the answer modulo 10^9+7. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 500.

examples.explanation: Valid sequences are: (P1,P2,D1,D2), (P1,P2,D2,D1), (P1,D1,P2,D2), (P2,P1,D1,D2), (P2,P1,D2,D1), (P2,D2,P1,D1).

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of 2n elements (P1..Pn, D1..Dn) and count those where each Di comes after Pi.

optimal.explanation: For each new order i, there are (2i-1)*i ways to insert its pickup and delivery into the existing 2i-2 slots.

problems.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
problems.description: Given an n x n matrix, return the minimum sum of a falling path. A falling path starts at any element in the first row and chooses the element in the next row that is either directly below or diagonally left/right. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100, -100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100.

examples.explanation: The minimum falling path is 1->5->7 with sum 13.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively try all possible falling paths from each starting column in the first row.

optimal.explanation: Bottom-up DP modifying in-place (or using extra array): each cell becomes min sum to reach it from above.

problems.title: Largest Divisible Subset
problems.description: Given a set of distinct positive integers nums, return the largest subset such that every pair (a, b) satisfies a % b == 0 or b % a == 0. If there are multiple solutions, return any. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000, 1 <= nums[i] <= 2*10^9.

examples.explanation: Every pair in {1,2,4,8} satisfies the divisibility condition, giving the largest subset of size 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets, verify divisibility for all pairs in each, and return the largest valid subset.

optimal.explanation: Sort nums, use LIS-style DP where dp[i] is the longest divisible chain ending at nums[i], then backtrack to reconstruct.

problems.title: Combination Sum IV
problems.description: Given an array of distinct integers nums and a target integer target, return the number of possible combinations that add up to target. The order of the numbers matters. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 200, 1 <= nums[i] <= 1000, 1 <= target <= 1000.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively subtract each number from target and count paths that reach exactly 0.

optimal.explanation: Bottom-up DP where dp[i] is the number of ways to reach sum i, building from 0 to target.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
problems.description: Given an integer array bloomDay where bloomDay[i] is the day the ith flower blooms, and integers m and k, return the minimum number of days to make m bouquets. Each bouquet requires k adjacent bloomed flowers. If it is impossible, return -1.

examples.explanation: After day 3, flowers at indices 0, 2, 4 are bloomed (days 1, 3, 2). We can make 3 bouquets each with 1 flower.

bruteForce.explanation: Try each day from 1 to max(bloomDay) and check if we can make m bouquets by counting adjacent bloomed flowers. This runs in O(max * n) time.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the answer day between 1 and max(bloomDay). For each candidate day, check feasibility in O(n). Total time is O(n log(max)).

problems.title: Selling Pieces of Wood
problems.description: You have an m x n piece of wood and a list of prices where prices[i] = [hi, wi, pricei] gives the price for a hi x wi piece. You can cut the wood horizontally or vertically any number of times. Return the maximum money obtainable by selling pieces. Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 200.

examples.explanation: Cut the board into a 2x2 piece (price 7), two 1x4 pieces (price 2 each), and two 2x1 pieces (price 3 each): 7+2+2+3+3+2 = 19.

bruteForce.explanation: Use naive recursion without memoization: for each (h, w) try selling directly or cutting at every row/column and recursively solve sub-problems. This leads to exponential repeated computation.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP where dp[i][j] = max revenue from an i x j piece. Fill bottom-up, trying all horizontal and vertical cuts plus selling whole piece. O(m*n*(m+n)) time.

problems.title: Tallest Billboard
problems.description: You have rods of given lengths and want to build two steel supports of equal height for a billboard. You may weld rods together and discard some. Return the maximum possible height of the billboard, or 0 if it cannot be done. The sum of rod lengths is at most 5000.

examples.explanation: Weld rods [1,2,3] for one support and [6] for the other, both height 6.

bruteForce.explanation: For each rod, try assigning it to the left pile, right pile, or discarding it using DFS/backtracking. Track the difference between two piles and the height of the taller. Exponential in number of rods.

optimal.explanation: Use DP where dp[diff] = max height of the taller support when the difference between two supports is diff. Process each rod: add to taller, shorter, or discard. O(n * sum) time.

problems.title: Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum
problems.description: You have n dice each with k faces numbered 1 to k. Return the number of ways to roll all n dice such that the sum equals target. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7. Constraints: 1 <= n, k <= 30, 1 <= target <= 1000.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion without memoization: for each die try all k faces and recurse on remaining dice. This has O(k^n) time which is exponential.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP where dp[i][j] = number of ways using i dice to reach sum j. Transition uses prefix sums to avoid the inner loop over k faces in O(1). Total O(n * target) time.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
problems.description: Given a wooden stick of length n and an array cuts of positions to cut it, the cost of a cut equals the length of the stick being cut. Return the minimum total cost to perform all cuts. You may perform cuts in any order. Constraints: 2 <= n <= 10^6, 1 <= cuts.length <= min(n-1, 100).

examples.explanation: Cut at 1 (cost 7), then 3 (cost 6), then 4 (cost 4), then 5 (cost 3): total 20. Optimal order gives cost 16.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of cuts recursively, simulate each order, and return the minimum total cost. Time complexity is O(c! * c) where c is the number of cuts.

optimal.explanation: Use interval DP. Add 0 and n as sentinels, then dp[i][j] = min cost to make all cuts between cuts[i] and cuts[j]. Try each cut k as the last cut in interval. O(c^3) time.

problems.title: Zuma Game
problems.description: In the Zuma game, you have a board of colored balls represented as a string and a hand of balls. You can insert any ball from your hand into the board at any position. Consecutive groups of 3+ same-colored balls are automatically removed. Return the minimum number of balls to insert to clear the board, or -1 if impossible. The board length is at most 16 and hand size at most 5.
