examples.explanation: We need at least one W and one BB or RR to clear, but we can't clear WRRBBW with only R and B.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS/DFS with memoization: try inserting each hand ball at every position, collapse consecutive triples, and recurse. State is (board_string, hand_multiset). Exponential without pruning.

optimal.explanation: Use DFS with memoization and pruning: match groups in board with hand balls, only insert at group boundaries, and skip equivalent positions. Memoize (board, hand_freq) states for efficiency.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
problems.description: You have n piles of stones in a row. Each move merges exactly k consecutive piles into one; the cost equals the total stones in those k piles. Return the minimum cost to merge all piles into one, or -1 if impossible. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 30, 2 <= k <= 30.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: try merging every valid group of k consecutive piles and recurse on the resulting array. This has exponential time due to overlapping subproblems without memoization.

optimal.explanation: Use interval DP with prefix sums. dp[l][r] = min cost to merge stones[l..r] into as few piles as possible. A merge is only possible when (r-l) % (k-1) == 0. O(n^3/k) time.

problems.title: Minimum Score Triangulation of Polygon
problems.description: Given a convex polygon with n vertices labeled with integer values, triangulate it into n-2 triangles. Each triangle's score is the product of its vertex labels. Return the minimum total score of all triangles. Constraints: 3 <= n <= 50, 1 <= values[i] <= 100.

examples.explanation: Only one triangle: 1*2*3 = 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Enumerate all possible triangulations recursively: for a polygon with vertices l..r, pick each vertex k as the apex of a triangle with edge (l,r) and recurse on sub-polygons. Without memoization this is exponential.

optimal.explanation: Use interval DP with memoization. dp[l][r] = min score to triangulate sub-polygon from vertex l to r. For each apex k between l and r, dp[l][r] = min(dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + v[l]*v[k]*v[r]). O(n^3) time.

problems.title: Predict the Winner
problems.description: Two players take turns picking a number from either end of an array of integers. The player with the higher total score wins. Given the array, return true if Player 1 can win assuming both play optimally. If scores are equal, Player 1 also wins. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^7.

examples.explanation: Player 1 picks 1 or 2. If 1: Player 2 picks 5, Player 1 picks 2. Scores 3 vs 5. If 2: Player 2 picks 5, Player 1 picks 1. Scores 3 vs 5. Player 2 always wins.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion: the current player picks left or right end and the opponent then plays optimally. Return the max score the current player can get minus the opponent's best. Exponential without memoization.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP where dp[i][j] = max score difference (current player minus opponent) for the subarray nums[i..j]. Fill diagonals incrementally. O(n^2) time and space.

problems.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
problems.description: You are given intervals and queries. For each query q, find the smallest interval [l, r] such that l <= q <= r and return the length r - l + 1. If no such interval exists, return -1. Constraints: 1 <= intervals.length, queries.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: For query 2: smallest containing interval is [2,4] (len 3). For query 4: [4,4] (len 1). For query 5: [3,6] (len 4).

bruteForce.explanation: For each query, check all intervals to find which ones contain the query point, then return the minimum size among them. O(n * m) time where n is intervals count and m is queries count.

optimal.explanation: Sort intervals by start and sort queries. Use a min-heap keyed by interval size. For each query (in sorted order), add all intervals that start <= query, then remove intervals that end < query from the heap top. O((n+m) log n) time.

problems.title: Painting the Walls
problems.description: You have n walls to paint. A paid painter can paint wall i in time[i] at cost[i]. While the paid painter works, a free painter paints one wall per unit of time simultaneously. Return the minimum cost to paint all n walls. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 500, 1 <= cost[i], time[i] <= 500.

examples.explanation: Paint wall 2 with paid painter (cost 2, time 2). Free painter paints 2 walls simultaneously. All 4 walls painted at cost 2+1=3.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of walls assigned to the paid painter. For each subset, check if the free painter can cover the rest (free painter covers at most sum of time[i] for paid walls). Return minimum cost subset. O(2^n * n) time.

optimal.explanation: Use DP where dp[j] = min cost such that we can cover j extra walls via free painter. For each wall i, we can assign it to paid painter gaining time[i] free-painter slots. Equivalent to 0/1 knapsack. O(n^2) time.

problems.title: Maximum Earnings From Taxi
problems.description: A taxi driver starts at point 0 on a number line of length n. Given rides where rides[i] = [start, end, tip], the driver earns end - start + tip for ride i. At most one ride can be taken at a time. Return the maximum earnings the driver can achieve. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, 1 <= rides.length <= 3*10^4.

examples.explanation: Take ride [2,5,4]: earn 5-2+4=7. Taking both is impossible. 7 is optimal.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort rides by end point. Use recursion with memoization: for each position, either skip to next ride or take it and jump to its end. Without pruning this is O(m^2) where m is rides count.

optimal.explanation: Use a DP array indexed by position (1..n). dp[i] = max earnings reachable at position i. For each ride ending at e, update dp[e] = max(dp[e], dp[start] + profit). Fill with running max for O(n + m log m) total.

problems.title: Strange Printer II
problems.description: A printer can print a rectangle of cells with a single color in one turn, overwriting previous colors. Given a target grid of colors, determine if it is possible to print the grid using at most 60 different colors. Return true if achievable, false otherwise. Constraints: m, n <= 60, 1 <= colors <= 60.

examples.explanation: Print color 1 over the full grid first, then print color 2 in the bottom-right 2x2 region.

bruteForce.explanation: For each color, find its bounding rectangle. Then try all topological orderings of colors (color A must be printed before B if A's bounding box overlaps B's region but B appears inside A's box). Check for cycles. O(c^2 * m * n) where c is the number of colors.

optimal.explanation: Find bounding box per color, then build a dependency graph: color A must be printed before B if B appears inside A's bounding box but A is not B. Run topological sort (Kahn's algorithm). If no cycle, return true. O(c * m * n) time.

problems.title: Number of Music Playlists
problems.description: You want to make a playlist of exactly goal songs using n different songs, where every song is played at least once, and a song can only be replayed after at least k other songs have been played. Return the number of possible playlists modulo 10^9 + 7. Constraints: 0 <= k < n <= goal <= 100.

examples.explanation: There are 6 playlists of length 3 using all 3 songs where no song repeats back-to-back.

bruteForce.explanation: Use backtracking: build each playlist position by position, tracking which songs have been used and the last k songs played. This is O(n^goal) without memoization.

optimal.explanation: Use bottom-up DP: dp[i][j] = number of playlists of length i using exactly j unique songs. Transitions: add a new song (multiply by n-j+1) or replay an old one not in last k (multiply by max(0,j-k)). O(goal * n) time.

problems.title: Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule
problems.description: You have a list of jobs with difficulty[i] that must be done in order. You need to schedule them in exactly d days. Each day you must do at least one job, and days are contiguous partitions of the job list. The difficulty of a day is the maximum difficulty job done that day. Return the minimum total difficulty, or -1 if not possible. Constraints: 1 <= d <= n <= 300.

examples.explanation: Day 1: do job [6] (difficulty 6). Day 2: do jobs [5,4,3,2,1] (difficulty 5). Total = 11. Optimal: day 1: [6,5,4,3,2] (difficulty 6), day 2: [1] (difficulty 1). Total = 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion without memoization: for each day, try ending it at every possible job, taking the max difficulty for that day's segment, and recurse for the remaining days and jobs. O(n^d) time.

optimal.explanation: Use 2D DP: dp[day][i] = min difficulty scheduling first i jobs in exactly day days. Transition: for each last day starting point j, dp[day][i] = min(dp[day-1][j] + max(jd[j..i])). O(d * n^2) with O(d * n) space.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.description: Given a rotated sorted array nums that may contain duplicates, return the minimum element. The array was originally sorted in ascending order but rotated at some unknown pivot. Duplicates make worst-case O(n) unavoidable, but aim for O(log n) on average.

examples.explanation: The minimum element is 0, found after the rotation point.

bruteForce.explanation: Scan the entire array and return the smallest element found. This is straightforward but ignores the rotated sorted structure.

optimal.explanation: Use binary search, but when nums[mid] == nums[right], decrement right by 1 to skip duplicates. This achieves O(log n) average and O(n) worst case.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.description: Given a rotated sorted array nums that may contain duplicates and an integer target, return true if target exists in the array, otherwise return false. The array was rotated at an unknown pivot index. Duplicates may prevent you from determining which half is sorted.

examples.explanation: 0 is present in the array at indices 3 and 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Perform a linear scan of the entire array and check if any element equals target. This ignores the sorted and rotated property completely.

optimal.explanation: Use binary search with a special case: when nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], increment left and decrement right to skip duplicates, then continue standard rotated binary search logic.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
problems.description: Given a sorted array nums of integers and a target value, return the starting and ending position of target in the array as a pair [first, last]. If target is not found, return [-1, -1]. Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: 8 first appears at index 3 and last appears at index 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Do a linear scan to find the first occurrence from the left and another scan for the last occurrence from the right. This is O(n) and does not use the sorted property.

optimal.explanation: Run two separate binary searches: one to find the leftmost index (lower bound) and one to find the rightmost index (upper bound - 1) of target.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.description: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted in ascending order and the first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row, and an integer target, return true if target is in the matrix. Your solution must run in O(log(m*n)) time.

examples.explanation: 3 exists at row 0, column 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate over every cell in the matrix to check if any equals target. This runs in O(m*n) and ignores the sorted structure.

optimal.explanation: Treat the 2D matrix as a flattened 1D sorted array and perform a single binary search using index arithmetic to map mid to (row, col).

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix II
problems.description: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted left to right and each column is sorted top to bottom, and a target integer, return true if target exists in the matrix. The rows do not necessarily start greater than the end of the previous row.

examples.explanation: 5 is found at row 1, column 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Check every element in the matrix one by one. This O(m*n) approach doesn't exploit the sorted row/column property.

optimal.explanation: Start from the top-right corner: if current value equals target return true; if greater move left; if smaller move down. This eliminates a row or column at each step.

problems.title: Sqrt of x
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer x, return the integer square root of x (i.e., the floor of the square root). You must not use any built-in exponent function or square root function. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer.

examples.explanation: The square root of 8 is 2.828..., and since we return the floor, the answer is 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate from 1 upward and check if i*i <= x. Return i-1 when i*i exceeds x. This linear scan is O(sqrt(x)).

optimal.explanation: Binary search between 1 and x/2+1: find the largest mid such that mid*mid <= x. This reduces the search space logarithmically.

problems.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
problems.description: You are playing a guessing game where a number n is picked from 1 to n. A guess() API returns -1 if your guess is too high, 1 if too low, and 0 if correct. Implement guessNumber(n) that finds the picked number using the minimum number of calls to guess().

examples.explanation: Binary search converges on 6 using at most log2(10) calls to guess().

bruteForce.explanation: Try every number from 1 to n sequentially and call guess() until the result is 0. This takes O(n) calls in the worst case.

optimal.explanation: Apply binary search: check the midpoint using guess(), and narrow the search range based on whether the answer is higher or lower.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of sizes m and n respectively, return the median of the combined sorted array. The overall run time complexity must be O(log(m+n)). Both arrays may be empty, and the combined size is at least 1.

examples.explanation: The merged array is [1,2,3] and the median is 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Merge both sorted arrays into a single sorted array, then return the middle element (or average of two middle elements for even length). This takes O(m+n) time and space.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the smaller array to find the correct partition such that all elements on the left of both partitions are smaller than all elements on the right, then compute median from partition boundary values.

problems.title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
problems.description: Given n basket positions in a sorted array position[] and m balls to place, return the maximum minimum magnetic force (minimum distance) between any two balls. You must place all m balls into distinct baskets, maximizing the minimum distance between any pair of balls.

examples.explanation: Place balls at positions 1, 4, 7. The minimum distance is 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible minimum distances from 1 to max_position and check if it's feasible to place m balls with at least that distance apart. This is O(max_pos * n) which is too slow.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the answer (minimum distance). For each candidate distance, greedily check if m balls can be placed. This reduces the search to O(n log(max_position)).

problems.title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
problems.description: Given an array weights of package weights and an integer days, return the minimum capacity of a ship that can ship all packages within days days. Packages must be shipped in order; each day, you load packages until adding the next one would exceed the ship's capacity.

examples.explanation: With capacity 15, the packages can be split over 5 days: [1-5],[6-8],[9],[10] etc.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every possible capacity from max(weights) to sum(weights) and return the first capacity for which all packages can be shipped within days days.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights). For each candidate capacity, greedily simulate shipping to check feasibility in O(n) time.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.description: Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas and she has h hours to eat them all. Each hour she picks a pile and eats at most k bananas from it (finishing the pile in one hour if it has fewer). Return the minimum integer k such that she can eat all bananas within h hours.

examples.explanation: With k=4, Koko needs ceil(3/4)+ceil(6/4)+ceil(7/4)+ceil(11/4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every eating speed from 1 to max(piles) and check if Koko can finish all bananas within h hours at that speed. Return the first valid speed.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the eating speed k between 1 and max(piles). For each candidate speed, compute hours needed in O(n) time using ceiling division.

problems.title: Aggressive Cows
problems.description: Given n stalls at positions[] and c cows to place, find the maximum possible minimum distance between any two cows. You must place all c cows into distinct stalls to maximize the smallest gap between any pair of cows.

examples.explanation: Place cows at positions 1, 4, 9 giving minimum distance 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort stalls and try all possible minimum distances from 1 to max_gap. For each candidate distance, greedily check if c cows can be placed. Return the largest valid distance.

optimal.explanation: Sort the stalls and binary search on the minimum distance between 1 and (max-min). Greedily verify feasibility in O(n) for each candidate distance.

problems.title: Book Allocation Problem
problems.description: Given n books with pages[] and m students, allocate contiguous books to each student minimizing the maximum number of pages assigned to any student. Each student gets at least one book and books must be allocated in order. Return -1 if allocation is not possible.

examples.explanation: Allocate [12,34,67] to student 1 (113 pages) and [90] to student 2 (90 pages). Max is 113.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every possible maximum page limit from max(pages) to sum(pages) and check if books can be allocated to m students such that no student gets more than that limit.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the answer (maximum pages) between max(pages) and sum(pages). Greedily check feasibility by allocating books in order within the limit.

problems.title: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, split nums into k non-empty subarrays such that the maximum subarray sum is minimized. Return that minimized maximum sum. Each element must belong to exactly one contiguous subarray.

examples.explanation: Split into [7,2,5] and [10,8], giving maximum sums 14 and 18. The minimized maximum is 18.

bruteForce.explanation: Use dynamic programming where dp[i][j] = minimum largest sum splitting first i elements into j parts. This is O(n^2 * k) time.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the answer between max(nums) and sum(nums). For each candidate maximum sum, greedily count minimum splits needed and check if it is <= k.

problems.title: Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer threshold, find the smallest divisor such that the sum of ceil(nums[i] / divisor) for all i is <= threshold. The divisor must be a positive integer, and 1 <= divisor <= max(nums).

examples.explanation: With divisor=5, sum = ceil(1/5)+ceil(2/5)+ceil(5/5)+ceil(9/5) = 1+1+1+2 = 5 <= 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every divisor from 1 to max(nums). For each divisor compute the sum of ceiling divisions and return the first divisor where sum <= threshold.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the divisor between 1 and max(nums). For each candidate divisor, compute the sum of ceiling divisions in O(n) and narrow the search based on the comparison with threshold.

problems.title: Find K Closest Elements
problems.description: Given a sorted integer array arr, two integers k and x, return the k closest integers to x in the array. The result should be sorted in ascending order. If two integers are equally close, choose the smaller one. 1 <= k <= arr.length.

examples.explanation: The 4 closest elements to 3 are 1,2,3,4 with distances 2,1,0,1.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort all elements by distance to x (breaking ties by value), take the first k, then sort them in ascending order. This is O(n log n) and doesn't exploit the sorted property.

optimal.explanation: Binary search for the left boundary of the k-element window. Compare arr[mid] and arr[mid+k]: if x-arr[mid] > arr[mid+k]-x, the window should shift right, otherwise left.

problems.title: Count of Range Sum
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and two integers lower and upper, return the number of range sums that lie in [lower, upper] inclusive. A range sum S(i, j) is defined as the sum of elements in nums between indices i and j inclusive (0 <= i <= j < n).

examples.explanation: The three ranges are [0,0]=(-2), [0,2]=2, [2,2]=(-1), all within [-2,2].

bruteForce.explanation: Compute all O(n^2) range sums using prefix sums and count how many fall within [lower, upper]. This is O(n^2) time.

optimal.explanation: Use merge sort on the prefix sum array. During the merge step, use two pointers to count valid range sums [lower, upper] in the left half against the right half, achieving O(n log n).

problems.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
problems.description: Given a mountain array arr (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing), return the index of the peak element. The array has at least 3 elements. There is guaranteed to be exactly one peak. Your solution should run in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The peak is at index 1 with value 10, which is the maximum.

bruteForce.explanation: Do a linear scan to find the element that is greater than both its neighbors, or find the maximum element and return its index.

optimal.explanation: Binary search: if arr[mid] < arr[mid+1], the peak is to the right (lo = mid+1); otherwise the peak is at mid or to the left (hi = mid). Converges to the peak index in O(log n).

problems.title: Minimum Time to Complete Trips
problems.description: Given an array time where time[i] is the time for bus i to complete one trip and an integer totalTrips, return the minimum time for all buses together to complete at least totalTrips trips. Each bus operates independently and can make multiple trips.

examples.explanation: At time=3: bus 1 completes 3 trips, bus 2 completes 1 trip, bus 3 completes 1 trip, total = 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate time step by step: at each time unit, count how many total trips all buses have completed. Return the first time when cumulative trips >= totalTrips.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on the answer time t between 1 and totalTrips * min(time). For each candidate t, compute total trips completed across all buses in O(n) and check feasibility.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Removable Characters
problems.description: Given strings s and p and an array removable of indices, each round you remove the character at removable[i] from s. Return the maximum number k such that after removing removable[0..k-1] indices from s, p is still a subsequence of s. 1 <= p.length <= s.length.

examples.explanation: After removing indices 3 and 1, s becomes "a_c_cb" and p="ab" is still a subsequence.

bruteForce.explanation: For each k from 0 to removable.size(), mark the first k indices as removed and check if p is still a subsequence of s. Return the maximum valid k.

optimal.explanation: Binary search on k: for a given k, mark removable[0..k-1] as removed using a boolean array and check if p is a subsequence of s in O(|s|). Binary search reduces checks to O(log(|removable|)).

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
problems.description: Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same. Return the number of unique elements k. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4, -100 <= nums[i] <= 100.

examples.explanation: There are 2 unique elements. The first two elements of nums are modified to be 1 and 2 respectively.

bruteForce.explanation: Use a set to collect unique elements, then copy them back into the array in order. This uses extra space proportional to the number of unique elements.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers: a slow pointer tracks the position of the last unique element, and a fast pointer scans through the array. When a new unique value is found, write it at the slow pointer position.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
problems.description: Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, remove duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears at most twice. Return the number of elements k after modification. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The first five elements after modification are 1,1,2,2,3. Each element appears at most twice.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate through the array and use a count map to track occurrences, then rebuild the array keeping at most two of each element into a new array and copy back.

optimal.explanation: Use a two-pointer approach where the write pointer k tracks valid positions. An element is written only if k < 2 or it differs from nums[k-2], allowing at most two copies without extra space.

problems.title: Remove Element
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer val, remove all occurrences of val in-place. The order of the remaining elements may change. Return k, the number of elements not equal to val. Constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 50, 0 <= val <= 100.

examples.explanation: After removing all 3s, the first two elements are 2 and 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Copy all elements not equal to val into a temporary array, then copy back into nums and return the count.

optimal.explanation: Use a single write pointer k. Traverse the array; whenever nums[i] != val, write it to nums[k] and increment k. This is done in-place with O(1) space.

problems.title: 3Sum Smaller
problems.description: Given an array of n integers nums and an integer target, find the number of index triplets i, j, k such that i < j < k and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] < target. Constraints: n == nums.length, 0 <= n <= 3500, -100 <= nums[i] <= 100, -100 <= target <= 100.

examples.explanation: The two triplets are (-2,0,1) with sum -1 and (-2,0,3) -- wait, that's 1 < 2. Triplets: (-2,0,1) sum=-1 and (-2,1,3) sum=2 not valid. Valid: (-2,0,1)=-1 and (-2,0,3)=1. Count=2.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible triplets with three nested loops and count those whose sum is less than target. This is O(n^3) time.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array, then for each i use a two-pointer approach on the subarray [i+1, n-1]. When nums[i]+nums[lo]+nums[hi] < target, all pairs (lo, lo+1..hi) are valid, adding hi-lo to count.

problems.title: Boats to Save People
problems.description: You are given an array people where people[i] is the weight of the i-th person, and an infinite number of boats where each boat can carry at most limit weight. Each boat carries at most two people at the same time. Return the minimum number of boats to carry every person. Constraints: 1 <= people.length <= 5 * 10^4, 1 <= people[i] <= limit <= 3 * 10^4.

examples.explanation: Both people can fit in one boat since 1+2=3 <= 3.

bruteForce.explanation: Sort the people array and try all pairings using a greedy check, tracking who has been paired and counting boats. This is less efficient due to extra bookkeeping.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and use two pointers from both ends. Greedily pair the heaviest person with the lightest if they fit; otherwise send the heaviest alone. This runs in O(n log n) due to sorting.

problems.title: Sort Array by Parity
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, move all the even integers to the beginning of the array followed by all the odd integers. Return any array that satisfies this condition. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000, 0 <= nums[i] <= 5000.

examples.explanation: The outputs [4,2,3,1], [2,4,1,3], and [4,2,1,3] are also accepted.

bruteForce.explanation: Create two separate lists for even and odd numbers, then concatenate them and copy back to the result array.

optimal.explanation: Use two pointers from both ends of the array. The left pointer seeks odd numbers and the right pointer seeks even numbers; swap them when both are found. This is done in-place with O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Maximum Erasure Value
problems.description: You are given an array of positive integers nums. You want to erase a subarray containing unique elements. The score of erasing the subarray is the sum of its elements. Return the maximum score you can get by erasing exactly one subarray. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The optimal subarray is [2,4,5,6] with sum 17.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays using two nested loops, verify uniqueness using a set, and track the maximum sum of a valid subarray.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window with a hashmap to track element counts. Expand the right boundary and shrink the left when a duplicate is found, maintaining the current window sum for O(n) overall.

problems.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
problems.description: You are given a 0-indexed integer array nums where nums[i] represents the score of the i-th student. You are also given an integer k. Pick the scores of any k students from the array so that the difference between the highest and lowest of the k scores is minimized. Return the minimum possible difference. Constraints: 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 1000, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Pick 0,35,50,90 with difference 90-0=90; pick 35,50,90,100 with difference 65. Minimum is 65.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all combinations of k elements from the array using recursion or bitmask, compute the difference between max and min for each combination, and return the minimum.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and slide a window of size k. The minimum difference is always nums[i+k-1] - nums[i] for some i, since the best k elements are always contiguous after sorting.

problems.title: Number of Subsequences That Satisfy the Given Sum Condition
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the number of non-empty subsequences of nums such that the sum of the minimum and maximum element on it is less or equal to target. Since the answer may be too large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^6, 1 <= target <= 10^6.

examples.explanation: The subsequences are [3],[3,5],[3,5,6],[3,6]. Count = 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Enumerate all 2^n subsequences using bitmask, find the min and max of each, check the condition, and count valid ones. This is exponential and only feasible for very small inputs.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and use two pointers. For each left pointer, find the rightmost position where nums[left]+nums[right] <= target. All 2^(right-left) subsequences starting with nums[left] are valid.

problems.title: Bag of Tokens
problems.description: You have an initial power of power, an initial score of 0, and a bag of tokens where tokens[i] is the value of the i-th token. You can play each token at most once. Face-up: spend tokens[i] power to gain 1 score. Face-down: spend 1 score to gain tokens[i] power. Return the maximum score you can achieve. Constraints: 0 <= tokens.length <= 1000, 0 <= tokens[i] <= 10^4, 0 <= power <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Play token 0 face-up (power=100, score=1), token 3 face-down (power=500, score=0), token 1 face-up (power=300, score=1), token 2 face-up (power=0, score=2). Max score = 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of token plays using DFS/backtracking and track the maximum score achievable at each state.

optimal.explanation: Sort tokens and use two pointers. Greedily play the cheapest token face-up to gain score, or the most expensive token face-down to gain power, maximizing the peak score reached.

problems.title: Longest Mountain in Array
problems.description: Given an integer array arr, return the length of the longest subarray which is a mountain. A mountain subarray has at least 3 elements and strictly increases to a peak then strictly decreases. Return 0 if no mountain exists. Constraints: 1 <= arr.length <= 10^4, 0 <= arr[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The largest mountain is [1,4,7,3,2] which has length 5.

bruteForce.explanation: For every possible peak index, expand left while strictly decreasing and expand right while strictly decreasing, compute the mountain length, and track the maximum.

optimal.explanation: Use two passes to precompute up[i] (ascending run ending at i) and down[i] (descending run starting at i). For each peak where both up[i] > 0 and down[i] > 0, the mountain length is up[i]+down[i]+1.

problems.title: Fruit Into Baskets
problems.description: You are visiting a farm that has a single row of fruit trees. You have two baskets and can only hold one type of fruit per basket. Starting from any tree, pick one fruit from each tree you pass without stopping. Return the maximum number of fruits you can pick. Constraints: 1 <= fruits.length <= 10^5, 0 <= fruits[i] < fruits.length.

examples.explanation: Pick all three fruits. Basket 1 holds type 1, basket 2 holds type 2.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays using two nested loops and count the longest one that contains at most 2 distinct values.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window with a hashmap to maintain at most 2 distinct fruit types. Shrink from the left when a third type is added, tracking the maximum window size.

problems.title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the number of good subarrays of nums. A good array is an array where the number of different integers in that array is exactly k. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^4, 1 <= nums[i] <= nums.length, 1 <= k <= nums.length.

examples.explanation: Subarrays with exactly 2 distinct integers: [1,2],[2,1],[1,2],[2,3],[1,2,1],[2,1,2],[1,2,1,2]. Count = 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Enumerate all subarrays, use a set to count distinct elements, and count those with exactly k distinct integers.

optimal.explanation: Use the identity: exactly k distinct = at most k distinct minus at most k-1 distinct. Implement a helper that counts subarrays with at most k distinct values using a sliding window, then subtract.

problems.title: Maximum Consecutive Ones III
problems.description: Given a binary array nums and an integer k, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s in the array if you can flip at most k 0s. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, nums[i] is either 0 or 1, 0 <= k <= nums.length.

examples.explanation: Flip the two 0s at positions 9 and 10 to get [1,1,1,0,0,1,1,1,1,1,1]. Maximum consecutive 1s = 6.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays using two nested loops, count the number of zeros in each, and track the maximum length where zero count is at most k.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window: expand the right boundary and track zeros flipped. When zeros exceed k, shrink from the left. The window always represents a valid range with at most k zeros flipped.

problems.title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element
problems.description: The frequency of an element is the number of times it occurs in an array. You are given an integer array nums and an integer k. In one operation you can increment an element by 1. Return the maximum possible frequency of an element after performing at most k operations. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5, 1 <= k <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Increment 1 by 3 and 2 by 2 to make all elements 4. Frequency of 4 becomes 3.

bruteForce.explanation: For each element as the target value, count how many other elements can be incremented to equal it within k total operations.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and use a sliding window. The cost to make all elements in [left, right] equal to nums[right] is nums[right]*(right-left+1) - windowSum. Shrink the window when cost exceeds k.

problems.title: Grumpy Bookstore Owner
problems.description: A bookstore owner has customers[i] customers during the i-th minute. The owner is grumpy[i] for that minute. When the owner uses a secret technique for minutes consecutive minutes, they are not grumpy. Return the maximum number of customers that can be satisfied. Constraints: 1 <= minutes <= customers.length <= 2 * 10^4, 0 <= customers[i] <= 1000, grumpy[i] is 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: Keep the technique for the last 3 minutes. Satisfied customers: 1+1+1+2+1+1+7+5 = 19, but 5 are already satisfied from grumpy=0. Optimal technique window [5,6,7] adds 5+7+5 extra, total 16.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible starting positions for the technique window of length minutes, compute total satisfied customers for each, and return the maximum.

optimal.explanation: First compute base satisfaction (non-grumpy minutes). Then use a sliding window of size minutes to find the maximum extra customers gained by suppressing grumpiness in that window.

problems.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
problems.description: You are given an integer array nums consisting of n elements, and an integer k. Find a contiguous subarray of length exactly k that has the maximum average value and return this value. Any answer with a calculation error less than 10^-5 will be accepted. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= k <= n <= 10^5, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The subarray [12,-5,-6,50] has the maximum average: (12-5-6+50)/4 = 51/4 = 12.75.

bruteForce.explanation: Compute the sum for every window of length k using nested loops and track the maximum sum to derive the maximum average.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window of size k: compute the initial window sum then slide by adding the new element and removing the old, updating the maximum sum in O(1) per step.

problems.title: Longest Subarray of 1s After Deleting One Element
problems.description: Given a binary array nums, you should delete one element from it. Return the size of the longest non-empty subarray containing only 1s in the resulting array. Return 0 if there is no such subarray. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, nums[i] is either 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: After deleting the 0 at index 2, the subarray [1,1,1] has length 3.

bruteForce.explanation: For each index, try deleting the element and compute the longest run of 1s in the remaining array. Track the overall maximum.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window tracking the number of zeros in the window. Allow at most one zero (the deleted element). When zeros exceed 1, shrink from the left. The answer is window size minus 1 (for the deletion).

problems.title: Count Number of Nice Subarrays
problems.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the number of nice subarrays. A nice subarray is a contiguous subarray that contains exactly k odd numbers. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 50000, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5, 1 <= k <= nums.length.

examples.explanation: The nice subarrays are [1,1,2,1] and [1,2,1,1], each containing exactly 3 odd numbers.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays with two nested loops, count odd numbers in each, and increment the result when the count equals k.

optimal.explanation: Use prefix sums of odd counts and a hashmap. The count of subarrays with exactly k odds equals the count of prefix pairs whose difference is k, computed in O(n).

problems.title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
problems.description: There are several cards arranged in a row, and each card has an associated number of points. In one step, you can take one card from the beginning or the end of the row. You take exactly k cards. Return the maximum score of the k cards you take. Constraints: 1 <= cardPoints.length <= 10^5, 1 <= cardPoints[i] <= 10^4, 1 <= k <= cardPoints.length.

examples.explanation: Take the last three cards [5,6,1]? No, 5+6+1=12. Or take [6,1,1]=8. Max is taking 4,5,6 from right minus... optimal is 12 by taking [1,6,5] from ends.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible splits of taking i cards from the left and k-i cards from the right for i from 0 to k, computing each sum and tracking the maximum.

optimal.explanation: Equivalently, find the minimum sum subarray of length n-k in the middle (the cards you do NOT take). Total sum minus that minimum middle window sum gives the answer.

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Reduce X to Zero
problems.description: You are given an integer array nums and an integer x. In one operation, you can either remove the leftmost or the rightmost element from nums and subtract its value from x. Return the minimum number of operations to reduce x to exactly 0, or -1 if not possible. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4, 1 <= x <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: Remove 3 and 2 from the right. 5 - 3 - 2 = 0 in 2 operations.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible combinations of taking i elements from the left and j from the right using two nested loops, and track the minimum operations when left+right sum equals x.

optimal.explanation: Equivalent to finding the longest subarray with sum equal to total-x. Use a sliding window on the middle subarray: the answer is n minus the length of that longest subarray.

problems.title: Longest Turbulent Subarray
problems.description: Given an integer array arr, return the length of a maximum size turbulent subarray of arr. A subarray is turbulent if the comparison sign flips between each adjacent pair of elements in the subarray. Constraints: 1 <= arr.length <= 4 * 10^4, 0 <= arr[i] <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,2,10,7,8] is turbulent: 4>2<10>7<8. Length = 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays to find the longest one that satisfies the turbulence condition by verifying the alternating comparison signs.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window where the left pointer resets when the turbulence condition breaks. Track the previous comparison direction and reset or shrink accordingly.

problems.title: Max Consecutive Ones II
problems.description: Given a binary array nums, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s in the array if you can flip at most one 0. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, nums[i] is either 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: Flip the first 0: [1,1,1,1,0]. Maximum consecutive 1s = 4.

bruteForce.explanation: For each 0 in the array, temporarily flip it to 1 and compute the length of the consecutive 1s sequence containing that position.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window with at most one zero allowed. Track the position of the last zero seen (prevZeroPos). When a second zero is encountered, move left to prevZeroPos+1 and update prevZeroPos.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum Variant
problems.description: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray of which the sum is greater than or equal to target. If there is no such subarray, return 0 instead. Constraints: 1 <= target <= 10^9, 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,3] has the minimal length 2 under the problem constraint.

bruteForce.explanation: Check all subarrays using two nested loops, compute their sums, and track the minimum length where the sum is at least target.

optimal.explanation: Use a sliding window: expand the right boundary adding elements, and once the sum meets target, shrink from the left while the condition still holds, updating the minimum length each time.

problems.title: Sliding Window Median
problems.description: The median is the middle value in an ordered integer list. Given an array nums and a sliding window of size k, return an array of the medians for each window position from left to right. Constraints: 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5, -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1.

bruteForce.explanation: For each window position, copy the window elements into a temporary array, sort it, and extract the median. This is O(nk log k) overall.

optimal.explanation: Use two multisets (max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half) to maintain the sorted order. For each slide, insert the new element, remove the outgoing element, rebalance the two sets, and read the median from the tops.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.description: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order.

examples.explanation: All possible subsets of [1,2,3] including the empty set.

bruteForce.explanation: Use bit masking: for n elements, iterate through all 2^n bitmasks and include element i if bit i is set.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking: at each index, decide to include or exclude the element, generating all subsets recursively without duplicates.

problems.title: Subsets II
problems.description: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicates, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. Return the solution in any order.

examples.explanation: Even though 2 appears twice, each unique subset appears only once in the result.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all subsets and use a set to deduplicate by storing sorted subsets as strings.

optimal.explanation: Sort the array and use backtracking; skip duplicate elements at the same recursion level to avoid duplicate subsets.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.description: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all the possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: All 3! = 6 permutations of [1,2,3] are returned.

bruteForce.explanation: Use next_permutation iteratively starting from sorted array to enumerate all permutations.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking with a visited array; at each step pick an unused element, add it, recurse, then remove it.

problems.title: Permutations II
problems.description: Given a collection of numbers, nums, that might contain duplicates, return all possible unique permutations in any order.

examples.explanation: There are 3 unique permutations even though 1 appears twice.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations and store them in a set to remove duplicates.

optimal.explanation: Sort and backtrack; skip a duplicate element if the previous identical element was not used (preventing same-level duplicates).

problems.title: Combinations
problems.description: Given two integers n and k, return all possible combinations of k numbers chosen from the range [1, n]. You may return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: All C(4,2) = 6 combinations of size 2 from numbers 1 to 4.

bruteForce.explanation: Use nested loops or recursion to generate all k-size combinations from 1 to n without any pruning.

optimal.explanation: Backtrack with pruning: stop early if remaining numbers are not enough to fill k slots, reducing unnecessary branches.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.description: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target integer target, return a list of all unique combinations of candidates where the chosen numbers sum to target. The same number may be chosen from candidates an unlimited number of times. Combinations may be returned in any order.

examples.explanation: 2+2+3=7 and 7=7 are the only combinations that sum to 7.

bruteForce.explanation: Recursively explore all combinations, allowing repeated use of each element, collecting those that sum to target.

optimal.explanation: Sort candidates first and prune branches where remaining target becomes negative, improving practical performance significantly.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.description: Given a collection of candidate numbers (candidates) and a target number (target), find all unique combinations in candidates where the candidate numbers sum to target. Each number in candidates may only be used once in the combination.

examples.explanation: Four unique combinations sum to 8; note that 1 appears twice in input but combinations are unique.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all combinations using DFS and store results in a set to eliminate duplicates.

optimal.explanation: Sort and backtrack; skip duplicate candidates at the same level (i > start && candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]) to avoid duplicate combinations.

problems.title: Combination Sum III
problems.description: Find all valid combinations of k numbers that sum up to n such that only numbers 1 through 9 are used and each number is used at most once. Return a list of all possible valid combinations.

examples.explanation: 1+2+4=7, and it uses exactly 3 numbers from 1-9 with no repeats.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all combinations of k numbers from 1-9 using DFS without pruning, collecting those that sum to n.

optimal.explanation: Backtrack with pruning: stop if remaining sum is impossible given remaining digits or if we've picked too many numbers.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.description: Given a string containing digits from 2-9 inclusive, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent. Return the answer in any order. A mapping of digits to letters is provided (like on a telephone keypad).

examples.explanation: Digit 2 maps to abc and digit 3 maps to def, giving 9 combinations.

bruteForce.explanation: Iteratively build combinations by starting with one letter and appending all letters from next digit.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking to build combinations character by character, avoiding repeated string concatenation overhead.

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.description: The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing n queens on an n x n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. Given an integer n, return all distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle. Each solution contains a distinct board configuration where 'Q' indicates a queen and '.' indicates an empty space.

examples.explanation: There are two distinct solutions to the 4-queens puzzle.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of column positions for each row and verify no two queens share a diagonal.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking with bitsets for columns, left diagonals, and right diagonals to check queen conflicts in O(1) per placement.

problems.title: N-Queens II
problems.description: The n-queens puzzle is the problem of placing n queens on an n x n chessboard such that no two queens attack each other. Given an integer n, return the number of distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle.

examples.explanation: There are 2 distinct solutions for the 4-queens problem.

bruteForce.explanation: Try placing a queen in each column for each row recursively, incrementing count when all n queens are placed.

optimal.explanation: Use bitmask to track used columns and diagonals for O(1) conflict checks, significantly reducing constant factor.

problems.title: Sudoku Solver
problems.description: Write a program to solve a Sudoku puzzle by filling the empty cells. A sudoku solution must satisfy all of the following rules: each of the digits 1-9 must occur exactly once in each row, column, and 3x3 sub-box. Empty cells are indicated by '.'.

examples.explanation: The board is filled so every row, column, and 3x3 box contains digits 1-9 exactly once.

bruteForce.explanation: For each empty cell, try all digits 1-9 and check validity against rows, columns, and boxes by scanning.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(9^m) where m is empty cells

optimal.explanation: Use bitmask arrays for rows, columns, and boxes to check validity in O(1), dramatically reducing constant factor.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning Backtracking
problems.description: Given a string s, partition s such that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitioning of s.

examples.explanation: Both partitions have all substrings as palindromes: [a,a,b] and [aa,b].

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS to try all possible cuts and check if each substring is a palindrome by scanning.

optimal.explanation: Precompute palindrome checks using DP in O(n^2), then backtrack using the lookup table for O(1) palindrome queries.

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
problems.description: Given n pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses.

examples.explanation: There are 5 valid ways to form 3 pairs of parentheses.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all 2^(2n) sequences of parentheses and filter those that are valid balanced strings.

optimal.explanation: Backtrack by tracking open and close counts; only add '(' if open < n and ')' if close < open, ensuring only valid strings are generated.

problems.title: Restore IP Addresses
problems.description: A valid IP address consists of exactly four integers separated by single dots. Each integer is between 0 and 255 (inclusive) and cannot have leading zeros. Given a string s containing only digits, return all possible valid IP addresses that can be formed by inserting dots into s.

examples.explanation: Only two valid IP addresses can be formed from the string.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all combinations of three dot positions using three nested loops and validate each resulting IP.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking to place exactly 4 parts; prune when remaining string length is incompatible with remaining parts needed.

problems.title: Expression Add Operators
problems.description: Given a string num that contains only digits and an integer target, return all possibilities to insert the binary operators '+', '-', or '*' between the digits of num so that the resultant expression evaluates to the target value.

examples.explanation: Both 1*2*3=6 and 1+2+3=6 evaluate to the target.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all ways to insert operators between digits, evaluate each expression, and collect those equaling the target.

optimal.explanation: The same backtracking approach is already optimal; use prev to handle multiplication precedence without re-evaluating the entire expression.

problems.title: Beautiful Arrangement
problems.description: Suppose you have n integers labeled 1 through n. A permutation of those n integers perm is called beautiful if for every i (1-indexed), either perm[i] is divisible by i or i is divisible by perm[i]. Given an integer n, return the number of beautiful arrangements you can construct.

examples.explanation: Arrangements [1,2] and [2,1] are both beautiful: for [1,2], 1%1=0 and 2%2=0; for [2,1], 2%1=0 and 1%1=0.

bruteForce.explanation: Generate all permutations of 1 to n and count those satisfying the beautiful arrangement condition.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking from position n down to 1, only placing numbers that satisfy the divisibility condition at the current position.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(k) where k is much less than n!

problems.title: Unique Paths III
problems.description: You are given an m x n integer array grid where grid[i][j] could be 0 (empty), 1 (starting square), 2 (ending square), or -1 (obstacle). Return the number of 4-directional walks from the starting square to the ending square that walk over every non-obstacle square exactly once.

examples.explanation: There are 2 walks that cover every non-obstacle square exactly once from start to end.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DFS from start, exploring all 4 directions, and count paths that reach end after visiting all non-obstacle cells.

optimal.explanation: Use bitmask DP: represent visited cells as a bitmask and memoize (position, visited_mask) states to avoid recomputation.

problems.title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
problems.description: Given a string s that contains parentheses and letters, remove the minimum number of invalid parentheses to make the input string valid. Return a list of unique strings that are valid with the minimum number of removals.

examples.explanation: Both outputs are valid after removing exactly one parenthesis (the minimum needed).

bruteForce.explanation: BFS level by level removing one character at a time, stopping at the first level that produces valid strings.

optimal.explanation: First count minimum removals needed for left and right parentheses, then DFS with pruning to only generate valid strings with exactly those removals.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if it is possible to divide this array into k non-empty subsets whose sums are all equal.

examples.explanation: It's possible to divide into 4 subsets: (5), (1,4), (2,3), (2,3) each summing to 5.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all ways to assign each element to one of k buckets recursively and check if all buckets have equal sums.

optimal.explanation: Use bitmask DP where the state represents which elements have been used; memoize states to avoid recomputation across recursive calls.

problems.title: Factor Combinations
problems.description: Numbers can be regarded as the product of their factors. Given an integer n, return all possible combinations of its factors. Note that 1 and n are not included as factors, and the factors must be in ascending order.

examples.explanation: 12 = 2*6 = 2*2*3 = 3*4 are all valid factor combinations, not including 1*12 or 12.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible factors from 2 to n-1 recursively and collect combinations that multiply to n.

optimal.explanation: Iterate factors only up to sqrt(n) for the current level, which prunes the search space and ensures no duplicate factor combinations.

problems.title: Binary Watch
problems.description: A binary watch has 4 LEDs for hours (0-11) and 6 LEDs for minutes (0-59). Given an integer turnedOn which represents the number of LEDs currently on, return all possible times the watch could represent. The order does not matter.

examples.explanation: Each time has exactly one LED turned on in either the hours or minutes display.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate all hours (0-11) and minutes (0-59) and include those where the total number of set bits equals turnedOn.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking to enumerate bit combinations, placing bits in hours (bits 0-3) and minutes (bits 4-9) positions.

problems.title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
problems.description: Given an integer n, return the count of all numbers with unique digits x, where 0 <= x < 10^n.

examples.explanation: The answer should be the total numbers in the range 0 <= x < 100 excluding 11,22,33,44,55,66,77,88,99 — which is 91.

bruteForce.explanation: Iterate all numbers from 0 to 10^n and check if each number has all unique digits.

optimal.explanation: Use math: count numbers with exactly k unique digits using permutation formulas and sum for k from 0 to n.

problems.title: Generalized Abbreviation
problems.description: A word's generalized abbreviation can be constructed by replacing any number of non-adjacent substrings with their respective lengths. Given a string word, return a list of all the possible generalized abbreviations of word.

examples.explanation: All 16 possible abbreviations of 'word' are generated where digits replace consecutive characters.

bruteForce.explanation: Use bit masking: for each bit pattern, abbreviate consecutive 1-bits as their count and keep 0-bit characters.

optimal.explanation: Use backtracking: at each position either keep the character or start/extend an abbreviation count, building the string directly.

problems.title: Flip Game II
problems.description: You are playing a Flip Game with a friend. You are given a string currentState that contains only '+' and '-'. You and your friend take turns to flip two consecutive '++'  into '--'. The player who cannot make a move loses. Return true if the starting player can guarantee a win.

examples.explanation: The starting player can win by flipping the middle ++ leaving +--+, after which the opponent cannot guarantee a win.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible moves and check if the opponent loses in all resulting states using minimax recursion.

optimal.explanation: Use memoization with the game state as key to avoid recomputing results for the same board configuration.

problems.title: Assign Cookies
problems.description: You have g children and s cookies. Each child i has a greed factor g[i], and each cookie j has size s[j]. A child is content if s[j] >= g[i]. Assign cookies to maximize the number of content children. Each child can have at most one cookie.

examples.explanation: Only one cookie of size 1 satisfies child with greed 1.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of cookie assignments and track the maximum number of satisfied children.

optimal.explanation: Sort both arrays, then greedily assign the smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy child using two pointers.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(g log g + s log s)

problems.title: Two City Scheduling
problems.description: A company is planning to interview 2n people. costs[i] = [aCost, bCost] where aCost is the cost of flying person i to city A and bCost to city B. Return the minimum cost to fly exactly n people to each city. Constraints: 2 <= n <= 100, costs.length == 2n.

examples.explanation: Person 0 to A (10), person 1 to A (30), person 2 to B (50), person 3 to B (20). Total = 110.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all combinations of choosing n people for city A and the rest for city B, tracking the minimum total cost.

optimal.explanation: Sort by the difference (aCost - bCost); send the first n people to city A (most beneficial) and the rest to city B.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.description: Balloons are represented as intervals [xstart, xend] on a horizontal axis. An arrow shot at x bursts all balloons where xstart <= x <= xend. Find the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons. Constraints: 1 <= points.length <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Shoot at x=6 to burst [2,8] and [1,6]; shoot at x=11 to burst [10,16] and [7,12].

bruteForce.explanation: For each possible arrow position, count how many balloons it bursts, and use a greedy simulation removing burst balloons.

optimal.explanation: Sort by end coordinate; greedily shoot at the earliest end, which bursts all overlapping balloons and minimizes arrows.

problems.title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
problems.description: People are represented as [h, k] where h is height and k is the number of people in front with height >= h. Given a shuffled queue, reconstruct it. Return the reconstructed queue. Constraints: 1 <= people.length <= 2000.

examples.explanation: Each person is placed so that exactly k taller-or-equal people are in front.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of the people array and verify which one satisfies all k constraints.

optimal.explanation: Sort by height descending (ties broken by k ascending), then insert each person at index k in the result list.

problems.title: Partition Labels
problems.description: Given a string s, partition it into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part. Return a list of partition sizes. Each letter appears in at most one part, and the parts concatenate to give the original string.

examples.explanation: Partitions are 'ababcbaca', 'defegde', 'hijhklij' — each letter appears in only one part.

bruteForce.explanation: For each starting position, find the minimum ending position that includes all characters in the current partition by scanning the rest of the string.

optimal.explanation: Precompute the last occurrence of each character, then greedily extend the partition end as we scan and emit a partition when current index equals the end.

problems.title: Advantage Shuffle
problems.description: Given arrays nums1 and nums2, rearrange nums1 to maximize the number of indices i where nums1[i] > nums2[i]. Return any rearrangement of nums1 that achieves this maximum advantage. Both arrays have the same length n.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all permutations of nums1 and count advantages, returning the permutation with the maximum count.

optimal.explanation: Sort nums1; for each largest element in nums2, assign the largest winning element from nums1 or the smallest if none can win (greedy matching).

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers
problems.description: There are n workers with quality[i] and wage[i]. You hire exactly k workers such that every worker is paid at least their minimum wage expectation and all workers are paid in proportion to their quality. Find the minimum total wage. Constraints: 1 <= k <= n <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Hire workers 0 and 2; pay ratio = 7, wages = 70 and 35; total = 105.

bruteForce.explanation: Try every subset of k workers, compute the valid minimum wage for each subset, and return the minimum total.

optimal.explanation: Sort by wage/quality ratio; for each worker as the highest-ratio worker, use a max-heap to maintain the k smallest qualities and compute total cost.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(n log n + n log k)

problems.title: Lemonade Change
problems.description: Customers pay for $5 lemonade with $5, $10, or $20 bills. Give correct change to every customer using the bills received so far. Return true if you can provide change for every customer, false otherwise.

examples.explanation: Customer 4 pays $20; give back $10 and $5 as change. Works with bills collected.

bruteForce.explanation: Simulate each transaction maintaining counts of $5 and $10 bills, trying all possible ways to give change.

optimal.explanation: Greedily prefer giving a $10 bill over three $5 bills for $20 change, as $5 bills are more versatile — this is the same linear solution but with explicit greedy reasoning.

problems.title: Can Place Flowers
problems.description: Given a flowerbed array of 0s and 1s, determine if n new flowers can be planted without violating the no-adjacent-flowers rule. Flowers cannot be placed in adjacent plots. Return true if n flowers can be placed.

examples.explanation: Plant at index 2; no adjacent flowers are violated.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of empty positions and check if any valid subset of size n satisfies the no-adjacency constraint.

optimal.explanation: Greedily plant a flower at every valid empty spot (both neighbors empty or boundary) scanning left to right.

problems.title: Minimum Deletions to Make Character Frequencies Unique
problems.description: A string is good if no two different characters have the same frequency. Given string s, find the minimum number of character deletions to make it good. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^5, s contains only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Delete one 'b' and one 'c' to get frequencies {a:3, b:2, c:1} which are all unique.

bruteForce.explanation: Count character frequencies, then for each duplicate frequency, repeatedly decrement by 1 until unique, counting deletions.

optimal.explanation: Sort frequencies in descending order; for each frequency, reduce it to the largest unused value, accumulating deletions.

problems.title: Remove Covered Intervals
problems.description: Given a list of intervals, remove all intervals that are covered by another interval. Interval [a,b] is covered by [c,d] if c <= a and b <= d. Return the number of remaining intervals after removals.

examples.explanation: [1,4] is covered by [2,8]? No. [3,6] is covered by [2,8]. So 2 intervals remain.

bruteForce.explanation: For each interval, check if any other interval covers it using nested loops, then count uncovered intervals.

optimal.explanation: Sort by start ascending (ties broken by end descending); track the maximum end seen and count intervals that extend beyond it.

problems.title: Course Schedule III
problems.description: There are n courses, each with a duration and a deadline. You can take one course at a time. Return the maximum number of courses you can take. A course must be finished before or on its last day. Constraints: 1 <= courses.length <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Take courses 0, 1, 3 (or 0, 2, 3) for a total of 3 courses.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of courses, check feasibility by sorting by deadline and simulating, and return the maximum feasible subset size.

optimal.explanation: Sort by deadline; use a max-heap of durations. For each course, add it to the heap; if the total time exceeds the deadline, remove the longest course taken.

problems.title: Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations
problems.description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, modify nums by negating any element exactly k times (the same element can be negated multiple times). Maximize the sum of the array after k negations. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 1 <= k <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Negate 2 to get [-2] wait, negate the smallest: negate 2 -> [4,-2,3], sum=5. Actually negate 2: [4,-2,3] sum=5.

bruteForce.explanation: Use recursion or DP to try all choices of which element to negate at each of the k steps, tracking the maximum sum.

optimal.explanation: Sort, negate all negatives from smallest to largest, then if k is odd negate the smallest absolute value element.

problems.title: Break a Palindrome
problems.description: Given a palindromic string palindrome, replace exactly one character with any lowercase English letter so that the result is not a palindrome and is lexicographically smallest. If no such replacement exists, return an empty string.

examples.explanation: Replace the second 'b' at index 1 with 'a' to get 'aaccba' which is not a palindrome and is smallest.

bruteForce.explanation: Try replacing each character with every possible letter a-z and collect all non-palindrome results, then return the lexicographically smallest.

optimal.explanation: Greedily replace the first non-'a' character in the first half with 'a'; if all are 'a', replace the last character with 'b'.

problems.title: Minimum Time to Make Rope Colorful
problems.description: Alice has a rope with colored balloons. She wants no two consecutive balloons of the same color. Given colors string and neededTime array, return the minimum total time to remove balloons so no two consecutive are the same color.

examples.explanation: Remove the 'a' at index 2 (cost 3) to break the consecutive 'aa'. Total = 3.

bruteForce.explanation: For each group of consecutive same-color balloons, try all subsets of removals to keep exactly one, minimizing total removal cost.

optimal.explanation: For each consecutive group of same-color balloons, the optimal choice is to keep the one with maximum time and remove all others (sum - max).

problems.title: Largest Perimeter Triangle
problems.description: Given an integer array nums, return the largest perimeter of a triangle with a non-zero area formed from three of the values in nums. If no valid triangle exists, return 0. A valid triangle must satisfy: sum of any two sides > third side.

examples.explanation: Triangle with sides 1, 2, 2 has perimeter 5 and satisfies 1+2>2.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all triples (i, j, k) and check if they form a valid triangle, tracking the maximum perimeter.

optimal.explanation: Sort descending; check consecutive triples — the first valid triple (nums[i]+nums[i+1]>nums[i-1] when sorted descending) gives the largest perimeter.

problems.title: Wiggle Subsequence
problems.description: A wiggle sequence alternates between rising and falling. Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest wiggle subsequence. A subsequence is obtained by deleting some elements without changing the order of the remaining. Constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: The entire sequence is a wiggle sequence: 1<7>4<9>2<5.

bruteForce.explanation: Use DP where dp[i][0] is the longest wiggle subsequence ending at i going up, dp[i][1] going down.

optimal.explanation: Greedily count peaks and valleys; each directional change increments the length without needing to track subsequence explicitly.

problems.title: Patching Array
problems.description: Given a sorted integer array nums and an integer n, add the minimum number of patches (positive integers) to nums so that any number in range [1, n] can be represented as a sum of some elements. Return the minimum number of patches needed.

examples.explanation: Add 2 to cover [1,6]: sums possible are 1,2,3,4,5,6.

bruteForce.explanation: Use BFS/backtracking to find the minimum patches needed to cover all sums from 1 to n.

optimal.explanation: Track the furthest reachable sum 'miss'; if nums[i] <= miss, extend coverage; otherwise patch with 'miss' itself, doubling coverage.

problems.title: Maximum Units on a Truck
problems.description: You are given boxTypes where boxTypes[i] = [numberOfBoxes, numberOfUnitsPerBox] and truckSize (max boxes). Maximize total units on the truck. You can choose any boxes but cannot exceed truckSize. Constraints: 1 <= boxTypes.length <= 1000.

examples.explanation: Take 1 box of 3 units and 2 boxes of 2 units and 1 box of 1 unit: 3+4+1=8.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all combinations of box selections up to truckSize and return the maximum units.

optimal.explanation: Sort box types by units per box in descending order, then greedily take as many boxes of highest-value type as possible.

problems.title: Non-decreasing Array
problems.description: Given an array nums with n integers, check if the array could become non-decreasing by modifying at most one element. An array is non-decreasing if nums[i] <= nums[i+1] for all valid i. Constraints: n == nums.length, 1 <= n <= 10^4.

examples.explanation: Change 4 to 2 (or 1) and array becomes [2,2,3] which is non-decreasing.

bruteForce.explanation: Try modifying each element to make the array non-decreasing and check if any single modification works.

optimal.explanation: Track violations; when nums[i] > nums[i+1], greedily decide whether to lower nums[i] or raise nums[i+1] based on context, allowing at most one fix.

problems.title: Monotone Increasing Digits
problems.description: Given an integer n, return the largest number that is less than or equal to n with monotone increasing digits (each digit is <= the next digit). Constraints: 0 <= n <= 10^9.

examples.explanation: 299 <= 332 and its digits 2 <= 9 <= 9 are monotone increasing.

bruteForce.explanation: Count down from n and check each number for monotone increasing digits property.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n * d) where d is number of digits

optimal.explanation: Scan digits left to right; when a digit decreases, decrement the previous digit and set all following digits to '9'.

problems.title: Minimum Platforms
problems.description: Given arrival and departure times of trains, find the minimum number of platforms required at the railway station so no train waits. Both arrays are the same length n. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^4, times are in HHMM format.

examples.explanation: At time 950, trains arriving at 900, 940, and 950 are all present (departures after 950), requiring 3 platforms.

bruteForce.explanation: For each train, count how many other trains overlap with it and track the maximum simultaneous count.

optimal.explanation: Sort arrival and departure arrays separately; use two pointers to simulate train events and track peak simultaneous trains.

problems.title: Fractional Knapsack Problem
problems.description: Given weights and values of n items and a knapsack capacity W, find the maximum total value you can put in the knapsack. Unlike 0/1 knapsack, you can take fractions of items. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, 1 <= W <= 10^6.

examples.explanation: Take all of item 0 (60) and item 1 (100) and 2/3 of item 2 (80). Total = 240.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all possible fractions of each item in discretized steps and track the maximum value within capacity.

optimal.explanation: Sort items by value-to-weight ratio descending, then greedily take as much of each item as possible until the knapsack is full.

problems.title: Activity Selection Problem
problems.description: Given n activities with start and end times, select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities that can be performed by a single person. Two activities overlap if one starts before the other finishes. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5.

examples.explanation: Select activities (1,2), (3,4), (5,7), (8,9) for 4 non-overlapping activities.

bruteForce.explanation: Try all subsets of activities and check if each subset is non-overlapping, returning the largest valid subset size.

optimal.explanation: Sort activities by finish time; greedily select each activity that starts at or after the last selected activity's finish time.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Keypresses
problems.description: You have a phone keypad with 9 buttons (1-9), each mapped to some letters. Type a string s using minimum keypresses. Each button can be mapped to at most one letter per press position. Return the minimum total keypresses. Constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^5, s has only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Assign 9 most frequent letters to first positions (1 press each), next 9 to second (2 presses), remaining to third (3 presses).

bruteForce.explanation: Count character frequencies, try all assignments of characters to keys and press positions, and find the minimum total keypresses.

optimal.explanation: Count frequencies, sort descending, then assign the top 9 to 1 press, next 9 to 2 presses, and so on (greedily minimize cost per character).

problems.title: Implement Trie Prefix Tree
problems.description: Implement a trie (prefix tree) with insert, search, and startsWith methods. The trie should support inserting a word, searching for a word, and checking if any word starts with a given prefix. All inputs consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.input: insert("apple"), search("apple"), search("app"), startsWith("app"), insert("app"), search("app")
examples.explanation: After inserting 'apple', searching 'apple' returns true, 'app' returns false (not inserted yet), startsWith('app') returns true, after inserting 'app', searching 'app' returns true.

bruteForce.explanation: Store all inserted words in a set/list, then search by checking exact match or prefix match by iterating through all stored words.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n*m) per operation where n is number of words and m is word length

optimal.explanation: Use a trie data structure with TrieNode containing 26 children pointers and an isEnd flag, enabling O(m) insert and search where m is the word length.
optimal.timeComplexity: O(m) per operation where m is the word length
optimal.spaceComplexity: O(n*m) where n is number of words

problems.title: Add and Search Word
